      (2026-09-04).**
      Step 2 of `docs/project_libraries_design.md`. Measured on the user's real
      project: `specs/packages/` empty and `specs/project_spec.json` absent, so
      `Project.load` raised and a 14-key package library did not survive the
      session that built it. Cause: `save()` called `validate()` and raised on
      ANY issue, so one simulation embedding a numpy array refused the whole
      project -- reproduced, **0 package files written** for a project whose every
      package would have persisted on its own (`_save_package` already falls back
      to pickling).
      - **Two kinds of failure, handled differently on purpose.** An embedded
        array is nothing the caller can fix at save time, so that simulation is
        skipped and logged at WARNING. A **dangling `mf.ref`** (or a
        `derived_from` naming an unregistered simulation) is a mistake with a
        fix, so it still RAISES -- but *after* the write, so the error costs a
        message rather than the whole library.
        `test_project_save_rejects_unresolved_references` passes unchanged, which
        is the evidence the contract was kept rather than weakened.
      - **A skipped simulation is left OUT of the project document's listing**,
        not listed and absent. `Project.load` raises `FileNotFoundError` for a
        listed entry whose file is missing (pinned by
        `test_project_load_fails_loud_on_missing_file`), and that fail-loud
        contract is worth keeping.
      - **BREAKING: `save()` returns `SaveReport`, not `Path`.** It is
        `os.fspath`-able, so `Path(report)` / `open(report)` work, but it is not
        `==` a `Path` -- `__fspath__` does not participate in equality, so
        `test_project_spec.py`'s `saved_path == project.layout.project_spec_path`
        was rewritten rather than papered over with a custom `__eq__`.
      - **Counts are per-kind, not a single `written` total.** An earlier draft
        had `written` mixing simulations and packages, which made the number
        unreadable; it is now `simulations`/`packages`/`grids`/`pickled`.
        `pickled` is the one worth watching -- a pickled entry is a cache, not an
        archive.
      - **`strict=True` is the old behaviour** (raise before writing anything),
        kept for anyone who wants a project to be all-or-nothing.
      - **NOT fixed here:** the array-bearing simulation still cannot be
        persisted at all. Making `ModelContext`-borne grids/domains serializable
        was considered and refused for this pass -- it would flood
        `Project.validate()` for every real GIS model and silently break
        `SimulationSpec.to_yaml`, which goes through the same `to_dict`.

181. **The run manifest stores the rebuildable recipe, not just a readable
      summary (2026-09-04).**
      Step 1 of `docs/project_libraries_design.md`, revised after the user said
      "I don't care if you break old runs/projects ... as long as you don't do
      anything to my saved modflow files." That permission is what made this the
      right shape rather than the carry-forward workaround shipped in `265b897`.
      - **What was wrong:** `_spec_summary` records package *names*, so a
        reopened run had `spec is None` and could be read but never re-run or
        varied without its original build script. `265b897` stopped `to_dict`
        from erasing that summary; this stores what actually rebuilds.
      - **Measured cost: 348 bytes -> 3,277 bytes** on a Ten Trails-shaped
        simulation. Cheap because the packages are `mf.ref(...)` into the library
        and the arrays live there, pickled by `_save_package`. A simulation that
        embeds arrays inline gets no recipe -- `to_dict()` raises -- and stays
        summary-only, which is the pre-change status quo, not a regression.
      - **Both blocks are kept.** `spec` stays the readable summary (it carries
        model types, `package_metadata`, `context_metadata` and hook names that
        `to_dict` does not); `spec_recipe` is the recipe. Neither is ever
        overwritten with null by a run that did not author it.
      - **`Project.reopen_run` attaches the build context**, so a revived spec
        resolves its `mf.ref` packages against the library. `mf.load_run` and
        `Run.reopen` deliberately do NOT -- there is no library in scope, and
        silently resolving against some other project would be worse than
        leaving the refs unresolved. (2026-09-11: package refs now resolve from
        the run's OWN copy first, in every route -- still never from a library
        that is not the run's. Ledger 230.)
      - **An unrevivable recipe degrades rather than failing to open.** A builder
        whose module moved is caught by name (`ValueError`/`TypeError`/`KeyError`/
        `AttributeError`/`ImportError`), logged at WARNING, and the run opens
        summary-only. A run you cannot open is worse than one you cannot rebuild.
      - **Test contract changed:** `test_reopened_run_without_spec_cannot_be_rebuilt`
        became `test_a_run_whose_manifest_has_no_recipe_cannot_be_rebuilt` -- the
        limitation it pinned is the thing being removed, and it now pins the
        legacy/array fallback instead.
      - **Fixed in passing:** `docs/core_specs.md` claimed "Python builder
        callables are intentionally not serialized" (false since §5.6A) and used
        `Project.reopen(...)`, which has never existed.

182. **The three project spec libraries became `dict` subclasses (2026-09-04).**
      Step 3 of `docs/project_libraries_design.md`, and the original report:
      "`Project` doesn't seem to have a way to discover and inspect saved
      packages. At least nothing exposed and discoverable to Pycharm."
      `src/myflopy/library.py` (import layer 2) holds one `SpecLibrary` base and
      three subclasses that override exactly `_row` and declare `_kind`/`_columns`
      -- four hand-written near-identical classes is the cost §4.7.6 measured.
      - **`Project.package(key)` restores what the fold dropped.** git `10d7a87`
        (2026-06-17) folded `ProjectSpec` into `Project`, kept `simulation(name)`
        and dropped `package_spec(key)`. This was a regression, not a missing
        feature, and nothing caught it because `tests/api_snapshot.json` does not
        cover `Project` at all (it iterates `package_api.__all__`).
      - **`_project_name` is a CLASS-level default, never a constructor
        argument.** Measured: `dict.copy()` and `dict.__or__` return a plain
        `dict`, so a library holding required instance state would silently
        degrade to a bare dict -- losing every verb -- through either.
        `copy`/`__or__`/`__ror__` are overridden to preserve the type.
      - **`persists` is NOT a summary column.** It was, in the first draft.
        Deciding it means attempting `to_dict()`, measured at **119 ms** for one
        100,000-record list BC (an array-bearing package short-circuits at 0 ms,
        so the cost lands exactly on the packages that do not). Jupyter calls
        `_repr_html_` on every bare `project`, and the user's USG-derived list
        EVT is ~650,000 records. It is `packages.persistence()` instead.
      - **`repr(project)` touches no disk and does not count runs.** PyCharm
        calls `__repr__` on every debugger step and `Run.reopen` does an
        unguarded `json.loads(...)["run"]`, so counting runs would let one
        truncated manifest make `repr` raise. Pinned by a test that monkeypatches
        `Path.glob`/`rglob`/`iterdir` to raise.
      - **Keys are deliberately NOT attribute-completable.** They contain `/`
        (`npf/base`), so they are not identifiers; a `__getattr__` tier would
        reach only the minority without one, which is worse than a clean absence.
        Answered at runtime by `names()`, `summary()`, the repr, and a
        did-you-mean `KeyError` raised from `__missing__` -- chosen over a new
        `require()`/`fetch()` verb so the message lands on the spelling people
        already type, and so `.get(key, default)` keeps `dict.get`'s meaning.
      - **Fixed in passing, and it moved the API snapshot:** `_builder_label` did
        not unwrap `functools.partial`, so all seven list BCs plus lak/sfr/uzf/mvr
        labelled themselves `'partial'` in every repr, summary and snapshot
        entry -- 11 lines of `tests/api_snapshot.json` now name the FloPy class.

183. **Two library keys that name one file are refused before the write
      (2026-09-04).**
      Found while answering "are the keys with `/` an issue?" -- they are not,
      but the characters `_slug` REWRITES are. `_slug` maps every unsafe
      character to `_`, so `"npf/high k"` and `"npf/high_k"` are distinct keys
      naming one file. Measured before the fix:
      `in memory {'npf/high k': 111.0, 'npf/high_k': 999.0}` ->
      `after load {'npf/high k': 999.0, 'npf/high_k': 999.0}` -- the second write
      won and the reload handed the survivor's spec back under BOTH keys, with no
      warning.
      - **Checked BEFORE the write, unlike the dangling-ref case in 193.** A
        dangling reference can be written harmlessly and reported afterwards; a
        collision cannot -- by the time it is observable, a spec is gone.
        Refusing costs a rename; writing costs a package.
      - **Grids collide more readily than packages.** `grid_spec_path` slugs the
        whole key FLAT, so `"base/coarse"` and `"base_coarse"` collide;
        `package_spec_path` splits on `/` into nested directories, so the same
        pair is fine there. Both are checked; the test pins the asymmetry.
      - **The `/` itself is fine and stays.** It nests packages on disk
        (`specs/packages/npf/base.json`) and costs nothing in completion:
        measured, IPython completes `project.packages['npf` -> `npf/base`,
        `npf/high_k`, because its completer inspects the live dict. PyCharm
        completes neither slashed nor underscored runtime keys, so renaming would
        buy nothing anywhere.

184. **`status` is myflopy's verb, `outcome` is MF6's verdict (2026-09-04).**
      The other half of step 1 in `docs/project_libraries_design.md`. Measured on
      the real project: four runs, every one `status="written", success=None`,
      while three had reached `Normal termination` and one had not. The manifest
      could not tell a success from a failure.
      - **Two axes, never collapsed.** `status` truthfully reports what the
        LIBRARY did; it read as a lie only because nothing reported what MF6 did.
        New leaf module `src/myflopy/run_record.py` (import layer 0, stdlib only,
        so `workspace` gains no deferred import) reads `mfsim.lst`.
      - **`succeeded` is `None`, not `False`, for an unfinished run.** A killed or
        crashed run's listing simply stops mid-iteration -- that is what
        `from_usg` looks like -- and calling it a failure would be the same class
        of lie the entry exists to fix. `reconcile()` leaves such a run alone.
      - **NOT cached into the manifest, deliberately.** The listing is the
        authority and sits in the same directory; a stored verdict would be a
        second source of truth that can disagree with its own source, and would
        need carrying forward through `to_dict` like the spec blocks in 179/181.
        Reading is cheap: only the last 8 KB is read, since a long transient run
        writes one block per time step and the verdict is in the last few lines.
        Pinned by a test over a 5 MB listing.
      - **`stale` compares against MF6 INPUTS only.** Results are legitimately
        newer than the listing that announced them, so counting them would mark
        every completed run stale. Real finding: the user's `baseline` listing is
        older than its own `.rch` -- a real verdict describing superseded inputs.
      - **Never raises.** An unreadable or non-UTF-8 listing is classified
        `incomplete`; a run you cannot classify must still be listable beside the
        ones you can.

185. **`project.runs` -- the run ledger, deferred out of step 3 and built once the
      outcome reader existed (2026-09-04).**
      Held back from ledger 182 on purpose: its only worthwhile columns
      (`outcome`, `stale`, `elapsed`) come from `run_record.read_listing_outcome`,
      which landed in 184. A runs table whose one column was the `status` field
      already reading `written` for every run would have been a surface without
      an answer.
      - **Manifest-less workspaces are INCLUDED**, listed as `discovered`.
        Measured under `examples/`: 39 MF6 workspaces against 14 `run.json`
        files, and most notebooks call `sim.run_simulation` directly. On the
        user's real project it immediately surfaced `mounding_lower_L3_K`, a
        completed run with no manifest at all.
      - **Keying does not depend on having a manifest.** A workspace under
        `runs/` is keyed by directory name either way; one elsewhere in the
        project keeps its relative path, so `runs/from_usg` and
        `scratch/from_usg` cannot collide. The first draft keyed the two loops
        against different bases and produced `runs/mounding_lower_L3_K` beside a
        bare `baseline` -- caught on the real project.
      - **An unreadable manifest is a ROW (`status="unreadable"`), never an
        exception.** `_write_json` is a non-atomic `write_text` called several
        times per run, so a truncated file is a real state; one of them must not
        hide every other run. Caught by name (`OSError`, `ValueError`, `KeyError`
        -- `JSONDecodeError` subclasses `ValueError`), so the broad-catch
        allowlist does not grow.
      - **Cached, with `Project.refresh_runs()`.** `project.runs["x"]` must
        return the same object twice, or `run.metadata[...] = ...` silently
        vanishes. A property that rescanned per access would look convenient and
        be a trap.
      - **`outcome` is still not cached into the manifest** (see 184), so every
        `summary()` re-reads the listing tails. Measured cheap -- only the last
        8 KB of each -- and correct by construction, which is the trade taken.
      - **NOT added: `RunLibrary.open(key)`.** It would be a second spelling of
        `Project.reopen_run(name)`, which additionally attaches the build context.
        `project.runs` is the browse surface, not a second way to open a run.

186. **Forking and editing packages: built, never patched (2026-09-05).**
      Step 4 of `docs/project_libraries_design.md` -- the feature originally
      asked for ("see what package specs have been defined, and then fork them to
      new packages with edits").
      - **The obvious implementation is silently wrong, and was in the first
        draft of the design.** `PackageSpec` is `frozen=True, slots=True` and
        validates in `__post_init__` -> `_check_options`, but `copy.deepcopy`
        reconstructs a slots dataclass through `__reduce_ex__`, so
        `__post_init__` NEVER RUNS. Deep-copying the spec and writing into
        `copy.options` therefore accepts a typo silently -- measured,
        `cp.options["kk_typo"] = 1.0` sails through and surfaces at MF6 build.
        `fork_package` copies the option VALUES and hands them to
        `dataclasses.replace`, which is the ordinary construction path.
      - **`deep=True` is the default because the hazard is in the options nobody
        edited.** `with_options` rebuilds the options dict but not its values, so
        a fork could write through into the parent's numpy arrays. Measured 15.2
        ms / 0.50 MB on a Ten Trails-scale simulation -- cheap enough that
        sharing is the opt-in, not the default.
      - **`metadata` is excluded from `package_digest`.** It carries provenance
        (`forked_from`, `edited`), which says where a spec came from rather than
        what it builds; including it would make stamping a note look like a
        change to the model.
      - **A flat `swap=` reaches EVERY model carrying the label.** The
        alternative -- refusing an ambiguous match -- makes a coupled GWF/GWT
        simulation unswappable, since `ic`/`oc`/`dis` sit on both models. The
        model-qualified form (`{"tport": {"ic": ...}}`) is how you mean one, and
        a mapping value is what distinguishes the two forms.
      - **A swap matching nothing RAISES**, resolved against the SOURCE spec so
        the message names the simulation the caller asked about rather than the
        derived name they have not seen. A typo that silently swapped nothing
        would return a "variant" identical to its parent.
      - **A rename carries into `pname`/`filename`, and REFUSES anything else.**
        Caught by adversarial verification after the first commit: a package name
        is not just `PackageSpec.name`, since `advanced._named_options` bakes it
        into `options` as `pname=name` and `filename="{model_name}.{name}"`. A
        fork that renamed only the field left those stale, and MF6 kept ONE
        package of two under a FloPy "Replacing existing package" warning --
        measured, two CHD specs on one model wrote a single `flow.chd` holding
        only the second. Only those two are rewritten, and only when they still
        hold what the helper wrote; a `*_filerecord` still naming the old package
        raises, because uzf/lak/sfr write `{model_name}_{name}_<suffix>` while
        mvr writes `{model_name}.{name}.bud` and `PackageSpec` has no
        package-type field to dispatch on.
      - **That refusal is keyed on CALLER RESPONSIBILITY, not containment.** A
        containment test cannot decide it: the corrected
        `{model_name}_sfr_north_budget.sfr` still contains `"sfr"` twice, once
        because the new name embeds the old and once because `.sfr` is the file
        suffix. So the question asked is whether the caller supplied that key in
        this call -- which is answerable exactly. Overrides therefore merge
        BEFORE the rename check, or a caller would be refused for a value they
        had just replaced.
      - **NOT carried, and out of reach from one spec:** a sibling's `requires=`
        tuple, MVR's `options["packages"]` and its `perioddata` source/destination
        strings, and `MoverConnection.package`. Renaming a package another one
        names is the caller's to fix.
      - **`fork` refuses an existing key without `overwrite=True`; `edit` never
        refuses.** Replacing a package other simulations reference is the
        accident `fork` exists to avoid; revising `npf/base` deliberately is the
        normal case, and the consequence is made visible by drift tracking rather
        than prevented.

187. **Drift: which library packages a run used have changed since (2026-09-05).**
      The other half of step 4 (design §6a). `edit` is never refused, so the
      contract is that its consequence stops being silent -- this is that.
      Measured on the current code before it: two models differing **50x in K**
      produced byte-identical manifests, and `ModelGroup(...).diff().report()`
      called them "identical to reference".
      - **Digests are computed at `prepare_run`, not in `_spec_summary`.** The
        design put them there; that is impossible, because `_spec_summary` sees
        `_package_entry_label` only, and a `PackageRef` is stored UNRESOLVED --
        digesting it needs the project library, which the module function has no
        access to. `Project._package_digests` resolves refs and the block rides
        the manifest beside `spec`/`spec_recipe`, carried forward by `to_dict`
        under the same rule as those (ledger 179/181).
      - **Only `mf.ref` entries are fingerprinted.** An inline package is baked
        into the run's own recipe and cannot drift; recording it would report
        every inline `dis` as `removed`, since its label is not a library key.
      - **`metadata` is excluded from the digest** (see 186), so stamping a note
        does not read as a change to the model.
      - **A run with no digest block reports `unknown`, never `unchanged`.** A
        missing fingerprint is not evidence of sameness -- the same class of lie
        as `status="written"` reading as success, which is what ledger 184 fixed.
      - **`drift` reports; it never rewrites.** Pinned by a test that asserts the
        manifest is byte-identical after an edit and a drift call.
      - **`RunLibrary._packages` is a class-level default**, like
        `_project_name`: `dict.copy()`/`dict.__or__` drop instance state, so a
        detached library raises naming the cause rather than silently reporting
        everything unchanged.
      - **NOT built: drift on grids or simulations.** A grid is referenced by key
        the same way and could drift identically, but `GridSpec` has no
        copy-on-write verbs, so nothing can edit one in place yet -- the verb
        would have no way to be exercised. Revisit if `GridLibrary` ever gains
        `edit`.

188. **What adversarial verification found in 186/187, and what it cost
      (2026-09-05).** A 35-agent pass over the two step-4 commits returned 27
      confirmed defects, four of them making previously-working code fail or
      silently produce a wrong model. Recorded because the pattern repeats: every
      one came from a *reasonable-looking* shortcut.
      - **`swap=` replaced the WRONG package.** `_package_slot` is only the key's
        FIRST SEGMENT for a ref, so `wel/north` and `wel/south` both answered to
        `wel` and `with_package` replaced whichever came first. Measured: asking
        to swap `wel/south` DELETED `wel/north`, left `wel/south` pumping, and
        MF6 reported normal termination on the wrong model. It fired on exactly
        the `<type>/<variant>` keying this project teaches. Fixed by
        `_package_entry_index`, which matches the FULL LABEL first and falls back
        to the slot hint -- so `model.package("npf")` still finds whatever
        occupies the slot.
      - **`prepare_run` began RAISING on packages that ran fine one commit
        earlier.** `package_digest` called `_callable_ref` (which refuses a
        closure) and `pickle.dumps` (which refuses a file handle), so a
        bookkeeping column gated the primary build verb while `validate()`
        reported clean. `package_digest` now returns `None` instead, and drift
        reports `unfingerprinted` -- guessing `unchanged` would be the same lie
        as `status="written"` reading as success.
      - **The digest was ORDER-SENSITIVE, which made drift useless on its own
        headline workflow.** `Project.save()`/`load()` round-trips options
        through JSON and returns them in a different order, so every reloaded
        package fingerprinted as `edited`. `_canonical` now sorts mapping keys
        recursively, sorts sets (whose pickle varies BETWEEN PROCESSES,
        contradicting the stability the docstring claimed), sorts `requires`, and
        collapses list/tuple -- none of which MF6 can observe.
      - **The model-qualified `swap=` never validated its labels**, so a typo in
        exactly the form the docs recommend for coupled models registered a
        "variant" identical to its parent. Both forms validate now, mixing them
        over one entry raises rather than letting dict order decide, a
        simulation-level label says so instead of denying it exists, and a
        non-string value is named.
      - **The drift column was O(runs x packages) with no memo** -- measured 1 ms
        to ~3 s, re-hashing the same arrays once per run. `summary()` now
        fingerprints the library ONCE per call and discards the memo, so an edit
        is picked up next call without needing invalidation. 40 runs x 7
        packages: 13 ms.
      - **A detached `RunLibrary` printed "—" in the drift column** -- a clean
        bill of health for a library it could not see -- while `drift()` refused.
        It reports `unbound`, and `SpecLibrary.copy`/`__or__` now carry the whole
        instance `__dict__` so a copy keeps its binding at all.
      - **Still open, noted not fixed:** two distinct lambdas fingerprint alike
        (no shipped builder collides); `deep=True` does not unalias object-dtype
        cells inside a DataFrame option (no `mf.*` helper produces one); grid
        drift is untracked and 187's stated reason for deferring it was wrong --
        the real reason is that `GridLibrary` has no `edit`, not that nothing
        can change a grid. The "15.2 ms / 0.50 MB" fork cost quoted in 186 is a
        SMALL-model figure; a real Ten Trails package is 60-350x that.

189. **Package digests are cached, and the fork/digest cost figures were wrong
      (2026-09-06).** Found while auditing for loose ends, by measuring the
      claims rather than repeating them.
      - **The "15.2 ms / 0.50 MB" fork cost quoted in 186 is a small-model
        figure and misleads about the SHAPE of the cost.** It scales with the
        number of PYTHON OBJECTS copied, not with cell count. Measured: a
        9,405-cell `npf` forks in **0.1 ms** and a 72x9,405 recharge ARRAY in
        **1.7 ms** (arrays copy at memcpy speed), while the USG-derived
        72-period, 9,090-record list EVT takes **808 ms** for its 654,480
        records -- 53x the quoted number, on a package this project actually
        has. Corrected at all four sites.
      - **`package_digest` has the same shape, and it mattered more.** ~0.04 ms
        for a scalar package, ~5 ms for the 72x9,405 array, **1.3 s** for that
        EVT. `RunLibrary.summary` fingerprints the whole library on every call
        and Jupyter calls it on every bare `project.runs`, so the browse surface
        stalled on exactly the projects worth browsing. Ledger 188 had fixed the
        O(runs x packages) part but left the per-package cost paid per call.
      - **`PackageLibrary.digests()` caches until the library is mutated.**
        Measured 1051 ms then 0 ms on repeat. The cache is keyed on the LIBRARY,
        not on spec identity, so every mutating route drops it --
        `__setitem__`/`__delitem__`/`pop`/`popitem`/`update`/`setdefault`/`clear`
        are overridden, each pinned by a parametrized test. A stale fingerprint
        would report a changed package as unchanged, which is the one thing
        drift must never do.
      - **Known hole, and the same one `_check_options` has:** mutating a spec's
        `options` dict IN PLACE bypasses the cache, because a frozen dataclass
        does not stop you writing into its mutable field. That is already not a
        supported way to change a package -- it also skips validation -- and
        `edit`/`fork` exist precisely so it is not needed.

190. **Loose ends closed after the project-libraries work (2026-09-06).**
      Three found by auditing what the work PROMISED against what it built.
      - **`tests/api_snapshot.json` now covers the project surface.** It
        collected `package_api.__all__` only, so `Project`, `Run` and the
        libraries were guarded by nothing -- which is precisely how
        `ProjectSpec.package_spec(key)` vanished in the 2026-06-17 fold without a
        single test failing, the regression that started this whole line of work
        (ledger 182). A `members()` collector records every public method and
        property each class DEFINES, under `Project.members`, `Run.members`,
        `SaveReport.members` and one per library. Verified by deleting
        `Project.package` and watching the snapshot test fail.
        **Signatures are deliberately NOT captured** for this tier: these are
        hand-written verbs whose parameters change often, and the value is in
        noticing a verb appearing or vanishing, not in churning the snapshot on
        every keyword added.
      - **`RunRecord` was designed and never built -- correctly.** Every field it
        proposed already lives on `Run` (`status`, `success`, the timestamps,
        `metadata`, and `spec_block`, the verbatim `_spec_summary` payload), so
        the class would have been a second object holding the same state. The two
        genuinely useful parts are properties on `Run` instead:
        `run.package_keys` (model -> library keys, read from `spec_block` so it
        answers for a run whose recipe could not be revived) and
        `run.spec_name`. The design doc's own worked example called
        `run.record.package_keys`, which never existed; corrected there.
      - **The types public methods RETURN are now exported.** `project.save()`
        hands back a `SaveReport` and `run.outcome` a `ListingOutcome`, but
        neither was reachable as `mf.*` -- you got an object whose type you could
        not name without importing from a submodule. Both are exported now, along
        with the library classes that are the TYPES of `project.packages` /
        `.grids` / `.simulations` / `.runs`. Per D12 every one is in the
        `TYPE_CHECKING` block as well as `_EXPORTS`, or it is invisible to
        PyCharm.
      - **Also corrected in the design doc, which was marked BUILT while
        describing things that were not:** the `SaveReport` repr in its worked
        example (shipped as simulations/packages/grids/pickled, not
        written/pickled), the `runs.summary()` columns (shipped with
        stale/drift/elapsed, not a `manifest` column), and `ListingOutcome.stale`
        versus the designed `manifest` field -- staleness of the INPUTS is the
        question that bears on whether a verdict still applies, which the
        manifest's own timestamp does not answer.

191. **D5 recorded at last, and the two ways step 1 made it worse (2026-09-06).**
      `prepare_run(overwrite=True)` reuses a run directory: it resets
      `status`/`success`/`metadata` and leaves the previous run's files -- results,
      listing, and any orphan package file only the old spec wrote. Design §7.3
      deferred this and **no ledger entry was ever written**, contrary to the
      standing rule; a 92-finding sweep flagged that omission four times
      independently. Recorded now, and still deferred: an archive-or-refuse
      policy is a real design decision, and
      `examples/mf6/variant_workflow/01_package_library_and_variants.py` depends
      on today's behaviour.
      - **Step 1 turned it from "loses the record" into "reports the wrong
        result".** `Run.outcome` reads `mfsim.lst` fresh and nothing cleared it,
        so a re-prepared, NEVER-EXECUTED run reported the previous execution's
        verdict: measured `outcome='normal', elapsed='3 Hours, 53 Minutes, 1
        Seconds'` on a model that had not been run. That is precisely the class
        of lie ledger 184 exists to remove, reintroduced one axis over.
        `read_listing_outcome(..., since=)` now reports **`superseded`** when the
        listing predates the run's own preparation, and `succeeded` is `None`
        there so `reconcile()` will not adopt it. On the real project this
        immediately flags `baseline`, whose listing (19:50:17) predates its
        manifest's `created_at` (19:55:11) by five minutes.
      - **A scanned run fabricated its own timestamps.** `Run.created_at` and
        `updated_at` default to construction time, so a manifest-less workspace
        reported the SCAN's wall clock in `runs.summary()`'s `updated` column --
        measured on the real project as two `discovered` rows 55 microseconds
        apart, which is the loop, not the runs. They now read the newest file
        mtime in the workspace. `superseded` is deliberately NOT applied to
        those rows: a scanned run has no known preparation time to be older than.
      - **Docs corrected in the same pass:** the `Project.runs` docstring told
        readers to call `RunLibrary.refresh`, which never existed (it is
        `Project.refresh_runs`), and `model_building_cheatsheet.md` still said
        `save()` "raises rather than writing a project that cannot be reloaded",
        contradicting its own gotcha #9 two paragraphs later since ledger 193.

194. **The documentation tail, and four code bugs hiding in it (2026-09-06).**
      A 92-finding sweep over the whole project-libraries body of work. Most of
      it was prose, but four items filed as documentation were defects.
      - **`|=` left a STALE digest cache.** `dict.__ior__` does not route through
        `__or__` or `update` on a subclass, so it slipped past every other
        invalidation hook added in ledger 189. A stale fingerprint reports a
        changed package as `unchanged` -- the one thing drift must never do.
        `__ior__` is overridden and is now in the parametrized invalidation
        sweep, which is where it should have been caught.
      - **`SaveReport.pickled` never counted grids** although its docstring said
        "packages and grids", so a project whose grid is a built mesh
        under-reported what it had cached. `_save_grid` returns whether it
        pickled, like `_save_package` already did.
      - **`Project._package_digests` bypassed the cache**, re-paying the full
        fingerprint on every `prepare_run` -- 1.3 s per run on a project holding
        the record-list EVT.
      - **`drift()`'s docstring named four states; the code returns five.** It
        omitted `unfingerprinted`, added in 188.
      - **Docs that were simply never told.** `CLAUDE.md` had no entry for this
        surface at all and never linked `docs/project_workflow.md`;
        `codebase_structure.md` was missing both new modules;
        `package_api_reference.md` (the declared "map of the whole API") and
        `myflopy_context.md` (the "accurate, code-derived capability map") carried
        none of it. All four now do.
      - **Docs that were wrong rather than absent.** `manual/04_architecture.md`
        said array-bearing specs "cannot be serialized to disk" -- a library
        package carrying arrays has persisted via pickle since long before this
        work; it is an inline simulation that is skipped.
        `project_workflow.md` listed `GridSpec.structured`/`from_geopackage` as
        usable grid tiers (both fail fast) and its quickstart advertised
        `m.visualize`, deleted in plan 8.6b.
      - **Ledger numbering was broken and is now fixed**: `layer=` duplicated
        177 and is now 192; `Project.save()` duplicated 180 and is now 193. In
        both cases the number stayed with whichever entry outside documents
        already cite, and those citations were updated. Entry 42 appears twice
        deliberately -- the second is the struck-through resolution.
      - **The flagship example now exercises the new verbs.**
        `examples/mf6/variant_workflow/01_package_library_and_variants.py` gains
        a section 5 doing the same work through `packages.fork`/`edit` and
        `simulations.fork(swap=)`, and running `project.runs.drift()` over the
        runs it just executed. Verified end to end with real MF6. It
        deliberately shows BOTH edit outcomes: a note-only edit leaves every run
        `unchanged` (provenance is not content), and a value edit reports
        `edited` and names the run. Writing it caught two errors in my own
        example that only running it would find -- a simulation registers under
        its own name, not one I picked, and `swap` matches the label an entry
        carries, so it needs the ref-based variant rather than the inline base.
      - **`stale` now asks the name files instead of guessing by extension
        (fixed 2026-09-06).** It deny-listed seven output suffixes and treated
        everything else as an input, so `heads.png`, `notes.txt` and MF6's own
        `flow.cbb` each flipped a clean finished run to stale -- measured. The
        input set now comes from `mfsim.nam` and the model name files it points
        at, which is MF6 declaring its own inputs; output paths live INSIDE
        package files and never appear there. A workspace with no `mfsim.nam`
        yields an empty set, which reads as "cannot tell" rather than "nothing
        changed". Verified on the real project: `baseline` still reports stale
        (its declared inputs ARE newer than its listing) and the other five do
        not.
      - ~~PEST calibration trees flood `project.runs`~~ **FIXED 2026-09-06,
        ledger 195** -- excluded and reported via `project.runs.calibrations`.
      - ~~No notebook exercises the new verbs~~ **FIXED 2026-09-06:**
        `examples/mf6/notebooks/project_libraries_tour.ipynb`, following the
        `canonical_fast_tour` / `plotting_vocabulary_tour` pattern. **It is
        EXECUTED by `tests/test_project_libraries_tour.py`, not source-checked
        like the repo's other notebook tests** -- a tour whose whole claim is
        that the surface works end to end is worse than useless if it does not
        run. 0.4 s, a two-cell model in a temp directory, two real MF6 runs.
        All items in 194 are now closed.

195. **PEST calibrations are excluded from the run ledger, and reported
      (2026-09-06).** The last item left open by ledger 194.
      A calibration builds into `<model workspace>.pest/` -- a SIBLING of the run
      directory, so inside `project.root` -- holding the PstFrom template,
      `<name>_ies_master`, `<name>_prior_master` and every pyEMU worker (launched
      with `worker_root=master.parent`, `pest/project.py`). Each is a wholesale
      `shutil.copytree` of the model workspace, so each carries an `mfsim.nam`
      and `RunLibrary`'s `rglob` listed it as a run: one calibration with 8
      workers adds ~11 rows to a ledger whose job is telling you what you ran.
      - **Reported, not silently absent** -- the user's explicit requirement.
        `repr(project.runs)` names the count, `_repr_html_` names each tree under
        the table, and `project.runs.calibrations` is a one-row-per-calibration
        frame pointing at `model.pest_runs`, which returns handles that
        understand phi, ensembles and forecasts. Nothing is lost; it stops being
        conflated.
      - **The markers are DUPLICATED into `run_record.py`, not imported.**
        `myflopy.modflow.mf6.pest.runs` is import layer 0, so importing it would
        not break layering -- but it executes the pest package `__init__`,
        measured at **1.43 s** against an `import myflopy` that costs **0.02 s**.
        A 70x import regression to reach three string constants is not a trade
        worth making. Pinned equal by a test, plus a subprocess test asserting
        `myflopy.modflow.mf6.pest` is NOT in `sys.modules` after `import
        myflopy` -- that guard is the actual regression risk here.
      - **The OUTERMOST marker wins.** The template directory carries
        `myflopy_pest_metadata.json` and sits inside the `.pest` root, so
        returning the first match walking up split one calibration into two rows
        -- the tree, and its own template counted separately. Caught by running
        it.
      - **`discover_native_runs()` is deliberately unchanged.** Its documented
        job is every native MF6 workspace, and a PEST worker genuinely is one. It
        stays the raw sweep; `project.runs` is the curated ledger.

196. **`gdf_topbtm` is read positionally, and a physics keyword moved the column
      (2026-09-10).** Several consumers decode the layer-elevation frame by
      POSITION -- `iloc[:, 1]` is the model top, `iloc[:, 2:]` the bottoms
      (`choros.py:695`, `:1184`) -- and nothing enforced where the geometry
      column sat. `LayerSurfaces.sample` writes `gdf[["geometry"] + labels]`,
      then under `if reconcile:` (**the default**) `reconcile_surfaces` returns a
      plain frame and `gpd.GeoDataFrame(df, geometry=...)` APPENDS geometry at
      the end, undoing the ordering three lines above.
      - **Measured**, three-layer frame: the hover read the first bottom as the
        model top (5.0 against a truth of 10.0) and handed a Polygon back as the
        last bottom, raising nothing. The dry-cell dagger flipped with it.
      - **Column NAMES were the wrong diagnosis**, and the one three docstrings
        adopt (`geopackage.py:97`, `layers.py:679`, `usg/model.py:262` all frame
        the divergence as int-vs-named). Names cause loud `KeyError`s. The silent
        half is geometry's POSITION, which flips on a keyword about physics and
        which no docstring in the repo mentioned. Unifying names would have left
        it fully intact.
      - **Enforced on the GETTER, not the setter, and that is not a preference.**
        Two routes bypass the setter: `__setstate__` does `__dict__.update`, so a
        reloaded grid keeps whatever order it was saved in; and an in-place edit
        (`vor.gdf_topbtm[2] = ...`, which `canonical_model_template.ipynb` cell 6
        performs) mutates the frame the getter returned.
      - **The getter STORES what it normalized and returns that object.**
        Returning a normalized copy hands an in-place edit a temporary: measured,
        a bottom set to 99.0 read back as 5.0. That is a worse bug than the one
        being fixed, and it is what the obvious spelling produces. Pinned by
        `test_an_in_place_edit_survives_the_normalizing_getter`.
      - **Geometry is found by DTYPE, not by the name `"geometry"`** -- a frame
        whose column is `geom` was otherwise swept in as a layer bottom.
      - **`LayerStack.to_disv` now publishes `result.attach_to_grid(vor)`**
        rather than letting the second sampling attach. It was publishing the
        stack's string labels (`['top','sand','clay','geometry']`), which made
        `mf.sfr` and `vor.plot.section` raise `KeyError: 0` on the path
        `model_building_cheatsheet.md` §5 teaches, while `to_disv`'s own
        docstring promised those consumers work.
      - **`_nlay` invalidation** rides along: it cached on first read and nothing
        dropped it, so re-attaching a frame with a different layer count left the
        old count standing.
      - **Setter normalization is redundant with the getter** and kept anyway, so
        anything reading `_gdf_topbtm` directly sees an ordered frame. It is
        pinned against the private storage rather than through the getter because
        mutation testing showed every behavioural test still passed without it.
      - **NOT DONE, deliberately.** (a) `ModelContext.surfaces` is a captured
        reference, not the property, so normalizing the getter does not reach it
        -- and that is where the stale-snapshot divergence lives (`sfr.py:637`
        reads `grid.gdf_topbtm` while `lakes.py:604` and `geopackage.py:181` read
        `context.surfaces`; measured SFR reach top 70.0 against
        `CellSurfaceOffset` 60.0, truth 30.0, no exception). (b) The tolerant
        reader-side accessor decoding all six writer layouts. (c) `DisuGrid`'s
        `['top']`/`['bottom']` lookup, satisfied by no writer since 2024-05-11,
        whose `except ValueError` cannot catch the `KeyError` pandas raises. All
        three belong with the regrid work, where surfaces get resampled anyway.

197. **The declarative spec layer was pinned by nothing (2026-09-10).** Before
      this, `SimulationSpec` appeared in `tests/api_snapshot.json` exactly once --
      as a bare name inside `mf.__all__`. `ModelSpec`, `PackageSpec`,
      `ModelContext` and `GridSpec` appeared not at all. A verb or a field could
      appear or vanish on the layer the whole package-first API is built from and
      no test would notice. This is the same hole ledger 182 recorded for the
      project/run surface, one tier down, and it is why this had to land BEFORE
      any vocabulary work rather than alongside it.
      - **Fields as well as members.** `members()` sees methods and properties;
        it cannot see a dataclass field. `PackageSpec.enabled` is the worked
        example -- it participates in `package_digest`, so removing it would make
        every historical run manifest report `state='edited'`, and the vocabulary
        work has `disabled()` (the METHOD) on its cut list, one careless step
        from the field. `spec_fields()` covers that.
      - **Names only, not signatures, and that is a KNOWN limit.** `members()`
        deliberately captures no parameters (its own docstring says why), so this
        catches a verb appearing or vanishing and NOT a signature widening --
        `SimulationSpec.models` changing from `tuple[ModelSpec, ...]` to a union
        would still pass. Adding `with_packages(..., slot=)` in the vocabulary
        work will therefore show a zero-line diff here. If that matters when the
        time comes, a `spec.signatures` block is the fix; it is not built now
        because the parameters on these verbs are about to change wholesale.
      - Verified by deleting `ModelSpec.without_package` and watching
        `test_api_snapshot.py` fail naming `ModelSpec.members`.

198. **The coupled one-liner in `simulation()`'s own docstring could not run
      (2026-09-10).** `mf.simulation(flow, transport)` -- labelled there as "one
      IMS each (coupled-ready)" -- wrote `COMPLEXITY simple` onto the GWT solver,
      selecting conjugate gradient, and MF6 aborted: *"MODEL TRANS PRODUCES AN
      ASYMMETRIC COEFFICIENT MATRIX, BUT THE CONJUGATE GRADIENT METHOD WAS
      SELECTED. USE BICGSTAB INSTEAD."* Measured preset matrix: SIMPLE fails,
      MODERATE and COMPLEX pass, a bare IMS fails.
      - **Keyed on the MATRIX, not the model kind, and that is the whole point.**
        A rule written against `model_type` fixes the coupled case and leaves
        every unconfined model broken: `mf.gwf(..., newtonoptions="NEWTON")` fails
        identically under SIMPLE, because Newton makes a GWF matrix asymmetric
        too. Both measured, both pass with `linear_acceleration="BICGSTAB"`.
      - **BICGSTAB rather than bumping `complexity`.** MODERATE also passes, but
        complexity is the caller's knob and the requirement MF6 states is the
        acceleration. Only the asymmetric model's solver gets it; a plain GWF
        solver is untouched.
      - **NO TEST COVERED THIS**, which is how it survived: nothing in the suite
        built a spec-declared GWF-GWT and ran it. `test_gwt_gwe_results.py`
        hand-sets complexity AND a BICGSTAB override, so it exercised a
        simulation the helper would never synthesize. The new tests reach MF6.
      - **Solver ORDER rides along.** MF6 requires a GWF solution to be listed in
        `mfsim.nam` before the solution of any model it feeds; nothing enforced
        it, so a hand-written `solver=[transport_ims, flow_ims]` wrote a name file
        MF6 rejects for a reason that reads like a physics problem. Solvers are
        now sorted by MODEL DECLARATION order -- the order the caller already
        expressed. The sort is stable and a solver naming no known model keeps
        its place at the end.
      - **A caller's explicit `solver=` list IS reordered.** Deliberate: the
        order carries exactly one meaning to MF6 and there is no legitimate
        reason to want the GWT solution first.
      - **`complexity=` survives here**, even though it is on the vocabulary
        work's cut list (it is ignored the moment `solver=` is passed). This pass
        is bugs only; removing the parameter is a public-API change and belongs
        with that work.

199. **Three lookups, one question, three answers (2026-09-10).** On a model
      carrying `mf.ref("wel/north")` and `mf.ref("wel/south")`, asking about
      `"wel"` gave: `package("wel")` -> the north one, `with_package(x, slot="wel")`
      -> replaced the north one, `without_package("wel")` -> deleted **both**.
      Nobody chose that. `_package_entry_index` grew its label-first pass after a
      swap deleted the wrong well package and MF6 reported normal termination on
      the wrong model; the fix reached that lookup and neither of the other two.
      - **One resolver.** `_package_entry_indices` returns EVERY match, label pass
        first (exact, at most one, since names are unique within a model) then
        slot hint (a hint, so it can match several). `_package_entry_index` wraps
        it and RAISES on more than one, naming the model and both candidates.
      - **Ambiguity is the caller's to settle, not list order's.** The old
        behaviour was not a policy, it was whichever entry happened to be
        declared first.
      - **`without_package` raises on a name it cannot find.** It used to be a
        silent no-op that still returned a new object, so a typo -- or a package
        already removed -- read exactly like success, and the only way to know
        was to diff `package_names`. Both not-found messages now list what the
        model carries.
      - **`_package_entry_matches` is deleted**, not left beside its replacement.
        It was the second of the three implementations and had no other caller.
      - **Nothing in the suite depended on any of the old behaviour**: 2437
        passed with the silent no-op turned into a raise. That is evidence the
        no-op was never a feature, not evidence the change is small.

200. **A `chd` handed to a simulation was accepted, and died inside FloPy
      (2026-09-10).** A simulation carries timing and solvers; a model package
      given to `mf.simulation(packages=[...])` or `sim.with_package(...)` was
      accepted at declaration and failed much later as FloPy's `Invalid package
      type "chd". Unable to register package.` -- a message naming the type but
      not the mistake, arriving a long way from the line that caused it.
      - **Read from the BUILDER's first constructor parameter**, never the
        package name. Measured across every `flopy.mf6` package class, that
        partitions cleanly: `model` 78, `simulation` 15,
        `parent_model_or_package` 8, `parent_package` 7. A name-prefix heuristic
        is WRONG on 17 -- all six exchange classes (`gwfgwt`, `gwfgwf`, ...) carry
        a model-kind prefix and are simulation-scoped, and eleven `utl*` classes
        read as simulation while being model- or sub-package-scoped (and they
        split BOTH ways: `utllaktab` hangs off a model, `utlats` off a parent
        package).
      - **`functools.partial` must be unwrapped or the check inverts.** The seven
        list BCs all build through `partial(_build_named, ModflowGwfchd)` and
        measure as unknown without it -- so the check would wave through every
        BC it exists to catch while still catching `npf`. Mutation-tested.
      - **Abstain rather than guess.** Only a decidable `"model"` is refused;
        `parent_model_or_package` (MVR/GNC, genuinely either), a `PackageRef`
        (no builder until it resolves), and any plain callable all pass.
      - **The change's only casualty was the bug it was built to find.**
        `tests/test_workspace.py` declared an `oc` at the simulation tier and
        passed because it only writes a manifest and never builds -- and its
        assertion accepted the package in EITHER tier, which is what hid it. It
        now edits the model, using `sto` rather than `oc`: the model already
        carries an `oc`, and the manifest summary records package NAMES, so
        replacing one changes nothing to assert against.

201. **The project accepted specs into the wrong library, and went quiet when it
      lost work (2026-09-10).** Two failures with one shape: every signal said
      success, and the loss appeared in a later session.
      - **`project.add_package("flow_hi", mf.gwf(...))` was accepted.**
        `validate()` returned clean, `save()` reported success while silently
        writing no simulations, and the next session's `Project.load` raised
        `KeyError: 'builder'` -- the whole project unopenable from one wrong
        verb. `_refuse_wrong_library` refuses a spec that belongs to a different
        library, naming the verb that was wanted.
      - **Only a spec that clearly belongs elsewhere is refused.** `add_grid`
        legitimately takes a `GridSpec`, a `GridRef`, or an already-built mesh,
        and a built mesh is none of the four spec types, so it passes untouched.
      - **`add_simulation` now warns when the simulation will not persist.**
        Previously this was discoverable only as `SaveReport(simulations=0,
        skipped=1)` -- truthy, raising nothing -- and that is what left a real
        project's `specs/` directory empty. Said at the line that registered it,
        naming `mf.ref(key)` as the fix.
      - **`Run._spec_recipe_block` was announcing at DEBUG** that a run had
        stopped being re-runnable: the manifest keeps a readable summary,
        `reopen_run(...).spec` comes back `None`, and nothing said so. Now
        WARNING, and de-duplicated per run via `Run._warned_unserializable`
        because `_record_status` re-summarizes on every status change and would
        otherwise repeat it three or four times.
      - **Both warnings are `logger.warning`, not prints** -- a degraded input is
        exactly what the logging rule reserves that level for, and
        `test_no_library_prints.py` stays green.
      - **NOT done:** `add_package` still silently REPLACES an existing key. The
        `overwrite=False` guard belongs with the vocabulary work, where
        `packages.fork`'s refusal and this verb should end up consistent; adding
        it here would break every re-registration in the examples mid-stream.

202. **`mf.simulation` grew three ways to say one thing (2026-09-10).** `tdis=`,
      `solver=` and `packages=` were three channels into ONE
      `SimulationSpec.packages` tuple, and `complexity=` was a fourth that only
      reached the synthesized solver -- silently ignored the moment `solver=` was
      passed. `solver=` also had two shapes (a spec, or a list of them). All
      collapsed into `packages=[...]`, matching `mf.gwf(packages=[...])`.
      - **`models=` is now OPTIONAL on `mf.ims`/`mf.ems`.** A solver declaring
        none claims every model the others left, which is what lets a one-model
        simulation write `packages=[mf.ims(complexity="COMPLEX")]` and name
        nothing. Added because the migration would otherwise have been a
        REGRESSION for exactly the case `complexity=` existed to serve -- the
        real notebook it was written for goes from one keyword to naming its own
        model. `build_ims`/`build_ems` raise if such a spec reaches a build
        without a simulation having filled it in.
      - **The key is absent, not `None`.** `_claim_models` and `_ordered_solvers`
        both test truthiness of `options.get("models")`, so an unfilled solver
        carries no `models` key at all rather than a null one.
      - **PRT is never folded into an open IMS.** MF6 rejects an explicit model
        under IMS6, so a PRT model gets its own EMS even when an unnamed IMS is
        present and would otherwise have claimed it.
      - **Two refusals that used to be silent corruption.** Two TDIS packages
        used to survive into the spec, with FloPy warning "tdis package already
        exists. Replacing" and whichever built last winning; two unnamed solvers
        had no defined meaning at all. Both raise.
      - **A `mf.ref` in `packages=` does NOT suppress a default.** An unresolved
        reference carries no builder, so a ref standing for a TDIS cannot be told
        from one standing for anything else -- guessing would either drop the
        caller's timing or write two. Documented on the parameter.
      - **Blast radius was 3 test call sites and 1 notebook cell**, far smaller
        than the surface suggested: 44 `mf.simulation(` calls repo-wide, only 4
        of which used any of the removed keywords.
      - **`examples/mf6/notebooks/bearcreek_uncertainty.ipynb` is GITIGNORED** --
        a live working notebook, not repo content. Its cell was edited surgically
        so it keeps running; that edit is in the working tree and in no commit.

203. **The one name a coupled model needs, offered by no IDE (2026-09-10).** The
      four `build_*_exchange` functions resolve on `mf` but appear in NEITHER
      `mf.__all__` NOR `dir(mf)` -- they are second-tier exports -- so
      autocomplete never offered them. Worse, the spelling four docstrings taught,
      `mf.build_gwf_gwt_exchange("flow", "transport")`, raises `ValueError`: the
      real builder takes `(simulation, models, **options)` and must be wrapped in
      an `ExchangeSpec`. Four sites, all fixed.
      - **`mf.exchange(a, b)` infers from the KINDS**, which is safe precisely
        because three of the four exchanges carry no information beyond the model
        pair (`ModflowGwfgwt`/`gwe`/`prt` take only filename/pname).
      - **GWF-GWF is the exception and is treated as one.** It takes 18 options,
        and MF6 rejects a file written without `nexg`/`exchangedata` -- *Required
        block "DIMENSIONS" not found*. `mf.exchange.gwfgwf` refuses rather than
        writing that file.
      - **The GWF model is put first regardless of argument order.** MF6 wants
        that order and there is no reason to want the other; making the caller
        get it right buys nothing.
      - **Inference refuses bare NAMES.** Kinds are what select the class, so
        `mf.exchange("flow", "trans")` cannot work -- it raises, naming the
        explicit spellings, which do accept names.
      - **The four `build_*` functions stay second-tier.** They are the engine;
        `mf.exchange` is the front door. Not deleted, because `ExchangeSpec`
        round-trips through `_callable_ref` by importable reference.
      - **Still true and worth repeating**: nothing wires an exchange for you. A
        coupled simulation without one builds, runs, and moves nothing, under
        normal termination.

204. **Four spellings for add-or-replace, two for remove (2026-09-10).**
      `ModelSpec.with_package`, `ModelSpec.with_packages`,
      `SimulationSpec.add_package` and `SimulationSpec.replace_package` all added
      or replaced a package. The last two differed ONLY in the absent-slot case,
      and `add_package` recorded its own lineage entry as `'replace_package'`
      whenever the slot happened to exist. Collapsed to `with_packages` /
      `without_packages`, one or many, varargs or a list, with `on=` choosing the
      tier.
      - **`slot=` carries `replace_package`'s must-exist assertion**, which is
        the one piece of it that mattered. Without the assertion a swap that
        misses silently ADDS, and MF6 accepts two RCH packages on one model and
        sums them -- 0.8000 against an intended 0.4000, under normal termination.
        The NAME was redundant; the check was not.
      - **`without_packages` at the simulation tier is new capability**, not a
        rename: there was no verb for dropping a tdis or a solver at all, short
        of rebuilding the `packages` tuple by hand.
      - **The singular forms are DELETED, not kept as aliases.** English prefers
        `with_package(npf)`, and that is a real cost; the user asked for one verb
        and 54 call sites migrated mechanically. Reverting is cheap if the plural
        grates in practice -- it is one alias each.
      - **The lineage SHAPE changed**: `{"operation": "replace_package", ...,
        "package": "npf/high"}` became `{"operation": "with_packages", ...,
        "packages": ["npf/high"]}`, a list because the verb is now plural.
        Verified first that nothing reads lineage entries programmatically --
        they are written and displayed, never parsed -- so old manifests keep
        their old shape harmlessly.
      - **The automated migration damaged 9 of 54 sites and the tests caught none
        of it directly.** A regex rewriting `replace_package(model, pkg)` to
        `with_packages(pkg, on=model)` matched `[^,]+?\\)` against the FIRST
        closing paren, so a nested call like `mf.ref("npf/high_k")` swallowed the
        keyword: `mf.ref("npf/high_k", on="flow")`. It happened to still parse.
        Found by listing every migrated line rather than by trusting green tests.

205. **Four verbs nobody typed while building a model (2026-09-10).** Removed:
      `PackageSpec.disabled`, `PackageSpec.with_input`, `PackageSpec.with_inputs`,
      `ModelSpec.with_hook`, `ModelContext.with_metadata`. Each capability
      survives through the constructor or `dataclasses.replace`; only the wither
      is gone.
      - **`disabled()` had ZERO callers anywhere** -- src, tests, examples,
        notebooks, docs -- and was the only producer of `enabled=False` in the
        whole repo. So the disable capability was never exercised by anything.
      - **The `enabled` FIELD stays, and must.** It participates in
        `package_digest`, so removing it would make every historical run manifest
        report `state='edited'`. `dataclasses.replace(pkg, enabled=False)` still
        reaches it. Removing the verb is safe; removing the field never is.
      - **`with_workspace` was on the cut list and is KEPT.** The claim it rested
        on -- "`prepare_run` never reads `spec.workspace`" -- is true and
        incomplete: `SimulationSpec.build()` reads it (`specs.py`, the standalone
        path), and three tests exercise exactly that. Checking the second reader
        is what saved it.
      - **`PackageSpec.with_metadata` stays too**, on 7 src callers: it is how
        `fork_package` stamps `forked_from`/`edited`. Only the `ModelContext`
        namesake went, which had none.
      - Migrations: `with_hook(h)` -> `mf.gwf(..., hooks=[h])`; `with_input(k, s)`
        -> `dataclasses.replace(spec, inputs={k: s})`. Two call sites, both tests.

206. **The discretization was the one package with no `mf.` helper (2026-09-10).**
      Every other package in a model comes from `mf.<name>(...)`; DISV came only
      from `result.to_disv()`. That asymmetry -- not the character count -- is
      what the user was pointing at, and the first answer given to them argued
      length and missed the point.
      - **`mf.disv(layers)` DELEGATES to `result.to_disv()`**, it does not
        re-derive. Re-deriving would be a second resolution of the same stack,
        which `LayerStack.to_disv`'s own comment records as 8.5 ft of drift on a
        real model -- and the drift is silent, because `attach_to_grid` publishes
        the result's surfaces while the DISV carries the other resolution's.
      - **`mf.disv(ctx, res)` was the user's spelling and is NOT what shipped.**
        A `LayerBuildResult` carries `res.vor`, so the context is redundant --
        `ctx.grid` IS `res.vor`. One positional, `grid=` only for a stack
        declared without one.
      - **Mixing the two forms raises.** `mf.disv(layers, nlay=99)` describes two
        different meshes; silently preferring either is the class of bug this
        whole pass exists to remove.
      - **NOT DONE: renaming `LayerBuildResult`.** The workflow recommended
        `Layers`; the user asked for the call form, not the rename, and renaming
        a public class in `mf.__all__` on aesthetics alone is not a call to make
        on their behalf mid-pass. Their actual question -- "what is res for?" --
        is answered by the docs, and now by a helper that does not need the
        variable at all.

207. **`run.model().chd.` autocompleted list methods (2026-09-10).** The ten
      package accessors on `SimulationBase` carried no return annotation, and
      PyCharm and Pylance are STATIC -- they read the `def` line and never run
      the module -- so an editor offered `append`, `count`, `sort`.
      - **The annotation is a UNION, and that is honest rather than lazy.**
        FloPy's `get_package` returns a LIST when a model carries more than one
        package of a type: measured, two CHD packages give a two-element list.
        Annotating the single class would be a lie an editor then propagates into
        every call site downstream.
      - `package()`'s docstring now states the list behaviour once, where the
        accessors get it from, rather than repeating it ten times.
      - A test asserts every accessor is annotated AND that each admits the list,
        so one added later without an annotation fails by name.

208. **The guarded verb was the deliberate one (2026-09-10).**
      `project.add_package(key, spec)` replaced an existing entry silently, while
      `packages.fork(source, key)` refused exactly the same collision unless told
      `overwrite=True`. That is backwards: a fork is a deliberate new thing,
      while re-using a registration key is usually an accident -- a second script
      run, a copied line, a notebook cell executed twice. All three registration
      verbs now take `overwrite=False`.
      - **`packages.edit(key, ...)` stays deliberately unguarded.** Changing what
        a key MEANS is the supported operation; `project.runs.drift()` is what
        makes its consequences visible. The refusal message names it, so the verb
        is discoverable from the error.
      - **The deferral reason given in ledger 201 was WRONG.** It said adding
        this would "break every re-registration in the examples mid-stream."
        Measured: zero breakage. 2552 tests pass, and a static scan of every
        example and notebook found one apparent duplicate key that turned out to
        be an ASCII diagram in a module docstring. The cost was assumed, not
        checked.
      - **`Project.load` is unaffected** -- it registers into a fresh project, so
        nothing collides. Pinned by a test, because a future eager-reload path
        would hit this immediately.
      - **The snapshot did not move, and that is ledger 197's limitation biting
        for the first time.** `members()` captures names, not signatures, so
        adding `overwrite=` to three public methods produced a zero-line diff in
        `api_snapshot.json`. The behaviour change is real and the ratchet cannot
        see it. If that matters more than once, the fix is the `spec.signatures`
        block 197 describes.

209. **SFR and LAK read layer elevations from different places (2026-09-10).**
      The one route found to WRONG NUMBERS IN AN MF6 INPUT FILE, left open by
      ledger 196. SFR's `_default_reach_tops` read `grid.gdf_topbtm` directly and
      never looked at `context.surfaces`, although `SFRBuilder` carries the
      context. LAK and `CellSurfaceOffset` read `context.surfaces` first.
      `ModelContext(surfaces=vor.gdf_topbtm)` captures the frame OBJECT, so
      re-running a layer-build cell in a notebook -- which re-publishes
      `vor.gdf_topbtm` -- left two packages in ONE model on different elevations.
      Measured: SFR reach top 70.0 against `CellSurfaceOffset` 60.0, truth 30.0,
      no exception, normal termination.
      - **One resolver, `specs._layer_elevations`,** called by all three. This
        fixes the internal inconsistency, which is the part that wrote wrong
        numbers.
      - **`context.surfaces` still wins when given.** A deliberate pin and a
        stale snapshot are indistinguishable at the call site, so neither is
        overridden. What changed: every builder now agrees on it, and a
        DISAGREEMENT with the grid's live table is logged at WARNING rather than
        written into the model. Compared by value, not identity -- a `.copy()` is
        not a stale snapshot, and warning on identity would cry wolf.
      - **SFR now reads elevation columns by POSITION** among the numeric ones
        (`[top, botm0, botm1, ...]`), not by label. It read `.loc[cell, 0]`, which
        only worked because the grid's table happened to be integer-labelled;
        reading `context.surfaces` would have made a unit-labelled table raise.
      - **A `LayerBuildResult` in `surfaces` is converted**, without publishing it
        onto the grid -- resolving a builder's input must not mutate the grid. It
        is a documented `surfaces` value, and LAK used to die on it with
        `'LayerBuildResult' object has no attribute 'drop'`.
      - **Reach-top derivation from the grid had no test at all** before this;
        `_default_reach_tops` appeared only in `api_snapshot.json`. Six mutants,
        all die, including one that reinstates the original grid read.
      - **NOT done:** the tolerant reader-side accessor decoding all six writer
        layouts (ledger 196). With these three readers sharing one source and
        the positional readers covered by the geometry-first getter, it is no
        longer load-bearing.

210. **A polygon drawn on cell faces was also written to the cells outside it (2026-09-11).**
      `GeoPackageSource._cell_shares` measured each piece of a feature by the
      PIECE's own extent -- area if it had any, else length. A polygon meets each
      face-adjacent cell along the edge they share, a line with no area, so every
      neighbour of a polygon drawn on cell faces was admitted with a pseudo-share
      of edge / area (L / L**2). All seven `.gpkg` list BCs and
      `GeoPackageSource.k_array` inherited it. Measured: a DRN polygon that is
      exactly one cell wrote 5 records and 500 of conductance where 1 and 100 are
      right; on an 8x8 grid a face-aligned polygon wrote 12 records and 1,200, and
      MF6 terminated normally with DRN outflow -6,053.84 against -2,811.84 for
      the same polygon inset by 0.1; a K zone that was one cell painted five.
      - **The FEATURE picks the measure now, never the piece.** An areal
        feature's pieces are measured by area, a line's by length, a point's not
        at all.
      - **`mf.Spread` hid it sometimes, and by units.** The pseudo-share fell
        under `min_share=0.01` at one scale and not at another, so the same
        geometry resolved to different cells in feet and in metres.
        `mode="retained"` renormalized the pseudo-shares: the total was conserved
        and 16% of it sat outside the polygon.
      - **"Refinement triples totals" was this bug, misdiagnosed.** A 4x4 -> 8x8
        refinement did triple a total, but only because the polygon's edges were
        faces on the finer grid. Refining under an unaligned polygon conserves.
      - **JUDGMENT CALL: a piece narrower than 0.01 is dropped too**
        (`geopackage._SLIVER_WIDTH`, in the grid's length unit). Exact
        coincidence has commoner near misses, each leaving a neighbour a sliver
        that carried the WHOLE unsplit value -- the same defect. A perturbation is
        a WIDTH, so the test is a piece's mean width, 2 x area / perimeter.
        Measured, the same on 5 ft and 500 ft cells: 3e-7 after a double-precision
        reprojection (4326, 32610); 3.4e-4 after NAD83 <-> NAD83(HARN) (2285, which
        PROJ closes through WGS 84 without a grid, and which vanishes at the
        origin); 3.5e-3 to 5e-3 for cells read back from a DISV FloPy wrote at 9
        significant digits. A feature itself narrower than the tolerance is kept
        whole, and a 0.015 strip into a neighbour reaches it (both tested). It
        also drops REAL corner clips that thin, deliberately -- the call
        `Spread.min_share` makes: on real overlays of independent meshes, 46
        such nicks, at most 1.5e-3 ft2 and 8.3e-6 of a cell. **Not covered:** coordinates ROUNDED on export (GeoJSON at 7 decimal
        degrees, 0.003 to 0.018, straddling the tolerance), and a datum shift of
        feet, which is geometry, not noise.
      - **Revised the same day, after a second review** (all LOW; none bites the
        real grids here, whose narrowest cell is 0.31 ft wide):
        - the width is measured on a piece's AREAL parts only -- a piece that also
          touches its cell along a face is a GeometryCollection holding that face
          as a line, and counted in the perimeter it made a 1.2 ft square a 0.00998
          "sliver";
        - a sliver must ALSO be under 1% of its cell (`_SLIVER_SHARE`). Noise is
          width / cell width of a cell, under 0.5% on any cell wider than half a
          unit, so real grids are untouched; on 0.05-unit cells the rule dropped
          pieces holding 14-27% of their cell;
        - if EVERY piece of a feature is a sliver, none is dropped -- they are the
          feature. A strip 0.015 wide centred on a face is two 0.0075 halves and
          lost both; a lab-scale grid of 0.01-unit cells lost all its coverage.
        - **Limit, recorded not fixed:** 9-digit DISV rounding is covered only while
          |coordinates| < 1e7 grid units. Texas State Plane northings and Web
          Mercator exceed it (slivers to 0.044); no grid here does.
        - Cost measured on the Ten Trails mesh: `_cell_shares` 1.07-1.17x.
        - Four mutants for the revision, all killed: the width counting a
          collection's lines, no 1% cap, all-sliver features dropped, and mixed
          collections refused again.
      - **The first version of this fix used a share of the cell, and was wrong.**
        Dropping a piece under 1e-6 of min(cell, feature) held on the 500 ft cells
        it was tested on, at the origin. Below ~340 ft cells the NAD83 shift got
        through, and 17,416 of 18,107 one-cell zones on the real Ten Trails mesh
        still leaked. An adversarial review caught it before commit; the test now
        runs 25, 100 and 500 ft cells at State Plane coordinates.
      - **A GeometryCollection mixing dimensions is measured by its highest one.**
        The first version refused it -- measured as a polygon, its line part
        vanished without a message -- and the second review REVERSED that: it is
        what `gpd.clip` and `gpd.overlay` return by default
        (`keep_geom_type=False`) wherever a zone runs along the clip edge, the lines
        being zero-area artifacts of the coincidence, so the refusal refused the
        commonest GIS operation's default output (and misfired on an EMPTY member).
        A deliberate line inside a polygon feature adds no area and reaches
        nothing: write one feature per geometry type.
      - **`edges_only` with a polygon that only BORDERS the grid edge** -- an ocean
        polygon on the coastline -- reached the edge cells through this bug and
        reaches none now: draw it overlapping the edge cells. The same polygon
        through the legacy `Boundaries` engine still reaches them. The next entry
        makes the miss loud.
      - **Real data, old vs new, every feature** -- the Ten Trails mesh (18,107
        cells), the old USG mesh (9,405), the demo site (4,107), the canonical
        grids, and every GIS file in `examples/` and the Ten Trails / USG-export
        data: no cell added, no share changed on a kept cell, no feature emptied.
        Every removal was a zero-area touch or a piece under the width. Polygons
        made from a mesh's own cells now resolve to exactly one cell each; the four
        USG lake polygons to 707 cells, the export's 707 CLN lake nodes (956
        before); the CHD a real run wrote reproduces exactly (120 cells).
        Last-feature-wins K painting changes painter in 5 of 18,107 cells, each of
        which the old painter covered by 1e-8 to 8e-6. The widest real noise was
        0.00494, from a written DISV -- 2x under the tolerance. Coordinates of 8 or
        more integer digits would round about 10x wider; none of the data has them.
      - **Eight mutants, all killed, each by the test written for it:** the
        original piece-picks-the-measure code (27 tests fail), the areal test
        decided per piece (16), no tolerance (11), the first version's share rule
        (5), no thin-feature guard, a 0.05 tolerance, the width without its factor
        of 2 (one each; the 0.015 strip pins the last two), and a mixed collection
        not refused. Run on a copy of `src/`, behind an import probe.
      - **NOT in this entry:** a LINE on a face still counts in both cells and a
        POINT on a face or vertex still goes to 2-4 cells (the tie rule, next);
        features that miss the grid are still dropped silently.

211. **A GeoPackage that landed nowhere built an empty package (2026-09-11).**
      A feature that resolved to no active cell was dropped without a word, by
      every `.gpkg` list BC and by `GeoPackageSource.k_array`. When EVERY feature
      missed -- a source in another location, a file with no CRS, a
      location-agnostic model placed at the origin -- the package came back
      empty: MF6 rejects an empty list package at read time with a message about
      the file rather than the cause, and with `maxbound=` runs without the
      boundary at all, under normal termination. `k_array` returned its defaults
      everywhere.
      - **All missed: RAISES**, naming the file and layer, each feature and why
        it missed (`outside the grid`, `only borders cells`, `on no active cell`,
        `on no active grid-edge cell` under `edges_only=`, `no geometry`), both
        extents, and both CRSs -- `the file has NO CRS` when it has none. A
        location mismatch is found by comparing two boxes, so the message prints
        them.
      - **`only borders cells` is its own reason** because entry 210 created it: a
        polygon on the grid's outer edge -- an ocean polygon on the coastline, with
        `edges_only=True` -- reached the edge cells through the face-touch bug and
        covers none of them. It says to draw the polygon overlapping the cells.
      - **Some missed: WARNS, by name** (the first ten, then a count). A partial
        miss can be deliberate -- one layer serving several grids -- so it is not
        refused. Decided 2026-09-11: raise on empty, warn on partial, and no
        `on_miss=` switch. **The switch part is SUPERSEDED by ledger 288**, which adds
        `gaps=`; the rest of this entry stands, including raise-on-empty, which 288
        keeps ORTHOGONAL to the mode. It fell because the channel this assumed -- a
        `logger.warning` -- was measured to reach nobody: `import myflopy` installs a
        `NullHandler`, so `logging.lastResort` never fires and the partial-miss line
        produced zero bytes on stderr.
      - **An empty layer raises too**; zero features make the same empty package.
      - **CRS strictness was considered and rejected.** Location-agnostic models
        sit at the origin in EPSG:2927 on purpose, and refusing a defaulted CRS
        would block them. The guard is on the RESULT -- zero cells -- not on the
        CRS.
      - **`Spread`'s own "covers no active cell" warning is gone.** A feature with
        no cells now stops before reaching it, so a partial miss is reported once
        rather than twice; the branch was unreachable afterwards and was removed.
      - **Twelve mutants, all killed:** a full miss that only warns, a partial
        miss not warned, an empty layer passed, every miss called "outside", a
        bordering polygon not named as such, the consequence left out of the
        refusal, the no-CRS case unnamed, the source CRS not recorded,
        `edges_only` not passed on, a missed feature still reaching `Spread` (a
        second warning), and both `k_array` hooks. The consequence mutant exists
        because a draft of this change named a loop variable `empty`, shadowing
        the message parameter, and printed "False" in place of the consequence --
        caught by one test only, so a second now asserts it.

212. **A line on a face counted twice; a point on a vertex, four times (2026-09-11).**
