      `GeoPackageSource._cell_shares` gave every cell a feature touched its own
      piece of it. A line lying ON a face is in both cells' pieces, so its shares
      summed to 2 and a `Spread` conductance doubled; a point on a face or a
      vertex went to 2-4 cells, each at the WHOLE value -- a well on a vertex
      pumped four times its rate. The tie rule was decided 2026-09-11:
      - **A stretch of line on a face is split EVENLY between its two cells**, so
        shares sum to one and a `Spread` total is conserved. The grid's outer edge
        and a face whose far side is inactive have one cell, which keeps the whole
        stretch. A face shared with two smaller cells (a hanging node) splits by
        the length each shares. The split is found pairwise, but only among cells
        whose piece runs along their own boundary -- usually none -- so a line off
        every face pays nothing for it.
      - **A point goes whole to the lowest-numbered active cell it touches**, one
        per point of a MultiPoint. Lowest-numbered is arbitrary but deterministic,
        and so would any other choice be; `edges_only` picks among edge cells.
      - **An unsplit field still reaches both sides of a face at its whole value**
        -- an elevation, a head. That is the documented broadcast, and the reason
        `Spread` exists for extensive fields.
      - **Shares now come back in cell order**, not spatial-index order.
      - **Nine mutants, all killed:** no split on a face, a split by the whole
        stretch, only neighbours-in-sort compared (a hanging node needs all
        pairs), a point taking the highest cell, a point taking every cell (the
        old code), a point ignoring activity, a point ignoring `edges_only`, a
        MultiPoint keeping its first point only, and the usable cells left in
        spatial-index order. The last one SURVIVED the first test set: the index
        returned hits in cell order on every grid the tests built, and out of
        order on 481 of 685 queries of a scrambled one -- so a test now numbers
        its cells out of spatial order.
      - **NOT done, and CLOSED by entry 237** (a line piece under the noise floor is
        dropped now, as SFR's has been since 214): a line within floating noise of a
        face zigzags across it; its
        length is conserved but falls to the two cells unevenly, as for any line
        through two cells.

213. **`ZoneSpec.from_raster` gave zone 0 to every cell too small to hold a pixel centre (2026-09-11).**
      `_majority_sample` burns cell ids onto the raster grid and takes each cell's
      most common label. `rasterize` burns a pixel only where its CENTRE falls in
      a cell, so a cell finer than the raster's resolution held none and took
      `nodata_zone`. That was documented, and wrong in effect: 24% of a refined
      grid frozen at zone 0 -- on an array target a frozen parameter, on a list
      target a spurious lumped zone. The surface sampler (`_area_weighted_sample`)
      had the answer all along, a centroid fallback.
      - **Such a cell now takes the label under its CENTROID.** The majority
        still decides every cell that holds a pixel centre: one odd pixel under a
        centroid does not outvote the rest of the cell (tested).
      - **Bounds are checked rather than trusted to `rasterio.sample`**, which
        returns its fill value -- 0 when the file declares no nodata -- for a
        point off the raster: a real-looking label for a cell the raster never
        covered. Off the raster, or on its no-data, a cell keeps `nodata_zone`.
      - **Centroids are taken in the GRID's CRS, then reprojected** -- a centroid
        computed in a geographic CRS is not the cell's centre.
      - **Four mutants, all killed:** no fallback, no bounds check, nodata
        ignored in the fallback, and the fallback overriding the majority.

214. **A stream centerline on a cell face was two streams' worth of reaches (2026-09-11).**
      `SFRBuilder.reaches` intersected each cell with the centerline, and a closed
      cell polygon includes its boundary, so a stretch lying ON a shared face came
      back full length from BOTH cells. A stream along a row line of a 4x4 grid gave
      8 reaches and 200 ft of rlen for a 100 ft stream -- streambed conductance
      doubled -- and the two copies' projected midpoints tied, so the stable sort
      interleaved the rows and the chain routed back and forth between them. MF6
      accepts every record: each is a valid cell, a positive rlen, an adjacent
      neighbour. Found by the vector-to-cell sweep that followed entry 210; the
      GeoPackage fix does not reach `sfr.py`.
      - **The lower-numbered cell keeps a face stretch** (decided 2026-09-11). The
        `.gpkg` rule splits a line on a face evenly (entry 212); for SFR that makes
        two parallel reaches and breaks the chain, so one cell it is. A stretch is
        claimed only by a reach that is KEPT, so a lower cell whose piece falls
        under `min_reach_length` does not take it from the cell that would have.
      - **A piece under `_SLIVER_WIDTH` (0.01) is dropped whatever
        `min_reach_length` says.** A diagonal through vertices sent through EPSG:4326
        and back clipped three corner cells by ~9e-7 ft and put three micro-reaches
        in the chain; the code's own comment records MF6 dying (SIGFPE) on a
        0.005 ft reach. `min_reach_length` keeps its 0.0 default -- it is the
        user's deliberate minimum; noise is not the user's to configure.
      - **The tolerance now lives once, in `grid/geometry.py`**, shared with the
        GeoPackage resolver (entry 210), so the two cannot drift apart.
      - Exact coincidence only: a centerline 1e-9 ft off the face was already
        right. The triggers are streams snapped to grid vertices, drawn along row
        lines of a structured or quadtree DISV grid, or derived from cell
        boundaries.
      - **Five mutants, all killed:** no claim subtracted, the higher-numbered cell
        claiming, no noise floor, claims not accumulated, and a stretch claimed
        before the length check.

215. **A tributary was connected where it started, not where it joined (2026-09-11).**
      `receiver_location="nearest"` -- the default for every `StreamConnection`
      and `StreamDiversion` -- projected the SOURCE stream's
      `representative_point()` onto the receiver, and for a two-vertex tributary
      that point is its upstream START. A tributary coming in from the east and
      joining mid-grid was connected to the main stem's LAST reach: its water
      entered downstream of the confluence and skipped every reach between. MF6
      accepts the connection. Found by the critic of the vector-to-cell sweep.
      - **The receiver is where the source DISCHARGES**: the source's own resolved
        location -- its downstream end by default -- projected onto the receiver,
        and without one the nearest point between the two lines. A stream running
        beside the main stem and discharging at its end enters there, not wherever
        the two lines happen to be nearest (tested).
      - **At a reach boundary the DOWNSTREAM reach takes the water.** Water joining
        at x=50 enters the reach in cell 6 at its upstream end; the reach in cell 5
        would carry it along a stretch above the confluence. It was `idxmin`, the
        lower reach number. A tie is anything within `_SLIVER_WIDTH`.
      - **Diversions had the same bug and get the same fix:** water leaving the
        main stem's downstream end was delivered to the canal's start.
      - **Four mutants, all killed:** the representative point (the old code), ties
        to the upstream reach, connections ignoring the outlet, and diversions
        ignoring the outlet.

216. **A fault trace resolved to the faces it crossed, and 68-100% of the flow still crossed it (2026-09-11).**
      `barrier_faces` accepted a cell pair when the trace crossed the pair's shared
      face. That is right only for a trace drawn exactly along faces. A trace
      through cells crosses the faces between consecutive cells ALONG the fault,
      which block nothing across it; the connections carrying cross-fault flow --
      the straddled cell to its neighbours on either side -- have faces the trace
      never touches. Measured with MF6 at hydchr 1e-10: 100% still crossed on a
      square grid through cell centres or off-centre, 93-98% on an irregular
      Voronoi grid, 79% on one refined along the fault, 95% on the canonical grid
      with the tests' own `crossing_line`, and 69% in the canonical model -- where
      `packages.hfb.results.q.summary()` read as a SEALED barrier, because it sums
      |q| on the barrier's own faces. A 45-degree trace through grid vertices
      resolved to zero faces. `test_a_tighter_barrier_passes_less_water` measured
      that same self-referential sum and passed on a barrier leaking 95%.
      - **A barrier now cuts the CONNECTIONS whose centre-to-centre segment crosses
        the trace** -- the DISV `cell2d` centres, `vor.points`, the points MF6
        connects. A trace along faces resolves exactly as before (20 faces at
        x=1000 on a 50 ft grid).
      - **A centre ON the trace belongs to its left**, looking along the trace as
        drawn. Without a side, both of its connections across the trace touch it
        only at an end and neither is cut: on a Triangle grid, whose boundary
        generators sit on the bisected segments, the connection rule without one
        leaked 52%. Which side is arbitrary, and moves the staircase by one cell;
        that it is fixed is not. A connection running ALONG the trace (both centres
        on it) is not cut.
      - **`strict=` is gone** from `mf.hfb.line`, `mf.hfb.gpkg` and
        `vor.barrier_faces`. It suppressed end-point touches of the face test and
        has nothing to act on now; a parameter that cannot act is the defect
        ledger 176 names. `api_snapshot.json` records the removal.
      - **Existing `.line`/`.gpkg` models get different faces** -- the correct ones.
        Accepted 2026-09-11. `mf.hfb(pairs=...)`, `.enclose`, `.flopy` and the USG
        importer (explicit pairs) are untouched.
      - **JUDGMENT CALL: no length correction.** The cut is a staircase up to half a
        cell off the trace and longer than it (about 1.4x at 45 degrees on a square
        grid), and MF6 multiplies hydchr by face width, so a FINITE-hydchr barrier
        is up to that much more conductive than the trace it stands for. A
        near-impermeable barrier is unaffected. Every grid-snapped HFB has this.
      - **A closed ring through `.line` is watertight now** (82 cuts on the
        canonical ring against `.enclose`'s 83). `.enclose` stays: it decides inside
        by centroid, and refuses a cut that leaks.
      - **A trace that ENDS at a centre or on a connection cuts nothing there.** The
        side rule is for a centre on a trace's interior; a draft that gave a
        trace's start a side cut the connection to its right from a 0.01 stub
        inside one cell. Elsewhere the test is a proper crossing (`crosses`, not
        `intersects`) for the same reason.
      - **Five mutants, all killed:** no side for a centre on the trace, the right
        side for the left, `intersects` for `crosses`, a trace's end given a side,
        and the old rule itself (faces the trace crosses: 10 tests fail).
      - Tests: a flood fill proves each trace seals -- along faces, through centres,
        off-centre, at 45 and 68 degrees, and across an irregular Voronoi grid with
        generators on the trace -- and a slow MF6 test measures the flow across the
        trace itself, which is what the barrier is for.

217. **Particle tracking failed on every converted USG model (2026-09-11).**
      `UsgModel.to_mf6` wrote NPF with `save_flows` only. PRT reads the specific
      discharge and the saturation GWF saves to its budget, so a PRT run on any
      converted model failed. Both are saved now. The 2026-09-10 bug sweep had to
      patch the NPF by hand before it could reproduce entries 218 and 219 at all.
      - Cost: two more budget records per step, which particle tracking cannot do
        without.
      - **NOT done:** a `PRTProject` precheck naming the missing flags for a model
        built some other way; such a model still fails inside MF6 rather than with
        a myflopy message.
      - One mutant, killed: the flags left off (the NPF test fails, and so do the
        end-to-end PRT tests entry 219 adds).

218. **Release points were written in the world frame on an offset grid (2026-09-11).**
      MF6 reads a PRP record's x/y in the model's OWN frame. `PRTReleasePoints`
      `.from_cells` wrote FloPy's cell centres, which are WORLD coordinates, and
      `.from_points` wrote the caller's world points unchanged. On a grid whose
      origin is not zero -- every USG import, since `to_mf6(local_origin=True)` is
      the default -- the particles were placed 1,340,000 ft off the grid and the
      run failed. Both convert with `modelgrid.get_local_coords` now;
      `from_points` still TAKES world points, in the grid's CRS, and its docstring
      says so.
      - Tested on the synthetic USG model moved to State Plane (1,340,000,
        650,000): a cell centred at (X0+5, Y0+5) is released at (5, 5).
      - Two mutants, killed: each conversion removed.

219. **Pathlines were drawn 282 miles from an offset grid (2026-09-11).**
      MF6 writes particle tracks in the model's own frame, and
      `results.pathlines.map()` reprojected them as if they were world coordinates:
      on an offset grid the tracks landed the length of the origin vector away --
      282.1 miles for a (1,340,000, 650,000) ft origin -- off-screen, with no
      warning. `mosaic` inherited it through `map`. The 3-D scene put the grid mesh
      at x 1,340,000 and the pathline mesh at x 5..20. `backend="mpl"` was right
      only because FloPy's `plot_pathline` applies the transform itself.
      - Both convert with `modelgrid.get_coords` before drawing.
      - **JUDGMENT CALL: `pathlines.get()` / `summary()` still return MF6's own
        frame**, as MF6 wrote it -- the table was never wrong, the drawing was.
        World columns, naming the frame the way the q sign convention does, are
        deferred until something needs them.
      - Tested end to end: GWF, then PRT released with `from_cells` on the offset
        synthetic USG model; every map vertex lies on the grid, and the pathline
        mesh inside the grid mesh.
      - `test_interactive_plotting`'s scene stub gained a grid at the origin: the
        scene now needs the model's grid to place the tracks, which is the fix, and
        at the origin that is the identity, so its pass-through assertion holds.
      - Two mutants, killed: the map's conversion and the scene's.

220. **A reopened run reloaded on every read, and dropped your edits (2026-09-11).**
      `LoadedMf6Run` recorded the package NAMES FloPy reports (`CHD_0`) and checked
      the TYPE asked for (`CHD`) against them. On any workspace whose names are not
      their types -- FloPy's defaults, a name file without pnames, a myflopy
      `name=` override -- every read reloaded the whole simulation (one full load
      per `get()`, 0.03-0.9 s measured, linear in input size), and so did probing a
      package that is not there. A reload replaces the in-memory simulation, so an
      edit made before one was silently dropped from the files `run_simulation`
      wrote: a WEL rate of -999 written back as -50. myflopy's own runs name every
      package for its type, so they escaped the per-read reload but not the
      absent-package one.
      - **A package request on a run that is not fully loaded triggers ONE full
        load, and a full load never reloads**: a package still missing is absent,
        and `package()` raises `AttributeError`. The partial `load_only` branch is
        gone -- it also served core packages (OC, DIS) from a partial load that the
        full load `run_simulation` needs then discarded, edits and all (tested on
        OC). The fast core load behind `vor` and `modelgrid` stays.
      - **Package TYPES are recorded.** With the early return, no reachable state
        tells names from types -- the mutant restoring names SURVIVES -- but every
        reader of that set compares types, so it holds types.
      - Three mutants: names recorded (survives, above), a full load reloading for
        an absent package (killed), core packages served from a partial load
        (killed).

221. **Reopening a run printed at verbosity 0 (2026-09-11).** `_load_simulation`
      floored its verbosity at 1, so FloPy's load chatter and myflopy's progress
      lines printed the first time a reopened run touched a package -- although
      `load_mf6_run(verbosity_level=0)` is the default, and asks for silence. The
      floor is gone. `test_no_library_prints` could not see it: the print IS gated
      on a flag, the flag was just overridden.
      - One mutant, killed: the floor restored.

222. **Every saved project with shared strings or NumPy scalars drifted as 'edited' (2026-09-11).**
      `package_digest` hashes a pickle of the package's canonical fields, and a
      pickle records object IDENTITY: one object used twice is written once and
      back-referenced, two equal objects are written twice. `_canonical` passed
      leaves through unchanged, so a string shared across records -- OC's two
      `"ALL"`, the boundname a GeoPackage feature puts on every one of its records
      -- was one object before `Project.save` and several after, and the digest
      changed. Separately, `np.float64` subclasses float, so JSON kept it and handed
      back a plain `float`, which pickles differently. `runs.drift()` then reported
      packages nobody touched as `edited`, in-process and in a fresh interpreter
      alike: measured on OC, a boundnamed WEL, a NumPy-rate WEL, `drn.gpkg` and
      `riv.gpkg`. The error only ran one way -- never a false `unchanged`.
      - **Leaves are normalized**: a NumPy scalar becomes its Python value, and a
        string is interned, so equal strings are always one object.
      - **JUDGMENT CALL: no digest version.** A manifest recorded before this whose
        packages held NumPy scalars reads `edited` ONCE. The user's standing line is
        that old run records may break but MF6 files never; these are records.
      - Two mutants, killed: each normalization removed.

223. **`load_mf6_run` opened the alphabetically first model, not the flow model (2026-09-11).**
      With no `model_name=`, the loader took the stem of the first `*.nam` in sorted
      order. In a coupled GWF+GWT/GWE/PRT run whose transport or tracking model
      sorted first, it opened that model as if it were flow. It now takes the
      first `gwf6` in `mfsim.nam`'s models block -- the order MF6 reads them -- and
      the name files decide only where there is no `mfsim.nam`. The models-block
      parser `_discover_model_type` already carried is factored out and shared
      (`_declared_models`), so the two cannot read the block differently.
      - Two mutants, killed: the model type ignored, and a model declared without
        a name not taking its name file's stem.

224. **A reopened run was drawn in EPSG:2927 whatever CRS it ran in (2026-09-11).**
      `run.json` recorded no CRS, and a reopened run's models came back through
      `load_mf6_run`, whose `crs=` defaulted to EPSG:2927: a run built on a UTM grid
      reopened labelled State Plane, and every map of it was drawn in the wrong
      place.
      - **The manifest records each model's grid CRS as built** -- a `"crs"` block,
        `{model: crs}` -- and a reopened run carries it forward when its manifest
        is rewritten.
      - **`load_mf6_run(crs=None)` now means the CRS the run recorded, else
        EPSG:2927.** A plain MF6 workspace with no manifest still opens at the
        default, and location-agnostic models still sit at the origin there on
        purpose. An explicit `crs=` still wins. `Run.model()` goes through
        `load_mf6_run`, so it needed no change of its own.
      - Old manifests have no block and open at EPSG:2927, as before.
      - Four mutants, killed: the manifest omitting the CRS, reopening dropping the
        block, `load_mf6_run` ignoring the manifest, and a reopened run forgetting
        the block on rewrite.
      - **NOT done:** the other ~19 hard-coded `2927` defaults -- the next LOW item.

225. **The default CRS was spelled three ways at 19 sites (2026-09-11).**
      `"EPSG:2927"` (11 sites), the integer `2927` (5, all legacy OO classes) and the
      bare string `"2927"` (3, `epsg=` parameters): finding the default meant a grep,
      and a new site could pick any spelling. They are now `DEFAULT_CRS` and
      `DEFAULT_EPSG` in `myflopy/_defaults.py`, a layer-0 module, and
      `tests/test_default_crs.py` fails naming any code-level `2927` elsewhere --
      docstrings and comments excepted, since they document the value.
      - **Every default keeps its value**, so no signature changed:
        `api_snapshot.json` is identical. An editor now shows
        `crs: str = DEFAULT_CRS` where it showed the literal.
      - **The default itself is unchanged, and pinned by a test.**
        Location-agnostic models sit at its origin on purpose, which gives a map a
        clean blue background; a defaulted CRS is never refused or warned about.
      - `import_layers.json` gains `myflopy._defaults` at layer 0 and moves
        `modflow.utils.contour_interp` from 0 to 1, since it now imports it.
      - Found by the 2026-09-10 sweep, as bug 18 of 21.

226. **SFR runoff grew with the number of reaches (2026-09-11).**
      MF6's RUNOFF is a volume per time on each reach, and `SFRBuilder` wrote a
      scalar runoff to EVERY reach -- so a stream's total runoff scaled with its
      reach count, and refining the grid under a stream multiplied it. A
      `{stream: amount}` mapping put the whole amount on the stream's upstream
      reach. Decided 2026-09-11, with the Phase 2 remap design:
      - **A number is each stream's TOTAL, split across its reaches in proportion
        to `rlen`**; `{stream: total}` gives each named stream its own, split the
        same way. An integer key names a reach and takes its amount as given, as
        do explicit per-reach rows.
      - **A time-series name is refused** unless given per reach: a series cannot
        be split by length. None of the user's models used runoff.
      - RAINFALL and EVAPORATION stay per-reach rates broadcast to every reach;
        INFLOW stays a point source at the headwater.
      - A per-stream total spread by length does not depend on the grid, which is
        what Phase 2 needs to carry runoff onto a new mesh.
      - Three mutants, killed: the old broadcast, an even split instead of by
        length, and a time series let through.

227. **ModelContext units were dropped on every save (2026-09-11).**
      `ModelSpec.to_dict` wrote only the context's `metadata`, and `from_dict` rebuilt
      `ModelContext(metadata=...)`, so the `feet`/`days` dataclass defaults filled in
      silently: a metres/seconds model came back as feet/days through `to_dict`,
      JSON, YAML and `Project.save` alike. Ledger 180's refusal to serialize grids and
      domains never covered two plain strings; they went with the arrays by
      accident, not decision. The round-trip tests compared `to_dict` with
      `to_dict`, which cannot see a field `to_dict` never writes.
      - **Latent, not live, until now:** the only readers, SFR and LAK, turn units
        into conversion floats at declaration, and those floats serialize. Grid-lazy
        packages (Phase 2) read the context AFTER a reload, where this would have
        become wrong numbers; a guard test pins that path (SFR on a reloaded
        metres/seconds context keeps conversions of 1.0).
      - **Written always**, not only when non-default. A file saved before this
        has neither and loads as feet/days, which is what it meant.
      - **NOT done:** `ModelContext.dates` is dropped the same way; the USG importer
        builds its context without the model's units; nothing checks the context
        units against DIS `LENGTH_UNITS` / TDIS `TIME_UNITS`.
      - Three mutants, killed: units not written, not read, and no fallback for an
        old file.

228. **A model's package names and types, shown both -- live and reopened alike (2026-09-11).**
      A live model's `package_names` were FloPy's NAMES (`CHD_0`); a reopened run's
      were file-suffix TYPES (`CHD`), matched against the registry's ten packages, so
      they missed every GWT/GWE/PRT package, array recharge, MAW, CSUB and any custom
      filename. The same model said different things live and reopened, and code
      that meant "is there a CHD?" asked a list of names. Decided 2026-09-11: show
      both.
      - **`package_names` are the packages' own names everywhere**; a reopened run
        reads them from the model's NAME FILE, so it stays cheap before any FloPy
        load and agrees with the live model.
      - **`package_types` is new: each type once**, array recharge/ET folded into
        RCH/EVT -- MF6 has one recharge package, and its name file lists an array
        one as `RCH6`. `packages.summary()` gains a `type` column, one row per
        package, still following `package_names` in order.
      - **A name file entry without a pname gets the name MF6 and FloPy give it**:
        `CHD-1`, `CHD-2` for a type FloPy's dfn marks `multi-package`, the bare type
        otherwise -- tested equal to FloPy's own load of the same file.
      - **Consumers that meant types read `package_types`**: the validators, the
        canonical contract check, transport setup (`lak`/`sfr`/`uzf`/`mvr`), the
        loader's own bookkeeping. MVR validation keeps names -- MVR records name
        packages. The diff tier's prefix match (`chd_0` counts as `chd`) is left:
        it already answers by type.
      - **`valid_package_names_3ltr` raised NameError on every call**: it tested
        `isinstance` against a class imported only for type checking (the layering
        rule keeps it there), taking `package_name_validator` and the legacy
        datalists with it. It is duck-typed now. Found by this entry's test.
      - `api_snapshot.json` gains `package_types`; `test_package_explorer_registry`
        pins the summary's columns, which gain `type`.
      - Seven mutants, killed: pnames ignored, unnamed packages not numbered, array
        recharge not folded, loaded names as types again, the validator reading
        names, the NameError restored, and the summary's type column dropped.

229. **Two packages of one type gave an empty table, or half of one (2026-09-11).**
      `build_cell_package_input_table` asked `model.package(type)` for ONE package.
      With two of a type under FloPy's default names, `get_package` returned a
      LIST, which the builder read as an array package with no fields: 0 rows,
      silently, for `packages.chd.inputs.head.get()` on a model with two CHDs.
      With explicit names it returned the package NAMED like the type, dropping
      the others; and an array recharge package (FloPy's `rcha`) was never asked
      for at all -- measured, a third of the applied recharge missing from the
      table while MF6's budget carried it. Decided 2026-09-11: include them all,
      with a column saying which is which.
      - **A table for a TYPE is every package of it, array form included** (RCHA
        counts as RCH, per entry 228), one frame per package, stacked. Each row
        carries **`pname`**, its package's own name. A token that is not a type
        -- `"rch_array"` -- is one package by its own name.
      - **The consumers keep or ignore it correctly**: the field explorer and the
        group tier keep `pname` in the rows they return; `inputs.summary()` does
        not count it as a value; the value-column pickers and the map hover
        already filtered by dtype, and the hover now lists the contributing
        packages per cell.
      - **Where two packages share a cell, a map ADDS them**: the per-cell
        aggregation was already `"sum"` -- which is what MF6 applies (tested:
        list 1e-4 plus array 5e-5 on one cell maps as 1.5e-4).
      - **Closes the diff-tier asymmetry recorded in the exception-narrowing
        entry**: an array RCHA was "present" by prefix but yielded no cell keys, so
        two such models compared as identical. The table reads it now.
      - Mutants, killed: the first package only, array recharge not counted as
        RCH, a package name preferred over its type, rows not tagged, and the field
        explorer dropping `pname`.

230. **A reopened run rebuilt from the library as edited since (2026-09-11).**
      A run records its library packages by KEY, and `Project.reopen_run`
      resolved those keys against the library as it stood when reopened. Edit
      `npf/base` after a run, reopen the run in a later session and rebuild it,
      and it came back with the NEW K -- silently, while its manifest still
      carried the old fingerprint, so `drift()` and the rebuilt model disagreed.
      The user chose to freeze at prepare time (2026-09-11).
      - **`prepare_run` copies each library package the simulation references
        into `<run>/_library/packages/`**, in the library's own format (JSON, or
        a pickle for an array-bearing package), and the manifest's new
        `package_snapshot` block maps each key to its copy. A rebuild resolves
        `mf.ref` from those copies first, by every route: `reopen_run`,
        `project.runs[key]`, and `mf.load_run`/`Run.reopen`, which could not
        resolve a ref at all before. Ledger 181's rule stands: a run never
        resolves against a library that is not its own.
      - **Read at build time, never at reopen.** `project.runs` reopens every
        manifest on each browse, and unpickling copies there would make browsing
        pay for arrays nobody asked to build. A run prepared in this session
        builds from the objects it copied and reads nothing back.
      - **Cost: one more copy per run of each referenced package.** Small for a
        JSON-able package; for an array one, the size of the library's pickle --
        a 72x9,405 float64 recharge array is 5.4 MB. The run folder already holds
        MF6's text input for the same package, which is larger.
      - **Runs prepared before this have no copies**, and still resolve against
        the library as it is now -- there is nothing else to build from. It is no
        longer silent: rebuilding one WARNS, naming each key whose current
        version differs from the fingerprint the run recorded, or that was never
        fingerprinted. Writing or executing it then records the versions it used
        and copies them, so from there on it is frozen like a new run and
        `drift()` tells the truth about its inputs.
      - **A missing or unreadable copy RAISES**, naming the run, key and file.
        It is not replaced from the library, which may now hold something else.
      - **A package that cannot be copied** (neither JSON-encodable nor
        picklable) is left out with a WARNING, because `prepare_run` must not
        fail over a copy; that key then behaves like an old run's.
      - **NOT covered: grid references.** They still resolve from the grid
        library, so editing a grid entry still changes what a reopened run
        rebuilds. The verified bug was about packages, and grids carry no
        fingerprint for `drift()` to compare. The user chose not to copy grids
        for now (2026-09-11).
      - `prepare_run(overwrite=True)` rewrites the copies it indexes and leaves
        any others in `_library/` unindexed, as it leaves the previous listing
        (design D5, ledger 191).
      - `_slug` is lossy, so two keys can share a file name. The index is by
        key, and a clash gets `~2`, which no slug produces.
      - `_save_package`'s JSON-or-pickle logic moved into `_persist_package`,
        shared by the library and the run copies, so both hold one format.
      - Fixed in passing: `docs/core_specs.md` still taught `replace_package`,
        removed by ledger 204.
      - Thirteen mutants, all killed: copies never used, the index dropped on
        reopen or never written, the library winning the merge, the old-run
        warning never or always given, `write` not recording, the missing- and
        unreadable-copy checks removed, clash handling removed, a copy failure
        uncaught, a fresh run reading its copies back, and `reopen_run` flagging
        no keys.
      - Found by the 2026-09-10 sweep, as bug 9 of 21.

231. **A lakebed from bathymetry had no supported route (2026-09-11).**
      `mf.lak(connection_modes="bathy")` needs a per-cell `lake_bottom`, and its
      docstring promised "a raster `Path` or a cell-indexed `Series`". Measured on
      `tests/test_lak_builder.py::_grid` (a pond on cells 3 and 4, neighbours 0, 1
      and 5), only `{lake_id: Series}` and a `Path` worked. A bare Series raised
      "must contain one value per lake"; a Series of the lake's cells raised
      "missing cell 0" -- a NEIGHBOUR, which nothing documented; a `str` path gave
      "could not convert string to float"; and `mf.Raster(...)` -- any `Surface`,
      so `mf.Contours` too -- gave "'Surface' object is not iterable", which a user
      hit on 2026-08-31 with `Surface.raster(...).below(10)`. The `Path` route
      area-sampled the WHOLE grid once per distinct cell it read. And the
      cheatsheet's `mf.lak` example omitted `lake_bottom`, so it raised.
      - **`lake_bottom` and `lake_top` take a `Surface`, a raster `Path` or `str`,
        or a bare cell-indexed Series**, bare or `{lake_id: ...}`. A `str` naming a
        column is still the column; one that is neither a column nor an existing
        file raises naming both, instead of reaching `float()`. A numeric string
        still works as a literal, as it did by accident.
      - **Sampled once per source**, through `Surface.values(grid,
        previous=model_top)`, then indexed per lake. Measured on a 2,729-cell grid
        with a 105-cell pond: **149 full-grid samples in 10.9 s before, 1 in 1.3 s
        after**, the same 421 connections. Passing the model top as "the surface
        above" makes a relative Surface a depth below ground
        (`mf.Surface.offset_below(6)`), and `units=` converts as it does in a
        `LayerStack`. The one sample is still full-grid; a window around the lakes
        was not worth the code.
      - **The neighbours are land, and default to the model top.** `bathy` reads
        the bed at each lake cell's non-lake neighbours to find the exposed steps.
        Where the source has none -- a raster clipped to the lake, a Series of the
        lake's cells -- it is now that neighbour's model top, deliberately. A
        raster's NaN used to reach `min(cell_top, nan)`, which returns the LAKE
        cell's top only because it is the first argument. The two agree except
        where the neighbour's ground is lower than the lake cell's top: the face now
        stops at the neighbour's ground, above which there is no aquifer to
        exchange with.
      - **Judgment call: a per-cell bed is capped at its cell's model top, and a
        capped LAKE cell warns.** A bed above ground lies in no layer and used to
        raise "does not intersect active cell". A bathymetry interpolation and a
        DEM are built independently and disagree a little at the shore -- in the
        GRASS end-to-end check below, 5 of 105 cells, by up to 0.48 ft -- so
        raising failed the Contours recipe on a correct model. The trade: a warning
        can be missed, and a bed that is wrong everywhere (a DEM passed as the bed)
        builds a zero-depth lake with one warning naming the count. **A scalar bed
        is never capped**: a rectangular facility's flat bottom is a design value,
        and still raises when it lies outside the cell. The USG export note and
        CLAUDE.md's Keevie trap said `mf.lak` rejects such beds; both now say it
        caps and warns, and ledger 169 is annotated.
      - **A lake cell a raster has no data for is set to the top (zero depth) and
        warns; one missing from a Series raises.** The first is a sampling artefact
        -- a sliver the polygon clips, holding no pixel centre, whose centroid
        falls outside the clipped raster (2 of 105 cells end to end). The second is
        an omission. A raster with no data on ANY lake cell raises: that is the
        wrong raster, not a sliver.
      - **"Model top" means column 0 of the layer-elevation table**, not the top of
        the highest ACTIVE layer. Where layer 0 is inactive and has thickness, a
        capped or filled bed lands in an inactive cell and still raises "does not
        intersect active cell", as it did before. Not handled.
      - **`lake_top` takes the same forms but is never filled or capped**: a
        facility top above ground is legitimate (a berm), and there is no natural
        default for a missing one.
      - **A Series keyed by lake id is now read by LABEL**, for every per-lake input
        (`starting_stage` and `bed_leakance` too). It was read by position, so one
        in a different order from the lake table was misassigned silently. For
        `lake_bottom`/`lake_top` a Series whose index is NOT the lake ids is read
        as cell-indexed, so a positional per-lake Series with a default index now
        raises naming the lake cells it misses, with a hint.
      - **Not done:** `mf.lak`'s `lake_bottom`/`lake_top` annotations stay `Any` (a
        union would show `Surface` in the editor, but needs pandas and `Surface`
        under `TYPE_CHECKING` in `package_api`); `LakeTableBuilder(dem=)` still
        takes a path, not a Surface (`surface.resolve_source()` gives one); a bare
        `{cell: value}` dict is still read as keyed by lake id (its error now
        points at the Series); an ncpl-length array is not read per cell
        (`mf.Surface.from_array` is the spelling).
      - **Verified end to end with GRASS** (`/usr/bin/grass`), outside the suite:
        digitized pond contours -> `mf.Contours(..., region_vector=pond.gpkg)` ->
        `mf.lak(lake_bottom=...)` on the 2,729-cell grid -> MF6 normal
        termination, lake stage 174.0 ft. The tests write their own GeoTIFFs, so
        none needs GRASS.
      - Docs: the `mf.lak` docstring (with a Contours example), cheatsheet §7 (the
        example now uses a contour bathymetry) plus a recipe,
        `package_api_reference.md` Advanced packages, `core_specs.md` Lakes,
        CLAUDE.md, and the USG export note.
      - 14 new tests (18 cases) in `tests/test_lak_builder.py`. Seventeen mutants,
        all killed: neighbours not read, the sample cache off, no cap, a NaN
        neighbour left unfilled, either warning dropped, a whole-lake miss not
        raised, a lake-id Series read by position, the model top not passed as
        `previous`, `units=` ignored, a `str` path not recognized bare or inside a
        mapping, `lake_top` treated as a bed, a Series missing a lake cell not
        raised, a Surface accepted for a per-lake input, and a bare cell Series
        refused.

232. **The cell-coverage rules could only be reached through a GeoPackage (2026-09-11).**
      Which cells a geometry reaches -- a polygon covers by AREA, a line lying on
      a face splits evenly between its two cells, a point goes to the
      lowest-numbered usable cell, a piece under `_SLIVER_WIDTH` is noise
      (ledgers 210-212) -- was decided inside `GeoPackageSource._cell_shares`,
      and `geopackage.py` is import layer 3. The three fixes queued behind this
      one -- head targets, the shared cell selector, grid-edge cells -- touch
      layer-1 modules that cannot import it, and each of the three reports
      proposed its own extraction of the same code. Extracted ONCE, first, with
      no behaviour change.
      - **`cell_shares(polys, geometry, *, usable=None)`, `domain_active(domain,
        layer, cell)` and `miss_reason(polys, geometry, *, target=)` now live in
        `grid/geometry.py`**, beside `_SLIVER_WIDTH`, `_SLIVER_SHARE` and
        `_mean_width`, which they already used. That module is layer 1, so
        `observations`, `boundaries` and the grid selectors can reach it;
        `geopackage.py` already imported it for the constants.
      - **Eligibility stays the CALLER's, through `usable`.** It is handed the
        cells a candidate touches and returns the ones that count, so a caller
        needing an edge set or one layer's activity computes it once and closes
        over it instead of deciding per candidate -- which is what
        `GeoPackageSource` does with `edges_only` and the idomain.
      - **The helper sorts what it is given, whoever chose it.** The spatial index
        answers in tree order (all nine interior vertices of the scrambled test
        grid) and a tie goes to the lowest-numbered cell, so with three callers
        coming the tie rule cannot rest on each of them remembering to sort a set
        before handing it back. No current caller is affected --
        `GeoPackageSource._usable_cells` already sorted -- and the returned pairs
        are now in cell order for every caller.
      - **The edge set is resolved only once a feature reaches something.**
        `get_grid_edge()` walks every cell and reads the grid's own
        `idomain_path` if it has one, so a row with NO geometry must not pay for
        it, and on a grid with a broken `idomain_path` would have begun raising
        where it used to return nothing. Extracting had lifted that call above
        the empty-geometry check; it sits below it again.
      - **No separate point helper**, as one report proposed: `cell_shares` on a
        point already returns `[(lowest usable cell, 1.0)]`.
      - **Nothing changed in behaviour, including the messages.** `domain_active`
        still raises `GeoPackage layer N is outside domain with M layers`, worded
        for the only caller there is; whichever fix adds the second should
        generalize the wording rather than leave two. `_extent` moved with them
        and is re-exported from `myflopy.geopackage`, where
        `tests/test_geopackage_spread.py` imports it.
      - **Size**: `geopackage.py` 958 -> 857 lines, `geometry.py` 504 -> 672. The
        difference is docstring: the rule now has to explain itself to callers
        with no GeoPackage in sight.
      - **What still kept its own copy at the time: `LAKBuilder._active`**
        (`lakes.py`), which counted a 1-D idomain as active everywhere where this
        one reads it -- CLOSED by entry 241. Neither were the other sites the
        sweep measured against these rules
        (`pest/zones.py`,
        `surfaces._cells_in_zone`, `PRTReleasePoints.from_points` (CLOSED by entry
        242), `get_vor_idx_from_geometry` (CLOSED by entry 245), the demo site's
        `_cells_for`), nor ledger
        212's open line case -- that one is CLOSED by entry 237: the line branch
        carries the same noise floor now, so a line overshooting a face by 1e-6
        no longer reaches the far cell here either.
      - 35 tests in `tests/test_cell_coverage_rules.py`, which pin the single
        copy by identity and by patching it, and exercise each rule directly on a
        4x4 grid. Twenty-three mutants, all killed: each delegation bypassed
        (`cell_shares`, `domain_active`, `miss_reason`), the candidate sort
        dropped and the sort narrowed to the default, slivers never detected and
        never dropped, the sliver SHARE guard dropped, a feature that is entirely
        slivers emptied, the even split on a face removed, a polygon measured by
        its pieces' length again, `_extent` preferring length, a point taking
        every cell it touches and a point taking the highest, `> 0` as `!= 0` in
        both idomain branches, the layer bound dropped, the eligibility closure
        not passed, the edge set resolved eagerly, a miss wording flattened,
        `miss_reason` ignoring its target, and two import probes.
      - Found by the 2026-09-11 sibling investigation.

233. **A head target on a cell face became four observations (2026-09-12).**
      `HeadTargets.match_to_model` joined its targets to cells with `intersects`
      and never reduced the result, so a well on a shared face got 2 rows and one
      on a vertex 4, all under one name. Measured on a 4x4 grid: `compare`
      returned 5 rows for 2 targets, `stats` said n=5, `to_flopy_obs` wrote 5 MF6
      records, and PEST disagreed with itself -- the build pivots `first` and read
      cell 5 where the forward run takes the last row and read cell 10.
      - **One cell per target, through the rules ledger 232 extracted**: the
        lowest-numbered cell active in the target's OWN layer. The same vertex is
        cell 1 in layer 0 and cell 0 in layer 1, so activity cannot be read at
        layer 0 for every target; an idomain -1 passthrough is not active, since
        MF6 writes no head there.
      - **The tie is the shared helper's, not a second copy.** `cell_shares` sorts
        whatever `usable` returns, so this caller decides eligibility only.
      - **Targets are reprojected to the grid's CRS first.** Two wells whose cells
        are 5 and 10 both resolved to cell 4 with their file in degrees over a
        State Plane grid.
      - **The nearest-cell snap is gone.** It moved an off-grid target onto the
        grid at ANY distance with no log -- 1.45e6 ft for State Plane coordinates
        on a grid at the origin -- and a target equidistant from two cells crashed
        the whole call with a pandas ValueError, losing the targets that HAD
        landed. Misses now follow ledger 211: all missing raises, with both
        extents and both CRSs; some missing warns by name and leaves them out,
        once per set rather than once per call, because every consumer calls
        `match_to_model` again.
      - **A non-point target is refused**: a polygon equal to one cell gave 9 rows
        and a MultiPoint 2, at x/y in neither cell.
      - **Explicit cell ids are validated** (user's decision, 2026-09-11): an id
        the grid does not have raises, where it reached the value table as NaN and
        dropped out of `stats` silently, and so does one inactive in its own
        layer. An id is an assertion about the model, so it raises where a missed
        point warns.
      - **The domain is read from the discretization package**, through the new
        `grid/domain.py` -- the loader's copy sat in `project.run_model`, the top
        import layer, where nothing else could reach it. `SimulationBase.idomain`
        is deliberately NOT consulted: it BUILDS a domain from an `idomain_path`
        and raises `TypeError` when there is none, so asking it turns "no domain
        declared" into an error. `observations.heads` moves to import layer 2 and
        its importers one each; the map is regenerated.
      - `domain_active`'s "GeoPackage layer ..." message is now caller-agnostic,
        as ledger 232 said the second caller should make it.
      - The PEST locations snapshot and its `n_locations` count now cover only
        matched targets.
      - **NOT done.** A name repeated in two layers still writes two mapping rows,
        so a two-screen well's build and forward run still read different layers;
        the user chose to key the mapping by (name, layer), which is its own
        entry. `examples/mf6/demo_site/calibration.py` keeps a third copy of the
        rule that crashes on a face point: the file is UNTRACKED, so it is left to
        the user (`scratchpad/ht/apply_demo_site.py` holds the change).
      - Ten mutants and an import probe, all killed: activity ignored, layer 0 for
        every target, a total miss only warning, misses ignored, no reprojection,
        a non-point accepted, both id checks dropped, and the once-only warning
        turned into never.
      - The 2026-09-10 sweep described this site wrongly: `contains` DROPS a face
        point, but that is `heads_observations.get_obs_cells`; here the predicate
        was `intersects` and the point was duplicated. Found by the 2026-09-11
        sibling investigation.

234. **PEST read a two-screen well's simulated head from the wrong layer (2026-09-12).**
      A target's observation identity was its bare NAME on the PEST side, while
      MF6's own records had always disambiguated a repeated name as
      `<name>_lay<layer>`. A well screened in two layers was therefore ONE
      simulated column: the build pivoted `first` and read layer 0, the forward
      run wrote each mapping row into that column and left layer 1 standing, and
      the two disagreed by whatever the layers differ by -- 5.0 against 1005.0
      measured. The user chose to key the mapping by (name, layer) (2026-09-11).
      - **One definition of the label**: `HeadTargets.observation_labels(model)`,
        built by `_ensure_unique_observation_names` -- the function the FloPy
        records already used. A name used once IS its label, so nothing is renamed
        in the ordinary case and existing pst files keep their observation names.
      - It reaches all four places that keyed on the name: the simulated CSV's
        columns, the MF6 `continuous` records, the mapping CSV the forward run
        reads, and the pst rows -- pyEMU names an observation after the CSV's
        column, so `col_label` had to follow. The residual map reads the same
        label when the mapping carries one.
      - **Concentration targets inherit it**, through the same two blocks in
        `pest/observations.py`.
      - A mapping written before the label existed has no such column, and its
        name still serves, so a calibration prepared earlier keeps working.
      - An observed row whose target matched no cell is now dropped from the pst
        rows (an inner join) rather than becoming a row for a column that does not
        exist.
      - **The observed values stay keyed by name.** A well with two screens has one
        measured series, so both of its observations compare against that series.
        That is what keying by (name, layer) means here; splitting the measurements
        per screen would need the values table to carry a layer, and it does not.
      - Five mutants and an import probe, all killed: the build pivoting on the
        name, the label being the name, the forward run keying on the name, the pst
        rows keeping the name, and the mapping dropping the label.
      - **A mutation harness can lie.** Two of these first read as killed because
        the harness ran pytest in a stripped environment where
        `tests/test_mf6_pest.py` failed at COLLECTION, and `-x` turned that into an
        immediate non-zero exit for every mutant. It now asserts a passing baseline
        under the same command before any mutant counts.
      - Found by the 2026-09-11 sibling investigation, as the second half of the
        head-target decision; ledger 233 is the first.

235. **The shared cell selector took any touch (2026-09-12).**
      `get_vor_cells_as_series` joined geometries to cells with `intersects` and
      no measure, so a polygon that was exactly cell 5 selected 9 cells, a
      face-aligned block of four selected all 16, a point on a vertex selected 4,
      and a diagonal line selected 10 where 4 are right. Everything that asks
      "which cells does this shape pick?" goes through it: regions and
      `map(select=...)`, mp3du particle release, cross-sections,
      `adjust_top_btm_overlaps`, the legacy boundary classes' inactive-cell set,
      and the observation-cell helpers.
      - **The default is the measured rule** (ledgers 210-212, through the shared
        `cell_shares` of 232): a polygon reaches the cells it covers by AREA, a
        line those it runs through, a point the one cell holding it. An explicit
        `predicate=` keeps the raw spatial join as a documented escape hatch -- no
        in-repo caller needs it now, and leaving it costs nothing.
      - **All five forwarders flipped too.** The default was restated at
        `VoronoiGridPlus.get_vor_cells_as_series`/`_as_dict`,
        `selection.get_vor_cells_as_dict`, `RegionRegistry.add_from_geometry` and
        `SimulationBase.add_region_from_geometry`, so fixing the free function
        alone would have reached almost nothing. A test pins every one, and each
        has its own mutant.
      - **An empty result is an empty Series**, not the empty GeoDataFrame callers
        indexed as a Series one line later, and features that reach nothing are
        named in a WARNING. The selector does not RAISE: an empty `map(select=)`
        is documented as a warning, and the callers that build model input
        (regions, particles) raise for themselves.
      - **The two `contains` callers** -- `heads_observations.get_obs_cells` and
        `datatypes/locs.py` -- dropped a point sitting on a face, since `contains`
        is false for every cell there, and then logged that it did not intersect
        the grid at all. They take the default now, and a ratchet test fails on a
        `predicate='contains'` anywhere in `src/`.
      - **`get_vor_cells_as_dict` asks once for the whole frame** rather than once
        per feature, keeping the `{name: [[cells]]}` shape ledger 192 left alone.
      - **What changes for callers**, on a 4x4 grid: a region from a cell-sized
        polygon is 1 cell where it was 9; a particle release from one is 1
        particle, not 9; a diagonal section crosses 4 cells, not 10, with no
        duplicated stations; `adjust_top_btm_overlaps` moves one cell's bottom,
        not nine. The legacy `Boundaries.inactive_cells` inherits the rule through
        the wrapper default, which the user accepted on 2026-09-11.
      - **Cost.** The rule measures per feature where the join was vectorised: the
        investigation measured 300 boxes on 10,000 cells at 0.025 s joined against
        1.43 s looped. A typical call carries a handful of features, and at ~441
        cells the measured path is faster than the join's own overhead.
        Vectorising the polygon case is left undone, and recorded here.
      - `select=`/`clip=` wording in the plot reference was corrected and
        `scripts/derive_docstrings.py` rerun (20 docstrings rewritten).
      - **NOT done at the time**: `get_grid_edge_cells`' own ring code (CLOSED by
        entry 236); the three consumers that hand the selector a list of lists
        (build_idomain, `InterpolatedSurface(clip=)`,
        `get_overlapping_area(shp_gpkg=)`) (CLOSED by entry 240); and the
        deprecated `PrtPrp`, which is still left alone.
      - Ten mutants and an import probe, all killed.
      - Found by the 2026-09-11 sibling investigation.

236. **Grid-edge cells came from a ring, and the ring was wrong four ways (2026-09-12).**
      `get_grid_edge_cells` answers "which cells are on the model's edge". Given an
      idomain it outlined the active area and asked which cells that outline
      touched. Measured on a 6x6 grid of 25 ft cells:
      - the inactive set came from the touch join (ledger 235's site), so a cell
        merely BORDERING the inactive polygon counted as inactive: a face-aligned
        strip returned 14 cells against a true 16, having lost the whole true edge
        column and gained four interior cells;
      - a ring runs through vertices, so a cell touching it at one corner was kept
        -- inactive corner cell 35 added its diagonal 28, and a one-cell hole added
        the hole's four diagonals;
      - outer-ring and hole-ring hits were concatenated without de-duplication: 36
        entries for the 27 cells around a one-cell hole;
      - `vor.idomain_path` was consulted BEFORE an explicit `idomain=`, and
        `idomain=[]` fell through to it.
      What that cost: `mf.chd/ghb/drn/riv.gpkg(edges_only=True)` on a grid carrying
      an idomain file wrote its boundary on the wrong cells, and
      `mf.build_simple_model(boundary_mode='drain')` on such a grid wrote 36 DRN
      records over 27 cells -- total conductance 3600 against 2400, with 7 interior
      cells drained.
      - **The fix is the rule the function already used with no idomain**: an
        active cell is on the edge when it borders the outside (more faces than
        neighbours) or when a face-neighbour is inactive. No ring, no geometry, no
        duplicates, and no dependence on how a line lying on a face is selected.
        The investigation's prototype of it matched a face oracle and a geometric
        ring oracle exactly on six meshes of 441 to 30,444 cells.
      - `include_interiors=False` keeps each active component's OUTER edge by
        flooding the mesh inward from the outside: what the flood cannot reach is a
        hole of that component. An island inside a ring keeps its edge, because
        that edge is the island's own boundary.
      - **`idomain=` is the list of INACTIVE cell ids** -- not a mask, and not MF6's
        array. Both are refused now, naming `np.flatnonzero(domain <= 0)`: the
        grid's own `idomain` property means the ACTIVE ids and MF6's means flags, so
        one word carried three meanings and a 0/1 list was silently read as the ids
        0 and 1. An id the grid does not have is refused by name.
      - **An explicit argument wins**, `idomain=[]` means nothing is inactive, and
        passing both raises.
      - **An idomain FILE is read as a frame**, so its CRS reaches the selector and
        is reprojected; the union this replaced dropped it, and a 4326 file raised
        `KeyError: 0` rather than saying where its features were. Coverage is by
        area (ledger 210): a 0.005 ft graze marks nothing, 40% of a cell marks it. A
        file covering no cell raises, naming it with both extents and both CRSs.
      - The edge set is found ONCE per `GeoPackageSource` now, not once per feature;
        `get_grid_edge` walks every cell and reads the grid's idomain file.
      - **NOT done**: what "edge" MEANS for `.gpkg(edges_only=True)` is unchanged --
        the grid's own edge, not the model's per-layer domain; a file with a layer
        column is unioned across layers; and `VoronoiGridPlus(idomain=)` /
        `GridSpec.voronoi(idomain=)` are still accepted and dropped on the floor.
      - The face-count test assumes shapely returns a LineString for a shared face.
        A hanging node that one cell splits with a collinear vertex its neighbour
        lacks would miscount; none were found on the six meshes checked.
      - Eleven mutants and an import probe, all killed -- two of them only after
        tests were added for the cases that let them live: an unsorted answer shows
        only when two active components interleave, and a bool mask SHORTER than the
        grid slips past the array check.
      - Found by the 2026-09-11 sibling investigation; the last of the three sites
        the user approved.

237. **A line overshooting a face by 1e-6 ft wrote a second full record (2026-09-12).**
      `cell_shares` has had a noise floor on its AREAL branch since ledger 210 -- a
      piece narrower than `_SLIVER_WIDTH` (0.01) and under `_SLIVER_SHARE` of its
      cell is a reprojection artefact, not coverage. Its LINE branch never had one.
      Measured on the 4x4 grid of 25 ft cells with a DRN line from (37.5, 37.5) to
      the face at x=25: ending exactly on the face, one record, cell 5; overshooting
      into cell 4 by 1e-6 ft or by 1e-3 ft, a full SECOND record, `((0, 4), 10.0,
      100.0)` -- the same elevation and the same conductance, because a field not
      wrapped in `Spread` is written whole. On a State Plane grid a
      2927 -> 4326 -> 2927 round trip moved the end by -2.95e-7 ft and did the same.
      `SFRBuilder` on that same geometry kept one reach in cell 5, having had the
      floor since ledger 214, so `.gpkg` and SFR disagreed about one line. The worst
      measured case is the geometry of ledger 214's own SFR test: a diagonal drawn on
      grid vertices, round-tripped through EPSG:4326 on a State Plane grid, clips three
      corner cells by ~9e-7 ft and became **SEVEN DRN records where four are right**,
      700.0 of conductance against 400.0. SFR gave 4 reaches on that same line.
      - **The floor is the shared rule's now, worded for a length**: a line piece
        SHORTER than `_SLIVER_WIDTH` and under `_SLIVER_SHARE` of its cell's mean
        width is noise. The shape is the areal branch's, not a second rule -- the
        same constants, the same share guard, and the same escape: if EVERY piece of
        a feature is a sliver they ARE the feature and none is dropped, so a 0.017 ft
        line across a vertex keeps both of its 0.0085 halves.
      - **This is the SHARED rule, so it is not a `.gpkg` fix.** Everything ledger 235
        routed through `get_vor_cells_as_series` moves with it -- regions and
        `map(select=...)`, mp3du particle release, cross-sections,
        `InterpolatedSurface(clip=)`, `adjust_top_btm_overlaps` and the legacy
        `Boundaries.inactive_cells` set -- and so does
        `observations/heads.py::match_to_model`, which calls `cell_shares` itself
        (ledger 233), so a LINE `HeadTargets`/`ConcTargets` takes it too. Measured on
        that same overshooting line, the selector answered `[[4, 5]]` and now `[[5]]`.
      - **The share guard is what keeps a sub-unit grid whole**, as it does for a
        polygon: on 0.02 ft cells a piece of 0.005 ft is half the cell's mean width --
        a quarter of its side -- and is coverage, not noise. A length is measured
        against the CELL's mean width, never against its perimeter, its area, or the
        feature's own length; on those cells the four guards are 1e-4, 8e-4, 4e-6 and
        whatever the feature is, so the choice decides real cases and each wrong one
        has its own mutant. `thin_feature` extends to a line as its LENGTH, so a
        0.009 ft feature split 0.006/0.003 across a face keeps both pieces instead of
        only the longer one -- two thirds of a feature that is entirely what was drawn.
      - **Ledger 212 is untouched**: a stretch of line lying ALONG a face is in both
        cells and is still split evenly between them (0.125 each across 8 cells,
        summing to 1). A dropped sliver leaves the face bookkeeping with its size,
        which is not cosmetic -- without that, a line running 0.004 ft along a face
        before turning into one of the two cells raised `KeyError` instead of giving
        the whole length to the cell that kept it, and CLEARING that bookkeeping
        instead leaves an untouched pair with the whole shared stretch each, which is
        exactly the doubling ledger 212 removed (shares summing to 2.0).
      - **Amends ledger 212's "NOT done"**, which recorded only "a line within
        floating noise of a face zigzags across it". That is the case where the line
        crosses and re-crosses; it did not cover a line that simply ends past the
        face, which is what a CRS round trip and a centerline drawn to a grid vertex
        produce. It also closes ledger 232's open bullet ("the line branch still has
        no sliver floor, so a line overshooting a face by 1e-6 reaches the far cell
        here while SFR drops it") -- amend both in place.
      - **A share is still a fraction of the WHOLE feature**, so the dropped tip is
        simply not applied: cell 5's share of the 1e-3 overshoot is 0.99992, not
        renormalized to 1. That is `Spread`'s documented "clip", and the areal branch
        does the same. Under `mode="retained"` the whole conductance now stays in
        cell 5 (100.0) instead of leaking 0.008 into cell 4.
      - **`Spread`'s own `min_share` hid this for a wrapped field** -- an 8e-8 share
        is below its 1% default -- which is why the defect lived: it was visible only
        on the plain unwrapped column, which is the default for every list BC, and on
        `min_share=0.0`.
      - **One existing test moved its geometry.**
        `test_geopackage_spread.test_min_share_drops_a_corner_clip` nicked a cell of a
        1-unit-cell strip by 0.005, and the margin there was ONE ulp: the nick measures
        0.004999999999999893 against a share guard of exactly 0.005, so had GEOS
        returned 0.005 + eps the piece would have been kept and the test would not have
        moved at all. Both conditions must hold to call a piece a sliver, and on a grid
        whose cells are about a unit wide the absolute floor and the share guard sit on
        top of each other -- that is the price of an absolute tolerance, and the one SFR
        has paid since ledger 214. The nick is 0.02 now (0.99% of a 2.02-long feature,
        2% of the cell), so the test pins `min_share` rather than the floor.
      - **NOT done**: the areal and line floors stay two branches of one function
        rather than one expression, because the measures are not interchangeable (a
        polygon is judged by its WIDTH, a line by its LENGTH) and collapsing them
        would have to pick one. `LAKBuilder.lake_cells` kept any area > 0 with no
        sliver rule at all (CLOSED by entry 241), and `usg/export._adjacency` still
        used `touches` (CLOSED by entry 244). No `Spread` renormalization was added.
      - **Cost: none measurable.** `_mean_width(polygon)` is evaluated only after
        `size < _SLIVER_WIDTH` short-circuits, so a line whose pieces are ordinary
        never computes it. A blast-radius sweep over 182 mixed geometries -- boxes,
        cell-sized boxes, random lines, points, a point on a face and on a vertex, a
        MultiPoint, a MultiLineString and a GeometryCollection -- is identical to
        HEAD's, 0 cases differing; the cut-over on the 25 ft grid is clean at the
        tolerance (0.0099 reaches one cell, 0.0101 two).
      - 27 tests in `tests/test_line_slivers_on_faces.py`, 18 of which fail at HEAD.
        Thirteen mutants and an import probe, all killed: no floor on a line piece
        (the old code), the absolute floor dropped leaving the share guard alone, the
        share guard dropped leaving the absolute floor alone, the guard taken against
        the cell's perimeter, against its area, and against the feature's own length,
        both comparisons flipped at their boundary, `thin_feature` not extended to a
        line, the all-slivers escape removed, a dropped sliver left in the face
        bookkeeping, that bookkeeping cleared entirely, and a sliver skipped outright
        as SFR does with no escape.
      - Found by the 2026-09-11 sibling investigation.

238. **A DRN seepage zone claimed every cell it touched (2026-09-12).**
      `DrnFlowTargets.zone_definitions` resolved a zone's cells with a spatial
      join on `intersects`, which is true of a shared edge and of a shared
      corner. Measured on a 4x4 grid of 25 ft cells: a zone drawn exactly on
      cell 5 gave `[0, 1, 2, 4, 5, 6, 8, 9, 10]` -- the cell and all eight
      neighbours -- a point on the 4|5 face gave `[4, 5]`, a point on a vertex
      gave `[5, 6, 9, 10]`, and a zone off the grid gave `[]` in silence, so its
      simulated seepage was a zero that read as a real number. Worst: two zones
      abutting on the column of faces at x=50 BOTH claimed
      `[1, 2, 5, 6, 9, 10, 13, 14]` (12 cells each, 8 of them shared), so every
      drain in that column was summed into two different observations and
      calibrated against twice.
      - **A zone COVERS its cells, through the rules ledger 232 extracted**: a
        polygon by AREA, a trace by the cells it runs through, a point the ONE
        cell holding it. The same five cases now give `[5]`, `[4]`, `[5]`, a
        raise, and `[0, 1, 4, 5, 8, 9, 12, 13]` / `[2, 3, 6, 7, 10, 11, 14, 15]`
        -- disjoint. The tie is `cell_shares`' own: this caller passes `usable`
        and decides eligibility only, so the lowest-numbered cell wins however
        the grid is numbered.
      - **Only cells active in the ZONE's own layer count**, since MF6 writes
        neither a DRN budget entry nor a DRN observation where there is no cell;
        an idomain -1 passthrough is not active either. That makes `layer` mean
        something for the first time, so it can now be WRONG: a zone declared in
        layer 3 of a two-layer model raised nothing and resolved 9 cells against
        layer 0, and now raises `Layer 3 is outside the model domain, which has
        2 layers.` from the shared `domain_active`.
      - **Zones are reprojected to the grid's CRS first**, as head targets are; a
        zone file in degrees over a State Plane grid matched on raw degrees, and
        geopandas said so in a `UserWarning` and returned `[]`. The frame handed
        back is therefore in the GRID's CRS, not the source's (EPSG:4326 ->
        EPSG:2927 measured) -- which `pest/observations.py` writes as the zones
        GeoPackage snapshot, so that snapshot's CRS moves with it. The cell ids
        beside it were resolved in that frame, and a snapshot whose geometry is
        in another CRS than its own ids would be the next bug.
      - **Misses follow ledger 211**: every zone missing raises, with both
        extents and both CRSs, in the SOURCE frame's own coordinates (a mismatch
        is two boxes; reprojecting one first would print two that agree); some
        missing warns by name and leaves them out, once per set rather than once
        per call, because all seven consumers in `drn.py` re-resolve the zones
        (`get`/`summary`/`_obs_column_map`/`_compare_from_obs`/
        `simulated_series`/`compare`/`to_flopy_obs`) and PEST's snapshot writer
        an eighth. `pest/ies.py`'s `_parse_cell_list` still tolerates an empty
        zone, which is now only the partial case.
      - **A zone given as several rows is ONE zone**, as the grouped join made
        it: the cells are unioned over its rows, and it counts as missing only
        when EVERY row of it does. Accumulating misses per row instead -- the
        first version of this fix -- warned `1 of 2 DRN zones land on no active
        cell and are left out: 'seep'` about a zone that had landed and was still
        in the frame, where the base code had silently got the union right. The
        `total` is a count of NAMES for the same reason.
      - **Membership is NOT restricted to cells that carry a drain**, and that is
        this entry's decision rather than an oversight. A zone is geometry,
        resolved with no reference to the DRN package -- which is also why the
        rule can be tested against a model-like object with no packages. A
        covered cell with no drain adds zero to the budget sum, and
        `to_flopy_obs` still writes an MF6 `continuous` record for it; whether
        MF6 rejects a DRN observation on a drainless cell was NOT measured (no
        MF6 run), and the intersects rule was putting far more such cells into
        every zone than the area rule can.
      - **Three pieces came out of `heads.py` rather than being copied**:
        `_in_grid_crs`, `_placement_note` (the extents-and-CRSs sentence, now
        taking the noun so "targets" and "zones" share one wording) and
        `_report_missed_features` (the raise-all/warn-some/warn-once shape).
        `HeadTargets` delegates to all three, so ledger 233's messages are
        unchanged byte for byte. The shared helper takes its `log` and its
        `where` from the caller -- `log` required, so a miss is never reported
        under `_shared`'s name, and `where` a callable, since only the raise uses
        the sentence and the deduped path would otherwise scan both extents for
        nothing. `geopackage.py`'s own `_where` is deliberately left alone: it
        reads `self._source_crs` rather than a frame, and another fix is landing
        in that file this week.
      - **Cost.** The vectorised `sjoin` became a per-zone loop with a
        per-candidate `.intersection`, as in ledgers 232 and 235: on a 100x100
        grid (10,000 cells) with two zones covering 7,500 of them, 0.007 s ->
        0.151 s per resolve, ~22x. Nothing caches it and seven methods re-resolve,
        so a `compare()` on big areal zones pays it repeatedly. A typical seepage
        zone is a handful of cells, where the loop is faster than the join's own
        overhead; caching `zone_definitions` per (model, locations) is left
        undone and recorded here.
      - **This closes the `observations/drn.py` line in 232's "What still keeps
        its own copy" list and the DRN half of 233's NOT-done bullet.** Both now
        misdescribe the code, so both are struck where they name DRN seepage
        zones (233's `heads_observations`/`locs.py` `contains` path was closed by
        235 and its bullet left stale -- the convention here is that a NOT-done
        bullet is a live index, not a historical record, so it is edited).
      - `observations.drn` moves from import layer 1 to 2 (it now imports
        `grid.geometry`/`grid.domain`); the map must be regenerated. That
        regeneration also picks up `grid.selection` 1->2 and
        `simulation.regions` 2->3, which ledger 235 left unregenerated and which
        are NOT from this change.
      - **NOT done**: `ZoneSpec.from_polygons` and `surfaces._cells_in_zone`
        still assign by centroid, and `PRTReleasePoints.from_points` took flopy's
        lowest cell2d (CLOSED by entry 242) -- each is its own entry. The canonical model
        defines its seepage zones as explicit cell lists, and the only existing
        geometry test (`test_mf6_pest.py`, a polygon inset to 0.95 of one cell)
        still resolves to `[0]`, so no in-repo expectation moved.
      - Twenty mutants and an import probe, all killed: the touch rule restored,
        activity ignored, layer 0 for every zone, misses ignored, no
        reprojection, the owner dropped from `zone_definitions`, explicit cell
        lists re-resolved as geometry, the miss reason dropped, the miss reason
        losing its layer, a total miss only warning, the once-only set dropped,
        the placement label ignored, the placement note built from the
        reprojected frame, the listing truncated to one name, the
        nothing-to-sum wording flattened, the resolved frame keeping source-CRS
        geometry, and four on the multipart zone (union dropped, first row wins,
        misses per row, the set counted by row). Eight of these are an
        adversarial review's own survivors against the first version of the tests.
      - Found by the 2026-09-11 sibling investigation.

239. **`sfr_connection(at=(x, y))` answered with the nearest reach CENTROID (2026-09-12).**
      The coordinate form of the semantic mover endpoint took the minimum of
      `(centroid_x - x)^2 + (centroid_y - y)^2` over the stream's reach pieces, so
      it answered with whichever piece happened to be centred nearest rather than
      the reach at the point. Measured on a 4x4 grid of 25 ft cells with a stream
      along y = 37.5 (reaches 0-3 in cells 4-7):
      - `at=(50, 37.5)`, the boundary between the reaches in cells 5 and 6,
        answered reach 1 -- the UPSTREAM reach, the opposite of ledger 215. Both
        centroids are 12.5 ft away, and `min` kept the first it saw. The 4|5 face
        was the same: reach 0 where 1 is right.
      - `at=(47, 37.5)`, 3 ft inside cell 5's own reach (9.5 ft from that reach's
        centroid), answered reach 2. Cell 6's reach is 10 ft long and centred at
        x = 55, 8 ft from the point, where cell 5's 25 ft reach is centred at 37.5.
        Not a tie -- simply the wrong reach, and the point is not in that cell at
        all.
      - `at=(37.5, 12)`, a whole row of cells below the stream, answered reach 1,
        and `at=(500, 500)`, off a 100x100 ft grid entirely, answered the outlet.
        Both silently.
      - **The grid decides which cell, and the reach follows from the cell**:
        `cell_shares` (ledger 232), the same rule that puts a head target or a
        GeoPackage feature in its cell. Reach centroids are gone from the index.
      - **Ledger 215 is restated here, and that is not free.**
        `SFRBuilder._reach_at` states the same rule and cannot be called: it needs
        the reach GEOMETRY and the `sequence` column, and a serialized index
        carries neither. `_reach_at_point` therefore orders by POSITION in
        `by_stream`, which is equal to `sequence` because `SFRBuilder.reaches`
        sorts a stream's pieces by projection along its line before numbering them
        -- an equivalence nothing pins today, and the thing to check if either
        side is ever reordered. The narrowing itself goes through `cell_shares`'
        `usable` hook: eligibility is "cells carrying a reach of THIS stream", and
        where the point sits on the face between two of them the set is cut to the
        DOWNSTREAM one, because the helper's general lowest-numbered-cell tie would
        otherwise hand the water upstream. Where two reaches of one stream share a
        cell the downstream one takes it for the same reason -- `reaches` emits one
        reach per (stream, cell) today, so that arm is pinned with a hand-built
        index rather than a grid.
      - **"Downstream" means down the STREAM, not up the cell numbers.** Every
        left-to-right fixture makes the two agree, so a reversed stream
        (`LineString([(100, 37.5), (0, 37.5)])`, reaches 0-3 in cells 7-4) is what
        pins the rule: there `at=(50, 37.5)` is reach 2 and `at=(25, 37.5)` reach 3,
        where "largest cell id" answers 1 and 2.
      - **A point on the face between a reach cell and a cell without one takes
        the reach cell**, which is what `usable` means and the shape
        `observations/heads.py` already has for inactive cells.
      - **A miss raises.** Outside the grid names the point, the grid's extent and
        the grid's CRS -- ledger 211's shape, and a bare `(x, y)` in the wrong
        frame is the commonest way to land there. Inside the grid but on no cell
        carrying a reach names the stream's reach cells AND the nearest of them
        with its centre, which is usually the reach the caller meant and is what
        the old rule handed back in silence. `miss_reason` is deliberately not
        used: it words a miss against the GRID, and would say "outside the grid"
        for a point that is inside it but off the stream.
      - **The index carries the reach cells' outlines, not the grid's.** Measured
        on a 97x97 grid (9,409 cells) with a 97-reach stream: 9,992 bytes of JSON
        for the whole index against 897,304 for the grid's own outlines -- which
        every fork deep-copies and every `PackageLibrary.digests()` hashes -- and
        every cell it would add is one the stream has no reach in. Building the
        index costs 4 ms once the reach table exists, which `mf.sfr` has already
        built by then (15 ms from cold, 11 of it the reach table itself); a lookup
        costs ~2 ms.
