      - **Its keys are strings now, and that fixed a second live bug.**
        `PackageSpec.to_dict` writes JSON, where an integer key comes back a
        string, and ledger 179 deliberately promotes those back to `int` only for
        `options`/`inputs`, never for `metadata`. So the int-keyed `centroids`
        lookup raised `KeyError: 0` on ANY saved-and-reloaded spec -- through
        `to_dict`/`from_dict` as much as through YAML. The round trip is pinned
        through the real seam, not a bare `json.dumps`.
      - An index written before this change still answers `"downstream"` /
        `"upstream"`, and says what to rebuild for `at=(x, y)`.
      - **Two tracked sentences taught the old rule and are corrected**: the
        comment above `with_metadata(sfr_index=...)` in `package_api.py` and line
        181 of `examples/mf6/package_first_full_stack.py`. The example is patched
        only where `examples/` exists, since the tree this draft was proven on does
        not carry it.
      - **NOT done.** `SFRBuilder.connection(stream_id, Point(...))` still resolves
        by distance to the reach GEOMETRY with the ledger-215 tie. Measured on the
        same fixture, the two public routes now AGREE wherever the point is on the
        grid -- `Point(47, 37.5)` -> 1, the 5|6 boundary -> 2, a point on the 1|5
        face -> 1 -- so the centroid half of the defect is genuinely absent there.
        The SILENT-MISS half is not: `sfr.connection("s0", Point(37.5, 12))` still
        answers reach 1 and `Point(500, 500)` still answers reach 3. It is left
        alone because the same `_reach_at` serves the network's own resolved ends,
        projections and intersections, where the point is on the line by
        construction, so making it refuse an off-stream point is a change to the
        network builder rather than to this endpoint. `at=` still takes an
        `(x, y)` pair only, not a shapely `Point`. A cell polygon with a hole would
        lose it to `.exterior`; no Voronoi/DISV grid builds one.
      - Seventeen mutants and an import probe, all killed: no downstream
        narrowing, the upstream reach at a boundary, a miss falling back to the
        outlet, off-grid not told from off-stream, a shared cell going upstream,
        the whole grid in the index, integer keys, an old index undetected, any
        stream's reach cell being eligible, downstream-most read as
        highest-numbered cell, coordinates truncated to whole units, the off-grid
        test excluding the grid's own edge, cell ids paired with the wrong rings,
        the layer stored instead of the cell, `cell_shares` replaced by a bespoke
        `contains` scan, the nearest reach cell named as the farthest, and the CRS
        dropped from the miss message.
      - Found by the 2026-09-11 sibling investigation.

240. **Three callers read the cell selector's answer as a flat list, and so raised on every input (2026-09-12).**
      `get_vor_cells_as_series` answers one entry per FEATURE, each a LIST of
      cells -- the shape ledger 192 kept and ledger 235 made measured. Three
      consumers read it as a flat list of cell ids, which ledger 235 named as not
      done and the user asked for next. Each failed on EVERY geometry:
      - **`build_idomain`**, through `assign_voronoi_cells_to_layers`
        (`utils/datatypes/readers.py`), put `[[5]]` in each layer column and then
        died with `TypeError: cannot use 'list' as a set element (unhashable type:
        'list')`. So `SimulationBase(idomain_path=...)` had no working read at
        all: `model.idomain`, `model.idomain_gdf` and `model.inactive_cells` every
        one of them raised that, for every idomain file.
      - **`InterpolatedSurface(clip=)`** (`grid/interpolated_surface.py`, in both
        `xs` and `ys`) and **`get_overlapping_area(shp_gpkg=)`**
        (`grid/geometry.py`) handed the list of lists to `.loc` and got
        `KeyError: None of [Index([(5,)], dtype='object')] are in the [index]`.
      - **One flattener, `selected_cells`**, in `grid/geometry.py` beside the
        coverage rules ledger 232 extracted. Four callers had already written it
        out for themselves and worked -- nine lines inside `adjust_top_btm_overlaps`
        in that same file, a set comprehension in `_inactive_from_file`
        (`grid/selection.py`, ledger 236, landed while this was being drafted),
        another in `RegionRegistry.add_from_geometry` (`simulation/regions.py`),
        and a fourth inside `build_idomain` itself, five lines above the code this
        entry adds. With `choros._resolve_cells` that is five, so fixing
        `get_overlapping_area` and the clipped surface in place would have made a
        sixth and a seventh. All four of the working copies call it now;
        `choros._resolve_cells` deliberately does not (below).
        Measured after: a cell-sized idomain polygon makes exactly cell 5
        inactive, a clipped surface's `xs` is `[37.5]`, `get_overlapping_area` is
        625.0.
      - **`build_idomain` asks the selector ONCE for the whole file**, not once
        per row. Per row, a row landing off the grid is a WHOLE-input miss, so the
        ledger-211 raise/warn policy fired on a single row; and the selector's
        setup was paid again for every row and every layer column -- on a 400-cell
        grid, 60 features over two layer columns measured 120 selector calls in
        0.0494 s against 1 in 0.0132 s, 3.7x. Answers map back by POSITION,
        not by index label: keyed by label, a frame carrying a repeated label gave
        both of its rows one row's cells.
      - **A file that lands on NO cell now raises** (ledger 211). It came back as
        a domain with every cell active in every layer, so the model runs to
        normal termination with the idomain doing nothing; the cause is almost
        always a location or a CRS, so the message carries both extents and both
        CRSs and each feature's reason from `miss_reason`. A PARTIAL miss keeps
        the rest and is warned by the selector, by name -- including a file whose
        layer-0 features land and whose only layer-1 feature misses, which is a
        good file and must not be refused.
      - **A domain now EXISTS where every read used to raise, and that reaches
        other code.** `mp3du`'s `collect_inactive_cells` lists `TypeError` in its
        own handler and fell through to the flopy `modelgrid.idomain` instead; it
        now reads the polygon-derived set, which is what `get_start_cell_diagnostics`
        counts its released-into-inactive-cells warning from, and the two can
        disagree. Two details of that, measured on the 2-layer 16-cell fixture:
        its docstring says "the model's top layer" but `SimulationBase.inactive_cells`
        is layer-FLATTENED (`[5, 21]` for cell 5 of both layers), so ids >= ncpl
        can never match a particle's cell and an inactive cell below layer 0 goes
        uncounted -- true before this and not fixed here; and the source of truth
        for that warning moves from the written DISV to the polygon file. Nothing
        else in `src/` reads `SimulationBase.inactive_cells` or `.idomain`: the
        legacy `Boundaries`/`recharge`/`kflow`/`drn` tier builds its own from
        `idomain`/`idomain_path` and is untouched, and model BUILDING never asks
        -- a package-first model's domain arrives as `ModelContext.domain`
        (`simulation/base.py:175`), which never calls `build_idomain`.
      - **The crash was hiding a second defect.** Under the pre-235 `intersects`
        join a one-cell idomain polygon claimed 9 of the 16 cells on the test

      - **`InterpolatedSurface.clipped_cells` is a property**, resolved once and
        memoised. `zs` read a cache that only `xs`/`ys` ever filled, so asking for

        the total-miss refusal removed, fired on a partial miss, its extents
        dropped and its features unnamed; `zs` reading the stale cache, the memo

      - `tests/import_layers.json` and `docs/import_layering.md` are derived and

241. **A lake kept every cell it grazed, and LAK had its own activity test (2026-09-12).**
      `LAKBuilder.lake_cells` took any cell whose overlap with the lake polygon had
      an area above zero, with no noise floor at all -- the last site that kept an
      overlap ABOVE ZERO with no floor, which is the clause ledger 237 left open.
      (It is not the last site off the shared rule: 232's list is still live, and
      `VoronoiGridPlus.get_vor_idx_from_geometry` is looser still -- it defaults to
      `predicate="intersects"`, keeping every cell a geometry merely TOUCHES.)
      Measured on a 4x4 grid of 25 ft cells: a lake drawn exactly on cell 5 gave
      `[5]`, but the same lake on a State Plane grid round tripped 2927 -> 4326 ->
      2927 gave `[4, 5, 8, 9]`, the extras overlapping by 7.41e-06, 9.07e-14 and
      7.41e-06 ft2; via EPSG:2285 `[5, 6, 9, 10]`, extras 1.41e-04, 8.58e-03 and
      1.94e-09 ft2; and grown by 1e-06 ft, all nine cells around it. Each of those
      becomes a **full LAK cell with its own vertical connection**, so the lake's
      sidewall topology and its budget moved with the projection the polygon had
      been digitized in, under normal termination.
      - **A lake COVERS its cells, through the rules ledger 232 extracted.**
        `lake_cells` is `cell_shares(polys, geometry)` now -- the same rule behind a
        `.gpkg` boundary, a head target, a DRN zone and a region -- and the four
        cases above all give `[5]`. Shares are discarded at the call: LAK connects
        to a cell or it does not, and nothing about a connection is apportioned by
        how much of the lake sits in one. Which LAYER each cell connects in is
        still `_layer_containing`'s, against that cell's own elevations.
      - **The floor is the PIECE's width, not its share of the lake**, which is
        what keeps a real clip. A lake reaching 0.1 ft into the next cell covers it
        (2.5 ft2, 0.4% of the lake and 0.4% of the cell, but a strip 0.0996 ft wide
        -- ten times `_SLIVER_WIDTH`), and a lake that is ITSELF that thin keeps
        every piece: a 0.004 ft strip centred on the 1|5 face is two 0.002 ft
        halves, and a rule that dropped them would have emptied it.
      - **A multipart lake is measured per PART, and that is the one place a cell a
        modeller MEANT can go.** Measured: a one-cell lake with a detached
        15 x 0.005 ft satellite (0.075 ft2, mean width 0.005) was `[5, 15]` and is
        `[5]` -- the satellite's cell is gone, silently, because the lake as a whole
        is 9.6 ft wide so the whole-feature escape does not cover it. A detached
        1 x 1 ft pond and a 15 x 0.1 ft strip both stay, and a multipart lake whose
        every part is thin keeps them all, so the loss is confined to parts that are
        themselves noise and a lake can never go from some cells to none this way.
        Accepted rather than special-cased: it is the answer a `.gpkg` zone of that
        shape already gets, and a second rule for lakes is what this entry removes.
        Pinned by test, and stated in `docs/package_api_reference.md`.
      - **`LAKBuilder._active` is `domain_active`**, closing 232's "What still keeps
        its own copy" line. It differed twice: a ONE-dimensional idomain counted as
        active EVERYWHERE, so a lake connected through cells the model had switched
        off (measured: `_active(0, 4)` True on a flat domain whose cell 4 is 0, now
        False, and a lake on a switched-off cell raises `bottom does not intersect
        active cell` where it used to build); and a layer beyond a `(nlay, ncpl)`
        domain raised `IndexError: index 3 is out of bounds for axis 0 with size 1`
        rather than `Layer 3 is outside the model domain, which has 1 layers.` The
        `-1` passthrough was already read correctly in the 2-D branch and still is.
      - **A lake reaching no cell follows ledger 211**: `1 of 1 lakes cover no grid
        cell, so they would carry no LAK connection: 'pond' (outside the grid). The
        lakes span (...) and the grid (...); both are in EPSG:2927.` It was `Lakes
        do not intersect the grid: pond`, which named the lake and nothing that
        would find it. **There is no partial tier** as there is for a `.gpkg`
        source, where one layer can deliberately serve several grids: a lake with no
        cells carries no connection, which MF6 refuses, so ANY lake missing raises
        and the message counts them (`1 of 2 ...`, naming only the one that missed).
        The raise stays in `validate()`, not in `lake_cells`, so reading
        `.lake_cells` to diagnose a miss still answers `{'pond': []}`. No `target=`
        is passed to `miss_reason`: a lake is areal and nothing filters its cells,
        so only "outside the grid" and "only borders cells" can come back and the
        argument would be text no run can print.
      - **The source CRS is now captured before `lake_table` reprojects** (a new
        `_source_crs`, as `GeoPackageSource` has), because the sentence is about two
        frames and the frame on hand had already been moved to the grid's -- it
        would have said "both are in EPSG:2927" of a file read in degrees.
      - **A collapsed lake outline is refused by name**, and that is this entry's
        own decision rather than a reported defect: `_extent` falls back to LENGTH
        for a geometry with no area, so `box(25, 25, 25, 50)` -- still a `Polygon`,
        so the existing geometry-type check passes -- came back as the two cells
        along that face instead of as the miss the old area test made it. `Lake
        geometry has no area: <names>` is raised from `lake_table`, beside the type
        check.
      - **No lake anywhere on disk moves a cell.** Measured old rule against new:
        the canonical valley lake at 21x21 (33 cells), 50x50 (130), 22x16 (25) and
        the default 100x100 (541); the demo site's `lake.gpkg` on its 4,107-cell GIS
        grid (60); and the Ten Trails USG export's four lakes on the 18,107-cell
        DISV mesh of `runs/from_usg` -- Keevie 47, Black Diamond 22, Horseshoe 18,
        Marjorie 15, **0 cells dropped**, matching that run's own written
        `tentrails.lak` exactly (161/69/64/44 connections). Those polygons are
        dissolved OLD CLN cells on a mesh drawn later, which is the case this rule
        was most likely to bite; shifting them 1, 8 and 68 ft across that mesh drops
        nothing either. Horseshoe is why the floor is two conditions and not an area
        tolerance: its smallest overlap is 0.107 ft2, 1.9e-06 of its cell -- under
        the share guard -- but 0.118 ft wide, so it is a real clip and is kept. So
        no expectation changed, no notebook output moves, and ledger 169's "249
        fringe cells over four lakes" stands.
      - **Ledger 231's bathymetry route is untouched and asks for LESS**: it raises
        where a per-cell `lake_bottom` Series misses a lake cell, and the cells this
        drops were exactly the edge clips its "no data at N of the M cells" warning
        was about.
      - **Cost: this is slower, as in 232/235/238.** One vectorised
        `GeoSeries.intersection` over the whole grid became a per-candidate loop:
        0.63 -> 0.94 ms for the canonical lake at 21x21, 2.04 -> 3.35 ms at 50x50,
        and 8.1 -> 22.4 ms (2.8x) for a 999-cell reservoir covering half the 50x50
        grid. It is cached per builder and read once per lake, so a build pays it
        once; `test_lak_builder.py`'s cache test had to change instrument (it
        counted `GeoSeries.intersection` calls, and the shared rule intersects
        shapely geometries), not intent.
      - **The extents are printed in the GRID's frame, where 238 prints the
        source's.** `lake_table` normalizes the lakes once, on read, and keeps no
        second copy to measure -- so a lake file in degrees reports
        `(1,146,072.9, 795,811.0, ...)` against the grid's `(0.0, 0.0, 100.0,
        100.0)`. The two boxes still disagree, which is what the sentence is for,
        and the clause names the reprojection; holding the source geometry (or
        reprojecting back inside the error path) for a tidier box was not worth the
        state. Ledger 211's own site (`geopackage.py`'s `_where`) prints the
        reprojected frame too. If a third caller wants source-frame extents, that
        belongs in `where_they_are`, not here.
      - **Amends 232 and 237 in place**, as 237 did to 212: 232's "What still keeps
        its own copy: `LAKBuilder._active`" sentence goes, and 237's NOT-done clause
        loses its `LAKBuilder.lake_cells` half (`usg/export._adjacency` still uses
        `touches` and is still its own site).
      - **NOT done**: `lake_cells` passes no `usable` -- membership is geometry
        alone, with no reference to idomain, and a lake cell inactive in every layer
        still raises from `_vertical_connection` naming the cell, which is a better
        error than silently dropping it. Nothing WARNS about a dropped sliver: the
        shared rule drops them in silence for every other caller and a per-lake
        warning here would be the only one. And no MF6 run was made: what a lake
        losing three sliver cells does to the LAK budget was not measured, only what
        it does to the connection set (four lake cells to one).
      - Twenty mutants and an import probe, all killed: the area-above-zero rule
        restored, the delegation bypassed with the touch rule, membership by share
        of the lake, cell order reversed, the cache dropped, `domain_active`
        bypassed, the layer bound dropped, idomain read as truthiness, the miss
        never raising, only a total miss raising, the miss reason dropped, the
        extents and CRSs dropped, the source CRS read off the reprojected frame,
        the source CRS captured after it instead of before, the source CRS never
        captured, a collapsed outline accepted, the zero-area guard narrowed to
        `is_empty`, the miss count counting the missing set as its own denominator,
        membership filtered by idomain through `usable=`, and the raise moved out of
        `validate()` into the property.
      - Found by the 2026-09-11 sibling investigation.

242. **PRT release points ignored idomain and took the lowest cell on a face (2026-09-12).**
      `PRTReleasePoints.from_points` located every point with FloPy's
      `modelgrid.intersect`, which answers with the lowest CELL2D and reads no
      idomain. Measured on a 4x4 grid of 25 ft cells with cells 0 and 4 inactive in
      layer 0:
      - a point on the face between cells 4 and 5, `(25, 37.5)`, gave cellid
        `(0, 4)` -- the INACTIVE cell -- where the rule gives `(0, 5)`;
      - a point on the vertex shared by cells 0, 1, 4 and 5, `(25, 25)`, gave
        `(0, 0)`, also inactive, where the rule gives `(0, 1)`.
      - **What that cost, measured with MF6 (the 2026-09-11 investigation could
        not: it needs a run).** Nothing was silent, and nothing was wrong in the
        output either -- it never got that far. FloPy's PRP validates each cellid
        against idomain, so `PRTProject(...)` raised
        `MFDataException: Cellid (0, 4) is outside of the active model grid` from
        `_check_valid_cellids`, naming an id the caller never wrote and neither the
        point that produced it nor the active neighbour that point equally touches.
        The same point in cell 5 runs: 3 track records, normal termination. So the
        defect's shape is a late, unattributable refusal of a release the grid could
        perfectly well have accepted, one cell over.
      - **The fix is `cell_shares` + `domain_active` (ledger 232), the shape
        `observations/heads.py::match_to_model` has had since 233**: eligibility
        ("active in the release layer") goes in through the `usable` hook, and the
        helper's own sort decides the tie, so the lowest-numbered ACTIVE cell wins
        without a second copy of that rule here. The release `layer=` is what
        activity is read in, so one point resolves differently per layer, and a
        passthrough (`idomain = -1`) is not active.
      - **It is also 400-500x faster**, which was not the point but is the larger
        number: one spatial-index query per point replaces FloPy's per-point scan of
        every cell. 200 points on a 100x100 (10,000-cell) DISV grid, same points both
        sides, 7.5 s -> 0.016 s (the old side measured 6.5-8.7 s across runs on a
        machine running other agents' work, the new side 0.015-0.017 s). It scales
        per point: the cost was in `intersect`, called once per release.
      - **Ledger 211 reaches release points too.** A point landing on no active cell
        is left out and named in a warning, with `irpt` renumbered over the
        survivors the way `merge` already renumbers across sets -- MF6 wants
        1..NRELEASEPTS with none missing -- and group labels stay indexed by the
        point GIVEN, not by the record written. When NONE of them land it raises,
        with both extents and both CRSs. The reason is measured where the point
        LANDED and the coordinates named are the ones the caller GAVE, which is the
        only way a reprojected point that misses reads as "on no active cell"
        rather than "outside the grid". That raise/warn split RELAXES a hard
        failure into a warning: FloPy's `intersect` raises `point given is outside
        of the model area` for an off-grid point, so one bad row in a well file used
        to cost the other ninety-nine. The house rule (211, 233, 238) is that a
        partial miss can be deliberate -- one file serving several grids -- so it
        warns by name; this follows it rather than keeping FloPy's all-or-nothing.
      - **Points are reprojected to the grid's CRS first**, as every other myflopy
        source does. Without it the new refusal would fire on a perfectly good frame
        read in degrees, and `where_they_are`'s sentence -- which says the points
        WERE reprojected -- would have been false.
      - **The frame handling of ledger 218 is untouched, and pinned.** Cells are
        resolved in the WORLD frame (the `vor`'s, which is the world frame in every
        path myflopy builds one: a USG import's comes from the .gsf while its DISV
        declares the origin the mesh was shifted by, and a reopened run's is rebuilt
        from `modelgrid.verts`, offset applied), and the record is still written in
        the model's own frame through `get_local_coords`. Three tests on an offset
        grid at (1,340,000, 650,000) hold the halves apart: a point inside a cell
        (only the frame can fail it), a point on a face (either can), and the grid's
        OWN coordinates, which must reach no cell because the frame is not guessed.
        218's line saying `from_points` "TAKES world points, in the grid's CRS" is
        now half of the story -- a frame in another CRS is converted to it first.
      - **A third copy of the ledger-211 raise/warn wrapper, deliberately.**
        `_refuse_or_report_missed` is the third after
        `observations/_shared.py::_report_missed_features` and
        `geopackage.py::_refuse_or_report_misses`, and the judgment is: reusing
        `_shared`'s would cost the layer. Its wording is fixed at "lands on an
        active cell" with no layer, and the layer is exactly what makes a release
        point's miss actionable (a mutant that drops it fails two tests); its
        `%ss` pluralisation cannot take a subject carrying one, and its `owner`
        dedupe exists for observation views that resolve the same features per
        call, which a release set does not. Promoting a layer-aware version into
        `grid/geometry.py` beside `miss_reason`/`where_they_are` is the real fix and
        wants its own pass, with all three callers in it. Same for `_in_grid_crs`,
        now a third spelling after `_shared._in_grid_crs` and
        `heads._locations_in_grid_crs`: `_shared`'s returns anything that is not a
        GeoDataFrame unchanged, so a GeoSeries of release points would have been
        located in its own degrees and nothing would have said so.
      - **NOT done: `from_cells`.** It still trusts the ids it is given, measured on
        the same grid: cell 4 (inactive) is written as `(0, 4)` in silence and fails
        later exactly as above; `cells=[-1]` wraps to cell 15's centre and writes
        cellid `(0, -1)`, which FloPy then refuses with `Invalid cellid (0, -1)`
        (its -1 case wants EVERY element of the cellid to be -1), so the wrong cell
        is silent only until the package is built; `cells=[99]` on a 16-cell grid
        raises numpy's `IndexError: index 99 is out of bounds for axis 0 with size
        16`, which does not name the grid. The rules approved for this pass cover
        resolving a GEOMETRY; refusing an explicit cell id is
        `heads.py::_validated_cells`' rule (233), and applying it here would refuse
        release sets that build today. Its docstring now says it takes the ids as
        given and points at `from_points`. It is its own entry.
      - **NOT done: structured (DIS) grids**, which keep FloPy's `intersect` -- and
        with it FloPy's own all-or-nothing refusal, so NEITHER half of this reaches
        a structured model, the activity or the ledger-211 message. The shared rule
        is indexed by cell id and a DIS cell is `(row, col)`; `grid/domain.py`'s
        reader does not read a DIS idomain either (it looks at DISV/DISU), so the
        activity half could not be honoured there without widening a helper three
        other callers share. `_cell_frame` returns `None` for that grid kind and for
        a model carrying no `vor`, and two tests pin what DIS still does, FloPy's
        `point given is outside of the model area` included, so half of it cannot be
        changed by accident. PRT supports DIS and DISV only (`_copy_grid_to_prt`),
        so DISU never arises.
      - `myflopy.modflow.mf6.prt` moves from import layer 0 to 2 (it now imports
        `grid.geometry` at L1 and `grid.domain` at L0); `tests/import_layers.json`
        carries the one changed line and `docs/import_layering.md` must be
        regenerated with `scripts/derive_import_layers.py`. The deferred-import
        allowlist and `tests/api_snapshot.json` do not move, and
        `scripts/derive_docstrings.py` has nothing to rewrite.
      - Twenty tests in `tests/test_prt_release_points_on_faces.py`; 15 of them fail
        on the unfixed tree. Twenty-two mutants and an import probe, all killed:
        activity never consulted, activity read in layer 0 for every release,
        activity by truthiness (so a passthrough counts), the domain never read, the
        domain left flat (so the layer stops mattering), the shared rule replaced by
        a strict containment scan (which loses every face point), the grid kind
        unchecked, the cell frame never found, the record left in world coordinates,
        x and y swapped reading the input, a GeoDataFrame read as a plain iterable
        (so its column names), no reprojection, `local_z` not the caller's, misses
        passing in silence, a miss falling back to the cell the activity filter
        rejected, a total miss only warning, the raise dropping both extents and both
        CRSs, the miss reason dropping its layer, the miss reason measured in the
        source frame, the listing truncated to one, `irpt` keeping the input
        position, and group labels shifting onto the surviving records. One mutant
        was retired as EQUIVALENT rather than left as a survivor -- `hits[0]` ->
        `hits[-1]`, since `cell_shares` answers a single-part point with exactly one
        pair.
      - Found by the 2026-09-11 sibling investigation.

243. **A zone boundary drawn through a row of cell centroids left that row in no zone (2026-09-12).**
      Both zone assignments -- `ZoneSpec.from_polygons` for PEST and
      `surfaces._cells_in_zone` for a layer surface -- asked whether a cell's
      centroid was `within` the zone polygon, which is FALSE for a centroid lying
      exactly ON the polygon's edge. A grid's centroids are where its data is, so
      that edge is where a boundary gets drawn. Measured on a 4x4 grid of 25 ft
      cells: two zones split at `y=37.5`, the line through the row-1 centroids,
      gave cells 4-7 the `nodata_zone` label 0, while a split at `y=37.4` gave them
      zone 2 -- and pyEMU gives a zone `<= 0` no multiplier (this module's own
      docstring), so that row of the model went uncalibrated under a definition
      that names it. Worse, a LONE zone `box(0, 0, 12.5, 100)`, whose east edge is
      the column-0 centroid line, selected NO cell at all: an all-nodata `ZoneSpec`,
      in silence, nothing calibrated. On the surface side
      `_cells_in_zone(grid, box(0, 0, 100, 37.5))` selected `[0, 1, 2, 3]` and not
      `[4, 5, 6, 7]`, and those four cells took the OUTSIDE elevation -- 2.0 ft
      where the zone said 15.0 -- which feeds `Surface.where`, hence botm, and
      through pinch-out idomain.
      - **The CENTROID rule is kept, deliberately.** A zone labels a WHOLE cell --
        a K zone, a layer's extent -- so its centre decides (ledgers 118, 213), and
        `cell_shares`' area rule is emphatically not what a zone wants: a zone
        drawn 0.1 ft short of the centroid line covers 49.6% of those cells by area
        and must still not label them. `tests/test_zone_edges.py` pins that, so the
        next reader cannot "fix" this by reaching for the area rule.
      - **A zone is CLOSED**: a centroid exactly on its edge is in it, outer
        boundary and shared boundary alike, corners included. With two zones
        sharing the line every centroid lands in exactly one; with one zone the
        boundary belongs to the only zone there is, which is why `box(0, 0, 12.5, 100)`
        now reaches the column it was drawn along.
      - **`covered_by` alone would NOT have been deterministic**, which is the part
        the obvious one-word fix misses. Both docstrings claimed a cell in several
        zones "takes the first match"; with `covered_by` the winner comes out of the
        spatial index's own tree order instead. Measured over 600 random frames of
        2-5 axis-aligned boxes whose corners are snapped to centroid lines (seed 11,
        this grid): the naive `sjoin` + first-match disagreed with the first row on
        433 of them, and an independent draw by the review measured 232 of 600 -- the
        count is the generator's, the disagreement is not. On a plain two-zone split
        it depends on which row is written first: rows lower-then-upper agree, and in
        the other order cells 4-7 took the SECOND row's label. So the shared rule
        reduces the index's pairs with `np.minimum.at` and the FIRST ROW wins by
        construction -- reversing the rows now swaps the shared row's label, and
        nothing else. Under `within` the join happened to agree with row order (0 of
        600 in both draws), so the tie is new only in the sense that the boundary
        case is what makes it reachable at all.
      - **One rule, one place**: `centroid_zones` in `grid/geometry.py`, beside
        `cell_shares`, which it deliberately is not. It answers ROW POSITIONS
        (-1 for none), because one caller maps them to labels and the other to a
        boolean mask, and both were already positional over `gdf_vorPolys`. Two
        copies of the predicate were two chances to fix one of them; an identity
        probe pins that neither keeps its own. This closes the `pest/zones.py` and
        `surfaces._cells_in_zone` entries in 232's "what still keeps its own copy"
        list only in that sense -- they share one rule now, and it is NOT
        `cell_shares`. 238's NOT-done bullet ("still assign by centroid") stays
        literally true and is deliberately kept, so it is left standing.
      - **A row whose LABEL is null is not a zone.** The old `sjoin` dropped it
        through a `notna` filter and the rewrite had to keep that: indexing the
        label array and casting gives `int(nan)` = `-9223372036854775808`, which
        `ZoneSpec.__post_init__`'s NaN guard cannot see and pyEMU calibrates like
        any other id. A NULL integer attribute is what `gpd.read_file` hands back as
        `nan` from a real `.gpkg`, so this is a file away, not a contrivance. The row
        keeps its POSITION (so `labels` still lines up) but is handed no geometry,
        which the shared rule never matches -- measured `[0]*4 + [2]*12` where the
        naive rewrite gave `[-9223372036854775808]*8 + [2]*8`. Found by an
        adversarial review of this entry's own first draft, which is why it is
        recorded here rather than in the NOT-done list.
      - **A polygon zone layer that reaches NO cell now warns**, with both extents
        and both CRSs (the shared `where_they_are` wording, ledger 211). It is a
        warning and not a refusal because `nodata_zone` is a legitimate "leave
        alone" id, but silence was wrong: for ARRAY targets (`k`, `k33`,
        `porosity` -- the headline zone use) `resolve_zone_array` returns before its
        zone-0 warning, so an all-nodata map parameterized nothing and said nothing
        -- a frame with `crs=None` that is really in another CRS gets no
        reprojection and lands exactly there. A PARTIAL miss stays silent: most zone
        layers cover part of a model on purpose. A test pins the silence as well as
        the warning.
      - **The array and raster routes do not move**, verified value for value:
        `from_array` is untouched, and `from_raster` majority-votes pixels with a
        centroid fallback (ledger 213) and asks no polygon predicate anywhere -- a
        test pins its output and a source probe pins the absence. A raster label
        boundary cannot be made to run along a centroid line without halving the
        cell, which is a majority TIE rather than a predicate question.
      - **Nothing in the repo's own expectations moved.** `test_pest_zones.py`
        splits its polygons at the middle of the canonical grid's bounds, which no
        centroid sits on (had one, the pre-fix `spec.ids` would already have
        carried the nodata label and that test would have been failing); the
        canonical PEST notebooks zone by raster or array. 1158 tests across the
        zone, surface, layer, geometry, coverage-rule and PEST modules pass
        unchanged. The swap is also not a cost but a saving: on 10,000 cells x 50 band
        zones the old `sjoin(within)` measured 10.9 ms per resolve against the shared
        rule's 5.2 ms (min of three, one process; a separate run measured 9 and 4).
      - **NOT done.** `_cells_in_zone` keeps its `union_all()` of a multi-row vector
        file -- one zone, no labels, so there is no row order to be deterministic
        about; a test now pins the union rather than leaving the choice untested.
        `_cells_in_zone` also does not warn when a zone reaches nothing: it answers
        a mask that a `Surface` pairs with an `outside=` value, so an empty zone is
        a whole-grid `outside`, not an absence. Two candidate mutants turned out
        EQUIVALENT and were dropped rather than reported as survivors: filtering
        null/empty geometry rows inside the shared rule, and short-circuiting an
        empty zone set -- shapely's index matches neither a `None` nor an empty
        geometry and accepts an empty query array, so the filter came out of the
        first draft and the early return is kept only because it saves building
        centroids and an index for nothing. A third, the review's own R7 (the
        reduction rewritten as last-write-wins over reversed pairs), is equivalent
        given that shapely returns its pairs sorted by input index -- the first-row
        PROPERTY is pinned, its independence from query order is not.
      - `tests/import_layers.json` and `docs/import_layering.md` are derived and
        move three modules a layer DEEPER: `pest.zones` 0 -> 2 (it now imports
        `grid.geometry`), and with it `pest.native_parameters` 1 -> 3 and
        `pest.pilot_points` 2 -> 4. Until they are regenerated
        `test_import_layering.py` reads the new import as pointing UPWARD and fails;
        `tests/deferred_import_allowlist.json`, `tests/api_snapshot.json` and the
        docstring splice are all unchanged.
      - Twenty-two mutants and an import probe, all killed: the strict interior
        restored, the shared edge given to the last row, the tie left to the index's
        order, no-zone reading as row 0, the unmatched sentinel counted as a match, a
        GeoDataFrame not unwrapped to its geometry, the cell POLYGON in the tree
        instead of its centroid, the touch rule on those polygons, the query pair
        unpacked the other way round, row 0's cells dropped, zones no longer
        reprojected, zones and cells swapped at the call, labels read one row off,
        the whole PEST route reverted to its sjoin copy, the missing label cast
        anyway, the missing label never detected, the nothing-landed warning
        silenced, that warning fired on a partial miss, that warning without its
        extents-and-CRS sentence, the surface mask back on `within` and with its
        first zone dropped, and a multi-row zone file reduced to its first row. Six
        of these are an adversarial review's own mutants, one of which survived the
        first version of these tests.
      - Found by the 2026-09-11 sibling investigation.

244. **A USG export chained cells that shared only a corner (2026-09-12).**
      `usg/export._adjacency` asked the spatial index for `predicate="touches"`,
      which is true of a shared edge and equally true of a single shared vertex.
      The chain it builds is what decides every exported `length_ft` and every
      `*_per_ft` twin, so on a structured or quadtree mesh -- both of which
      MODFLOW-USG writes and a `.gsf` describes -- the lengths were wrong wherever
      a feature ran diagonally. Measured on a 4x4 mesh of 25 ft cells, one DRN
      record of 100.0 per cell:
      - a **diagonal staircase** `[0, 1, 5, 6, 10, 11]` -- what a diagonal drain on
        a structured grid actually is, every step a real shared face -- walked
        `[0, 1, 5, 10, 11, 6]` with two corner jumps and measured **145.71 ft**
        where it occupies 125.0, three of its six segments 30.18 ft long inside a
        25 ft cell, `conductance_per_ft` 3.3137 where a straight run gives 4.00;
      - the **pure diagonal** `[0, 5, 10, 15]`, which shares no face at all, came
        back as ONE chain of **106.07 ft** against the 75.0 four such cells span,
        with `per_ft` 5.66/2.83/2.83/5.66;
      - the **2x2 block** `[0, 1, 4, 5]` came back a **clique** (every cell
        neighbouring all three others), so the walk stepped 1 -> 4 across the
        corner at (25, 25): 12.5/30.18/30.18/12.5 = **85.36 ft**, `per_ft` 3.31 on
        two of four. A 30.18 ft segment inside a 25 ft cell is the defect in one
        number.
      - **Adjacency is now a shared FACE**, through `grid.shared_face` -- the rule
        the HFB views already resolve a barrier's own face against, so no second
        copy of it was written. It agrees pair-for-pair with the older
        `adjacent_cells_idx` on every mesh measured (16-cell square; 441-cell
        irregular Voronoi, 2,494 pairs, 0 differences) while additionally handling
        a face interrupted into a MultiLineString -- measured, an 11 ft contact a
        bare `isinstance(intersection, LineString)` calls no contact at all -- and
        a face tolerance. The spatial index now only PROPOSES: the prefilter is
        `intersects` rather than `touches` because `touches` excludes a pair whose
        polygons overlap, which a degenerate mesh produces; `shared_face` decides,
        and on a 1e-3 overlap it says adjacent while reporting the 1e-3 sliver
        rather than the 25 ft contact -- right for this adjacency, worth knowing
        for anything that uses the segment. The same cases now give: the staircase
        in order at **125.0 ft** with `per_ft` 8/4/4/4/4/8 and no NaN, the diagonal
        as four one-cell chains, the block as a RING (75.0 ft, `per_ft` 4.00 --
        what four cells in a straight line give), the straight run `[0, 1, 2, 3]`
        unchanged at 75.0 and 8/4/4/8, and a quadtree coarse cell keeping both fine
        cells against its face while dropping the one diagonally off its corner
        (`{0: [1, 2]}`, was `{0: [1, 2, 3]}`).
      - **Nothing moves on a Voronoi mesh, which is why this survived ledger 169.**
        Over the canonical 441-cell irregular Voronoi grid the two rules are
        identical: 2,494 directed pairs each, 0 differing in either direction, mean
        degree 5.655 both ways -- a Voronoi vertex is 3-valent, so a corner-only
        contact is degenerate. The neighbour counts ledger 169 rests on (1.87 DRN /
        1.94 GHB / 2.52 CHD) therefore stand, and a re-export of Ten Trails is
        unchanged. `test_usg_export.py`'s expectations do not move either: its DRN
        runs along one row, and a straight run is the case that was always right.
      - **The documented rebuild does not break; the per-foot hand recipe does.**
        Reading the written `*_lines` layer back the way the manifest says --
        `mf.drn.gpkg(..., conductance=mf.Spread("conductance"))` -- recovers the
        feature total EXACTLY before and after, on the same mesh and on a 4x finer
        one (400.0 / 600.0 / 500.0 on all four shapes). What changes is which cells
        it occupies: the diagonal goes from 400.0 spread over 12 fine cells along a
        path MODFLOW never connected to 4 records on the cells that actually hold
        the old centres, and the staircase from 30 fine cells to 36.
      - **A cell alone on its chain is now REPORTED, not silent.** It keeps the
        degenerate line `_segment_line` has always given a lone cell -- `length_ft`
        0, and a NaN `*_per_ft` where the package has one -- and `pandas.sum` skips
        NaN, so the README's `per_ft x length` check reads a smaller total rather
        than failing. So the export counts them, logs a `logger.warning`, and
        writes `cells_alone_on_a_chain` plus a manifest note pointing at the POINT
        layer, which is exact for one cell. Two things the sentence had to get
        right: the count is of one-cell CHAINS, because a cell can be alone on its
        chain and still share a face -- a **branch arm the open walk could not
        extend through** lands there (a plus-cross `[1, 4, 5, 6, 9]` leaves two,
        both face-sharing with the centre) -- and the `*_per_ft` clause appears
        only where an extensive column exists, which **CHD has not** (`_EXTENSIVE`
        is `{cond, q}`; CHD carries heads), CHD being the most branched package
        ledger 169 measured at 2.52.
      - **Which direction the report moves is shape-dependent, and the loss it
        exposes is older than this change.** On a 20x20 mesh, a 12-cell spine with
        4 one-cell spurs: HEAD 2 cells alone and 1400.0 of 1600.0 recovered from
        the twin, now 3 and 1300.0. With 2 spurs it goes the other way -- HEAD 2
        alone and 1200.0 of 1400.0, now **0 and 1400.0**, the invariant restored.
        The corner links did not only lengthen a chain; they gave the open walk
        shortcuts that stranded face-connected cells. HEAD already lost 100.0 of
        500.0 on a 2x2 block with one cell hanging off it, silently: what is new
        is the warning.
      - **NOT done: no geometry is invented for a lone cell.** Giving it a real
        line means choosing a length AND a direction for a feature that occupies
        one cell -- the cell's mean width is available, the direction is not, and
        the only non-arbitrary direction (toward the corner-touching cells) would
        reintroduce as geometry exactly the connection just refused as adjacency.
        That is a design call about what a one-cell feature MEANS, so it is
        reported instead. Nor was `_chains`' arbitrary walk order pinned (a ring
        has no ends, so `component[0]` starts it and a set's iteration order picks
        the direction); the tests assert every step of a walk is a real shared face
        rather than an exact sequence. `_chains`' leftover recursion -- a
        pre-existing approximation of a branched feature -- is untouched.
      - **Cost: 3.3 ms -> 22.3 ms** for `_adjacency` on a 200-cell BC over a
        10,000-cell structured grid (3.5 -> 24.0 ms for the whole `_chains` build),
        paid once per package per layer per export. The prefilter keeps the work on
        the subset rather than reaching for the grid's full cached adjacency, which
        would walk all 10,000 cells to answer about 200.
      - Also fixed in passing: the README the export WRITES told the reader to read
        layer `drn_segments` and multiply `drn.cond_per_ft`. The export writes
        `drn_lines` and `conductance_per_ft`, so the recipe raised `KeyError` on
        both names.
      - 24 tests in `tests/test_usg_export_adjacency.py`, 21 of which fail at HEAD
        (13 of those reach `_adjacency`/`_chains` through the new grid argument, so
        at HEAD they fail on the call as well as on the answer). They build the mesh
        and a one-layer `UsgModel` by hand, so no MODFLOW-USG model is written and
        CI needs none. Twenty-one mutants and an import probe, all killed: the face
        test dropped (the `touches` bug restored), inverted, replaced by each of the
        two hand-rolled copies, taken as a length with `>= 0` so a corner's zero
        passes; self-pairs unskipped; neighbours recorded as subset positions; the
        prefilter narrowed to `contains`; the recursion and `_bc_frames` each handed
        the polygon frame again; a one-cell leftover DROPPED, which loses a BC
        record silently; a lone cell given an invented 1 ft line; and on the report
        side the count flipped, taken on the point frame, the warning's two counts
        swapped, a per-foot twin promised where there is none, the branch cause
        struck from the note leaving a false claim, the warning demoted to debug,
        the note dropped, the count dropped, and the report emitted
        unconditionally. Two mutants are recorded as EQUIVALENT and expected to
        survive: dropping the prefilter (same answer, O(n^2) face tests) and
        counting zero-length rows instead of one-cell chains (equal on every frame
        this writes -- counting chains is what makes the sentence about them true
        rather than accidentally true).
      - **Entry 237 deferred this site by name** ("and `usg/export._adjacency`
        still uses `touches`; both are their own sites"); that clause is struck
        above, and `LAKBuilder.lake_cells` remains the one it still names.
      - Found by the 2026-09-11 sibling investigation.

245. **Two public grid selectors took any touch, one answered about EPSG:2927 whatever frame the grid was in, and under an explicit predicate the pair asked opposite questions (2026-09-12).**
      `vor.get_vor_idx_from_geometry` and `vor.get_vor_idx_from_geometry_idx`
      (`grid/geometry.py`, forwarded from `VoronoiGridPlus`) are the "which cells
      does this shape pick?" pair a user's own script reaches for. Both asked the
      spatial index with a bare `intersects`, and the first also forced
      `crs=DEFAULT_CRS` and then compared in EPSG:4326. Measured on the 4x4 grid of
      25 ft cells, and on the same grid built in EPSG:32610:
      - a polygon that was exactly cell 5 came back as **9 cells** from both,
        `[0, 1, 2, 4, 5, 6, 8, 9, 10]`;
      - a point on the vertex shared by 5, 6, 9 and 10 came back as **all four**;
      - a point on the face between 4 and 5 had the two **disagreeing**: `[4, 5]`
        from the index one, taking both cells, against `[5]` from the dict one, which
        reached that through 2927 and then 4326 -- right by accident, on rounding;
      - on the **UTM grid** the cell-5 polygon came back as `[4, 5, 8, 9]` from the
        dict one -- a frame the grid was never in, one cell of four of them right --
        and as the same 9 cells from the other;
      - the reprojection detour **dropped** cells as well as adding them: a line
        running the length of the face between rows 0 and 1 came back from the dict
        one as `[0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 7]`, having lost 5 and 6 outright, where the rule
        gives all eight; and a corner-to-corner diagonal came back as 7 cells there
        and as 10 from the index one, against a true 4;
      - a query in any CRS **other than the grid's** (a cell-5 polygon handed over
        in degrees) came back **EMPTY** from the index one, degrees measured against
        feet, and as six cells from the dict one;
      - a query carrying **no CRS** raised `Cannot transform naive geometries` from
        the dict one, while the index one answered its 9 cells -- it never looked at
        a CRS at all;
      - a **filtered** frame -- `gdf.iloc[[2]]`, label 2 -- raised `IndexError:
        single positional indexer is out-of-bounds`, because keys were taken by
        label and rows by position.
      - **An explicit `predicate=` was two different questions under one name.** A
        predicate is asked of a PAIR, and the two functions handed the spatial index
        its sides opposite ways round: the dict one asked `predicate(cell, feature)`,
        which is what `get_vor_cells_as_series`' own `sjoin` asks, and the index one
        asked `predicate(feature, cell)`. Measured with a box strictly inside cell 5:
        `predicate='contains'` gave `[5]` from the dict one and the selector, and
        `[]` from the index one. The symmetric default hid it for years. Fixing this
        onto the INDEX one's orientation would have inverted a public answer and left
        two grid selectors disagreeing about one word, so both now ask it the
        selector's way, of the cell first.
      - **Both go through the shared rule now** (`cell_shares`, ledger 232, with
        `selected_cells` flattening the single-row answer): a polygon reaches the
        cells it COVERS by area, a line those it runs through, a point the one cell
        holding it. `predicate=` still asks for the raw index answer, as the
        selector's does, and the two now agree on an asymmetric one: over a box
        holding cells 5, 6, 9 and 10, `predicate='within'` gave `[5]` from the dict
        function (the lat/lon detour bulging three cells out of the box that
        contained them) against the selector's `[5, 6, 9, 10]`, which is what both
        answer now.
      - **`_idx` asks its sibling for that one row**, so the two cannot drift apart
        again. That is what makes a point on a face one answer instead of two.
      - **The grid decides where a cell is.** No forced CRS: a query carrying one is
        reprojected to the grid's, a query carrying none is read as the grid's.
        `crs=` defaults to None and keeps the only job it has left -- naming the
        frame of a query that carries none, a file of degrees with no CRS written
        into it. Passed **alongside** a query that carries its own frame it cannot
        act, so it warns instead of being dropped in silence; naming the frame the
        query already has is redundant, not wrong, and stays quiet.
      - **`to_grid_crs` is that reconcile, extracted into `grid/geometry.py`** beside
        the other shared rules, and `get_vor_cells_as_series` delegates to it: its
        inline block was the only copy, and these two would have been the second and
        third. It returns a NEW object rather than stamping a frame on the caller's,
        which the in-place `geometries.crs = ...` did through the `.geometry` view it
        was handed -- measured: a naive GeoDataFrame handed to the selector came back
        carrying `EPSG:2927`, and now comes back as it went in. Nothing in the suite
        or in `examples/` depended on the write-through, but a script that wrote that
        frame out afterwards was getting a georeferenced file by side effect.
      - **`crs_latlon` was the comparison frame and has no job left.** It stays in the
        signature so an existing call still works, and REFUSES any other value rather
        than being accepted and ignored -- a parameter that cannot act. Measuring in
        degrees over a grid in feet is the defect, not a setting. It is read as a
        CRS, not compared as a string: `4326` is an int geopandas accepts and did
        accept here, and a string test would have refused the default value spelled
        another way.
      - **A miss keeps its key**, with an empty list, which is the shape this always
        returned and what a caller's dict comprehension indexes; it is named in a
        warning with its reason from `miss_reason`. When EVERY feature misses, the
        warning carries `where_they_are`'s extents-and-CRS sentence -- the failure
        this site actually produced was a CRS mismatch, and "outside the grid" for
        every feature is not the diagnosis, two boxes and two CRSs are. The selector
        leaves such a feature out instead, and that is the one difference left
        between them -- flattened, the two agree on every input, including a miss.
      - **A plain `pandas.DataFrame` with a `geometry` column is coerced**, not
        refused: it reached the index function and answered (9 cells, any touch), so
        routing both through geopandas' CRS machinery would have broken a caller that
        worked, with `AttributeError: 'Series' object has no attribute 'set_crs'` a
        couple of frames from the call. A query with no geometry at all is named the
        way the selector names a bad `overlapping_geometry`.
      - **Nothing in the repo depended on the old answers**: neither function has an
        internal caller. The only in-repo assertions on them, in
        `test_mf6_refactor_smoke.py`, are an interior point and a polygon covering
        two whole cells, which the measured rule answers identically.
      - **NOT done, deliberately: deprecating either name.** Pointing both at
        `get_vor_cells_as_series` is the obvious follow-up -- between them they add
        only a dict keyed by a name column and a flat single-row answer, and the
        selector with `selected_cells` covers both -- but deprecating a public,
        documented method is the user's call, not this fix's. For the same reason the
        two dead parameters stay in the signature (`crs_latlon` refused, `crs`
        narrowed), and `_idx` gains no `crs=` of its own, so a naive query there is
        read as the grid's frame rather than one it can name.
      - **Also not done**: vectorising the measured rule (ledger 235's cost note
        stands); the rest of the list entry 232 left -- `pest/zones.py`,
        `surfaces._cells_in_zone`, `PRTReleasePoints.from_points` and the demo site's
        `_cells_for`; and one defect found in passing and left where it is --
        `get_vor_cells_as_series(predicate=...)` whose join matches NOTHING returns an
        empty GeoDataFrame rather than the documented per-feature Series, so
        `selected_cells` on it raises `ValueError: invalid literal for int() with base
        10: 'geometry'`. That is `selection.py`'s predicate branch, not this site, and
        other drafts are landing in that file.
      - 48 tests in `tests/test_vor_idx_selection.py`, every expectation worked out
        from row/column arithmetic; the four entry points are asked the same question
        and compared with each other and with the shared selector, including under
        two predicates that are each other's inverse. Twenty-six mutants and an
        import probe, all killed: each default flipped back at all four entry points,
        the predicate asked the old way round, the answer left in the grid frame's own
        order, row positions returned as cell ids, the reconcile skipped, the
        reprojection dropped or silenced, the assumed frame ignored or ignored
        silently, a naive query left naive, a plain frame left uncoerced, keys taken
        by position, the `crs_latlon` guard removed or reduced to a string compare,
        the escape hatch disabled, the single-row answer left nested, the miss warning
        silenced, truncated or stripped of its extents sentence, the wrong miss
        target, and the shared selector's own delegation cut.
      - Found by the 2026-09-11 sibling investigation.

246. **`edges_only=` on a GeoPackage source could not see the model's own idomain (2026-09-13).**
      `GeoPackageSource._edge_set` called `self.grid.get_grid_edge()` with **no
      argument**, so the only active domain that ever reached the edge test was the
      one a grid happened to carry as its own `idomain_path`. A
      `ModelContext(domain=...)` array -- the documented package-first route, and
      what `LayerStack` produces -- was never consulted, even though the very same
      class already honours it per cell in `_active`. So `mf.chd/ghb/drn.gpkg(...,
      edges_only=True)` asked about the GEOMETRIC rim of the mesh while every other
      question it asked was about the ACTIVE domain.
      Ledger 236 had already settled what an edge cell is: a cell bordering the
      outside of the mesh, **or one whose face-neighbour is inactive**. That fix
      landed in `get_grid_edge_cells`; this caller never passed it the domain, so
      for a `.gpkg` source the fix did nothing. Measured on a 5x5 grid of 25 ft
      cells with one inactive cell:
      - the package wrote **16 cells** where the active-domain edge is **20** --
        the four face-neighbours of the hole, silently missing, so a CHD boundary
        drawn around an active area stopped at the outer ring and left the hole's
        rim open;
      - with the **outer ring** inactive instead, the intersection of the geometric
        rim with the active set is EMPTY, so the source was **refused outright**
        (ledger 211's "no feature lands on an active grid-edge cell") on a model
        whose active edge is its nine interior cells. A correct request looked like
        a mislocated file.
      - the only workaround was `vor.idomain_path = Path(...)`, an undocumented
        back-channel on the grid, and it needed a vector file even when the domain
        was already in hand as an array.
      **The edge is now resolved per LAYER**, because activity is: `_active` is
      per-layer, so an edge that was not made every `edges_only` answer wrong in
      any model whose layers differ. Two features in two layers now get two
      different edges from one source. The cache is keyed by layer for the reason
      it existed at all -- `get_grid_edge` walks every cell, and a ten-feature
      source used to pay for that ten times -- so the cost is one walk per distinct
      layer used, not per feature.
      **The context's domain WINS over the grid's `idomain_path`** when both exist:
      it is the model's declared domain, the same precedence `specs._layer_elevations`
      settled for surfaces in ledger 209. With no context domain nothing is passed,
      so a grid built from an idomain file keeps working exactly as before -- that
      is the compatibility seam, and it is tested.
      NOT done, deliberately: no warning when a context domain and a grid
      `idomain_path` disagree. Ledger 209 warns on that class of conflict for
      elevations, but detecting it here means running `_inactive_from_file` -- a
      full selector pass over the grid -- purely to compare, on every source that
      has both, which is the cost `_edge_set` caches to avoid. The precedence is
      documented on the method instead.
      `tests/test_gpkg_edges_only_domain.py` (11 tests) pins the hole ring, the
      corner-only exclusion (a shared vertex is not a shared face), the inactive
      outer ring, the per-layer edge, a flat `(ncpl,)` domain, a `-1` passthrough
      cell as a hole, both precedence directions, one walk per layer, and that a
      layer past the domain still names itself. Seven mutants, all killed.

247. **A GeoPackage NULL became a non-finite number in a written MF6 package, by two routes (2026-09-13).**
      Found while auditing the legacy builders for deprecation, as the one thing
      `KFromVector`'s `fillna` did that the modern path did not.
      - **`GeoPackageSource.k_array`** did `result[layer, cell] = float(row[value])`.
        A null `k` attribute reads back as `None` or NaN, and `float()` of either is
        NaN, so the zone painted **NaN into the K array**, which reached `mf.npf` and
        a written NPF with no non-finite guard anywhere between. Measured on a 4x4
        grid, one zone with a real K and one with a null: cell 5 = `nan`, where the
        legacy `KFromVector.to_array` gave 1.0 (its `fillna` per layer, kflow.py).
      - **Every list BC** -- `_value` returned `_period_value(row, field, period)`
        raw, so a null stayed `None` all the way into the record. Measured: a GHB
        with null head and conductance produced `[(0, 0), None, None, 'a']`, and
        numpy casts that `None` to NaN when FloPy builds the recarray. So a NaN head
        or conductance is written, and MF6 answers a **NaN budget while reporting
        Normal termination** -- the same failure mode as the State Plane precision
        loss in ledger 159, and as hard to attribute.
      Both are guarded by one function now, `_finite`, at the single point every
      resolved value passes through, so chd/ghb/drn/riv/wel/rch/evt and `k_array`
      cannot disagree about it. It refuses a null, a NaN, an infinity, a string and a
      bool (`bool` is an `int` subclass, and `True` is not an elevation), and the
      error names the feature as a user would recognise it, the field, and what was
      found. `_field_name` spells out which field: a `Spread` says `(spread)`, a
      per-period list names every column, and a `CellSurfaceOffset` names the OFFSET
      and MINIMUM columns it read rather than the surface reference -- a null offset
      is what makes that sum non-finite, and blaming `cell_bottom` would send the
      reader to the wrong place.
      **AMENDED by ledger 289: that last claim was only half true.** A NULL reaching the
      surface SUM through `offset` was named; the `minimum` column was never checked at
      all, so a NULL there came back `nan`, `max(value, nan)` returned the UNFLOORED
      value, and the result was finite -- so this guard passed and the floor silently did
      not exist. Both columns go through `_finite` now, and the message names which of
      `offset=`/`minimum=` was empty as well as the column.
      **Refusing rather than defaulting is a deliberate divergence from the legacy
      behaviour.** `KFromVector` substituted the layer default for a null; that is a
      guess at a number the user never supplied, and it makes a mis-typed zone
      invisible rather than loud. A feature that ALSO lands nowhere still reports the
      MISS (ledger 211), because location explains more than the null does -- which
      needed its own test in `k_array`: a mutant dropping that `continue` survived
      the list-BC version of the test, since `_boundary_data` already skipped a
      missed feature and `k_array` did not.
      NOT done: `KFromVector`'s `defaults=None`, which leaves unpainted cells NaN so
      you can SEE what the zones missed. It is a real capability with no modern
      spelling (`k_array`'s `defaults` is required), but it is the OPPOSITE of this
      entry's rule and does not belong in a commit whose premise is refusing
      non-finite values. It stays on the gap list from the deprecation audit.
      `tests/test_gpkg_null_values.py` (17 tests) pins both routes, each refused
      type, the per-field message, the miss precedence in both loops, and the
      controls that an int, a scalar and a real K still pass. Nine mutants, all
      killed.

248. **A cell the raster gave no value for came back as a bare NaN, with nothing said (2026-09-13).**
      Reported from a real remap: copying initial heads from one model onto a
      different DISV grid, one cell of ~18,000 sampled to NaN, and the only way the
      user found out was by looking. They patched it by hand
      (`strt_sampled.loc[17832] = strt_sampled.loc[18205]`). Nothing was wrong with
      the patch; the problem is that `get_raster_vals_at_centroids` returns a frame
      whose NaN is indistinguishable from a real value until MF6 reports success and
      hands back a NaN budget.
      **The root cause is structural, not a fluke.** `InterpolatedSurface` builds its
      raster with `scipy.griddata(..., method='cubic')` and **no `fill_value`**, so
      the result is NaN everywhere outside the **convex hull of the input points** --
      and the input points are the source grid's CELL CENTROIDS. A model's outer
      cells extend past their own centroids, so such a raster is blank in a rim about
      half a cell wide around the entire footprint. Every boundary cell of a
      different grid can land in it. One cell was luck; a different mesh gives dozens.
      (`_area_weighted_sample` already falls back to the centroid for a cell holding
      no pixel CENTRE, which is why only the truly-off-the-data cells survived.)
      `gaps=` now says what to do, and defaults to being loud:
      - `"warn"` (default) keeps the NaN and warns, naming the count, the column and
        the first ten cells, and saying what a NaN does to an MF6 run;
      - `"nearest"` takes each gap from its nearest valued cell by centroid distance
        (a `cKDTree` over the cells that have values) and logs how many and which --
        the library doing what the reporter did by hand;
      - `"raise"` refuses;
      - `"ignore"` keeps the NaN silently.
      **`"ignore"` exists because gaps are legitimate mid-pipeline, and `Surface.sample`
      passes it.** A raster covering part of a model is normal for a layer surface:
      `Surface(fill="propagate")` inherits the rest from the surface above and the
      pinch-out rules turn what is left into idomain. Warning per cell there would
      have made the default useless through noise, which is the usual way a warning
      like this dies. `get_gdf_topbtm_multilyr` deliberately does NOT opt out -- a NaN
      in `gdf_topbtm` is a NaN cell elevation.
      **A raster that covers NO cell raises**, reporting both extents and both CRSs
      the way an off-grid vector source does (ledger 211) -- but only when the two
      extents are actually **disjoint**. An all-no-data column where the extents DO
      overlap is a blank raster, not a misplaced one, and gets the ordinary report:
      the first version claimed a location mismatch for both, which sent a one-cell
      test grid sitting on a single no-data pixel looking for a CRS bug. `_disjoint`
      answers "no" whenever it cannot know (a missing CRS, a transform that fails),
      because its only job is to decide whether to make that stronger claim.
      Also fixed, and the reason `gaps=` would otherwise have been unreachable from
      the scope a user samples from: `VoronoiGridPlus.get_raster_vals_at_centroids`
      forwarded **neither `method=` nor `nodata=`**, so the grid method could not ask
      for centroid sampling or override an undeclared sentinel either.
      NOT done: `InterpolatedSurface` still writes a hull-limited raster. Extrapolating
      past the hull is a modelling choice (nearest, or an RBF that runs away), and the
      honest fix for remapping between grids is not a raster at all -- it is an area
      overlay on the source grid's own cell POLYGONS, which has no hull and no rim.
      That is Phase 2's `sim.with_grid`/`import_run` work, and this entry is the
      stopgap that makes the rim visible until then.
      `tests/test_raster_sampling_gaps.py` (16 tests) pins each mode, the per-column
      independence, the constant-column exemption, both all-no-data branches, the two
      forwarded parameters, the `Surface` opt-out, and the interpolated-rim case end
      to end. Ten mutants, all killed.

249. **A model built against a grid its packages had never seen ran anyway (2026-09-13).**
      Phase 2 commit **A1**, the first of the reconciled plan. `SimulationSpec.replace_grid`
      swaps a model's grid and leaves every package's baked cellids, connection data and
      dimension counts on the old mesh -- and nothing anywhere looked. `ModelSpec.build`
      resolved the grid, built the packages, and returned, with no cross-check between the
      two. MF6 then applied the previous grid's cell numbers to the new geometry and
      reported **Normal termination**. Measured on that path (2026-09-10): a lazy CHD
      raised `IndexError` on a finer grid and resolved to **zero cells** on a coarser one,
      and a lazy disv beside one eager `drn.gpkg` ran the DRN on the old grid's cell
      numbers.
      `_discretization_complaints` now runs at the end of `ModelSpec.build` and raises
      listing EVERY disagreement at once -- one build, one error, rather than one fix per
      rebuild. It compares the built DISV's `ncpl`, its `nvert`, and its cell centres
      against the context grid; the context `domain`'s shape in cells AND in layers; and
      every leading cellid in each enabled package's `stress_period_data` against
      `nlay`/`ncpl`.
      **The cell-centre comparison was wrong twice before it was right, and an
      adversarial review caught the second one.**
      - A Voronoi cell's DISV centre is **not** its polygon centroid: measured **38.9
        length units apart** on one 4x4 grid, so comparing `cell2d` against
        `vor.centroids` fires on every model ever built. The comparison is against the
        grid's own `get_disv_gridprops()` instead -- the same definition on both sides,
        measured exactly 0.0 on a match.
      - A converted model's frame is deliberately **not** the world's:
        `to_mf6(local_origin=True)` shifts to a local origin because MF6 loses DISV
        conductance precision on State Plane coordinates (ledgers 159, 218), so the
        synthetic USG fixture's centres sit **1.34e+06 length units** from its grid's.
        Five `test_prt_offset.py` tests failed on the first version.
      - The fix for that was **sorted distances from each cloud's own centroid**, chosen
        to survive rotation as well as translation -- and sorting threw away the one
        thing a cellid means. **A renumbered mesh passed it.** Measured by the review on
        a 10x10 grid: a permuted `cell2d` moved the mean cell **509.4 length units** and
        the worst **1106.0**, every package cellid pointed somewhere else, and the build
        was clean. Mirroring and an x/y axis swap passed for the same reason. The
        comparison is now **index-aligned after removing each cloud's own centroid**,
        which is exactly translation-invariant -- so the local-origin case still passes --
        and is not order-invariant. Rotation between `cell2d` and the grid is not a shape
        this toolkit produces (the local-origin shift only translates, and `angrot` lives
        in the DISV options rather than in `cell2d`), so nothing was bought with that
        blind spot.
      - **The tolerance is a thousandth of a CELL, not an absolute distance.** A fixed
        1e-3 refused the same mesh written to a hundredth of a foot (centres move 0.005)
        and a float32 rendering at State Plane (the float32 step is already ~0.06 there),
        while on a grid in DEGREES the same number is ~110 m and a genuinely displaced
        mesh passed. The scale comes from the data: `sqrt(extent_area / ncpl)`.
      **A guard must not become the error it exists to prevent**, and four ways it did
      were found by review, each reproduced:
      - `int(disv.nvert.get_data())` raised `TypeError` on a DISV that leaves NVERT to
        FloPy -- which FloPy computes at write time, so the model is correct and the
        written file says `NVERT 34` while `get_data()` is `None`;
      - `props['nvert']` raised `KeyError` on a grid whose gridprops omit it, which
        FloPy's own `get_gridprops_vertexgrid()` does;
      - `int(grid_ncpl)` raised `TypeError` on a grid whose `ncpl` is per-layer, as a
        FloPy `UnstructuredGrid`'s is;
      - a **disabled** package was still scanned, so a package that never reached the
        model blocked the build.
      Every dimension is read through `_as_int`, which answers `None` rather than raising,
      and each comparison is skipped when either side is unknown.
      **The `context.surfaces` check was REMOVED rather than fixed.** It keyed on
      `.shape[0]` meaning "rows are cells", and `surfaces` is documented loosely -- "
      `vor.gdf_topbtm` or equivalent" -- so it legitimately arrives as a frame, a
      `LayerBuildResult`, or an array laid out `(nlay, ncpl)`. The check refused
      documented values with a message about a table, and there is no reliable invariant
      to replace it with. `specs._layer_elevations` is where surfaces are interpreted and
      where a disagreement belongs.
      **Deliberate limits, each a reason rather than an oversight:**
      - **A stale cellid that still falls inside a LARGER new grid is not caught.** A
        range check cannot see it. The grid PIN in commit A2 -- a hash of the mesh a
        package's cell numbers refer to -- closes it, and this entry is explicitly the
        decidable half. `test_a_refined_swap_is_the_documented_gap` pins the gap so that
        making it raise later is a deliberate change with its own entry.
      - **Advanced packages are not cellid-checked.** `_cellids_in` reads a record's
        LEADING tuples of ints -- one for a list BC, two for an HFB, which sits on a face
        between a pair -- and stops at the first non-cellid element, so it never reaches
        the value fields. It does not walk `packagedata`/`connectiondata`, where the
        position differs per package: SFR's `packagedata[1]` is a cellid, LAK's is a
        stage, and SFR's `connectiondata` holds reach numbers that would read as cells.
      - **A package attached by a post-build HOOK is not checked.** The guard runs before
        the hooks so that a stale grid is reported by name rather than as whatever a hook
        raises first, and a hook attaches FloPy objects directly rather than as specs, so
        its cellids are outside what this can read.
      - **DIS and DISU are not checked**: `ncpl` is a DISV concept.
      - **A `(1, ncpl)` domain on a multi-layer model is refused** even though the flat
        `(ncpl,)` spelling of the same intent is accepted. That reads as inconsistent
        until you read `domain_active`: a two-dimensional domain is indexed per layer and
        raises for any layer past its rows, so a one-row domain on a three-layer model is
        broken for every consumer. Refusing it here reports it once, by name, instead of
        deferring it to whichever package asks first.
      - **`ValueError`, not a named exception**, so A1 adds no public name and needs no
        `api_snapshot` regeneration. A named error can arrive with the pin.
      **Docs corrected, and one of them was actively dangerous.** `docs/project_workflow.md`
      and `docs/manual/04_architecture.md` both stated that GIS-driven packages "re-map onto
      whatever grid resolves, because they are evaluated against the model grid at build
      time". They are not: every `.gpkg` helper resolves its cells at DECLARATION. So the
      docs promised precisely the operation that silently produced a wrong model, with a
      tip recommending it. Both now say nothing re-maps, that a stale swap is refused, and
      that lazy resolution is planned work. Nine retired `with_package` / `replace_package`
      spellings were corrected across five files at the same time; the occurrences in this
      ledger and in CLAUDE.md are the historical record of ledger 204 and stay.
      `tests/test_build_grid_consistency.py` (33 tests) pins all four reproductions, the
      renumbering, mirroring, rounded-coordinate and float32 cases, both defensive reads,
      the disabled package, a bare-list `stress_period_data`, both halves of a barrier
      pair, the reader stopping before the value fields, the cap-and-count message, both
      context-domain shapes, and a model with no DISV at all. Twenty-one mutants, all
      killed -- one of which is the sorted-radii version itself, so the renumbering hole
      cannot reopen unnoticed.

250. **A package resolved on one mesh and built on another was only caught when the numbers went out of range (2026-09-13).**
      Phase 2 commit **A2**. Ledger 249 range-checks cellids against the built grid, which
      is decidable but partial: a package resolved on a SMALL grid and rebuilt on a LARGER
      one has every cellid in range and every one naming a different cell. That case built
      and ran, and 249 pinned the gap in a test rather than hiding it. This closes it for
      the seven `.gpkg` list BCs. (**AMENDED 2026-09-14:** this entry said "for every
      package the library resolved itself", which was false -- `mf.rch(context=)` and
      `mf.evt(context=)` resolve per-cell records through `RCHBuilder`, not
      `GeoPackageSource`, and carried no pin: built on a 36-cell grid, recharge landed on
      the wrong 16 cells and MF6 ran to completion. `mf.sfr`, `mf.lak` and `mf.uzf` were
      deferred by name here and were equally unprotected. Ledger 264 pins all of them
      through one shared `pin_metadata`.)
      `grid_pin(grid)` fingerprints a mesh's **connectivity** -- the cell count and each
      cell's own vertex ring **in cell order** -- and nothing continuous. (**AMENDED
      2026-09-14:** as first written it also hashed the VERTEX COUNT, and this entry and
      three other places said so. Ledger 257 removed it, because FloPy computes `NVERT`
      at write time and a correct package then fingerprinted differently from its own
      grid; the rings were canonicalised at the same time.) That choice is what makes it exact where comparing coordinates needs a
      tolerance, and it is the opposite trade from 249's geometry test:
      - the same mesh written to fewer decimals, rendered float32, or shifted to a local
        origin (`to_mf6(local_origin=True)`, ledgers 159/218) pins the **same**, with no
        epsilon to choose;
      - a **renumbering** pins differently, which is the case that matters, because cell
        numbering is the entire meaning of a cellid;
      - a mesh **stretched without being renumbered** pins the same. Its cellids do still
        name the same cells; the geometry test in 249 is what notices the stretch. The two
        checks are complementary and neither subsumes the other.
      **The pin rides in `metadata`, not in a new field.** It is provenance -- it says
      where the records came from, not what they build -- and `metadata` is already
      serialized by `to_dict`/`from_dict`, deep-copied by `fork_package`, and **excluded
