      driving four packages emitted four BYTE-IDENTICAL lines -- so a default caller
      would have seen one of four, in exactly the shape ledger 211 names as the
      legitimate reason to warn rather than refuse. The package name and the lost
      quantity are in the message; that makes each event distinct AND is the accounting.
      One change, both problems.
      **`gaps="nearest"` moves POINTS, and that is measured, not conservative.**
      Translating a feature by the minimal vector onto the grid recovers a point exactly
      (share 1.0000 at 3 ft off and at 30 ft off). It recovers a LINE only when the line
      happens to lie PARALLEL to the boundary it missed: the same line POINTING at the
      grid lands with its tip touching and resolves to **zero cells**. A polygon
      translated by exactly its gap only touches; with 0.01 ft of overshoot it finds the
      right cells but their shares sum to **0.0001**, so a `Spread` conductance would
      write 0.01% of what was declared, and the overshoot is a tuning knob with no
      defensible default. Orientation luck is not a rule. A point has no extent, which is
      the one case where "the same feature, slightly over" is well defined.
      **An areal feature is CLIPPED, never snapped** (user decision, 2026-09-18) -- and
      `cell_shares` already did that exactly: `sum(share)` equals the true in-grid
      fraction to four decimals (1.0000 / 0.5000 / 0.0909 / 0.0000). What was missing is
      that the loss was silent: a half-off polygon under `Spread(mode="clip")` wrote
      **497.1 of a declared 1000.0** with no warning at any level. The clipped fraction
      is reported per feature now, with the quantity where one means something.
      **A total is reported only where the library KNOWS the field is extensive** -- a
      well's rate, or any field the caller wrapped in `Spread(mode="clip")`, which IS a
      declaration that it is extensive. A declared-minus-written identity over every
      field is nonsense: an unwrapped conductance is copied WHOLE to each of the twelve
      cells a polygon covers, so a clean build would report -300% "loss". Ledger 169
      measured `corr(cond, cell area) ~ 0` over 205 real DRN records -- a conductance is
      not a leakance and summing it says nothing. Everything else lists per feature with
      no total.
      **`snap_within=None` in the signature AND in the recipe**, resolved at build
      against the `sqrt(area)` of the cell the feature would snap TO. A number resolved
      at declaration would carry the OLD mesh's cell width across `with_grid` -- the
      stale-cellid defect in another costume -- and a lazy declaration has no mesh to
      compute one from. LOCAL rather than grid-wide because cell areas span **3.9x** on a
      plain Voronoi mesh and 18.5x on a refined one, so one number is ~2x too generous
      beside the smallest cells and ~0.3x too tight beside the largest, in one model.
      Compared against the distance to the cell POLYGON, not its centroid: the two differ
      by **3.07x** on one real miss (3.00 ft against 9.21 ft). The raster sibling uses
      centroid distance; the divergence is deliberate.
      **The tolerance is the only discriminator that works, and no cleverer one does.**
      Snap-vector BEARING COHERENCE cannot gate it: legitimate one-sided digitizing slop
      measures R = 1.000, identical to a uniform 700 ft datum shift. Magnitude separates
      them -- a one-cell tolerance accepts **12 of 12** legitimate slop (median 0.12
      cells) and refuses **77 of 78** systematic misses (medians 11.8 and 25.5 cells). So
      R is worth reporting and worthless as a gate; the recorded `snap_max` is what makes
      a systematic error visible even when the tolerance refused it.
      **The all-missed refusal is ORTHOGONAL to the mode**, `"ignore"` included. Ledger
      211 decided raise-on-empty and this does not reopen it in one word. The raster
      sibling's `"ignore"` DOES return before its all-missing raise
      (`grid/surfaces.py:201` precedes `:203`) because `Surface.sample` has a documented
      next stage that fills the gaps; a boundary package has no such caller, and an empty
      one is rejected by MF6 naming the file or runs without the boundary under
      `maxbound=`. The vocabulary is shared through one `check_gaps`, so the four words
      cannot drift into two dialects; the one divergence is stated in both places.
      **Only "no `on_miss=` switch" falls out of ledger 211**, and it falls because the
      channel it assumed was never heard. Raise-on-empty, deliberate-partial-miss and
      guard-on-the-RESULT-not-the-CRS all survive intact.
      **The blind spot `gaps=` can never close, stated because it will otherwise be
      trusted there:** a unit/scale CRS error. Displacement is proportional to distance
      from the projection origin, so near features stay ON the grid in the WRONG cells,
      mid features land just outside and snap, and far ones are refused. Measured with
      EPSG:32149 against a 600 ft model at the origin -- the documented
      location-agnostic workflow -- **2 of 5 wells landed, 161 ft and 484 ft from where
      they were drawn**, 3 missed, 60% of the pumping gone. The tolerance does the right
      thing with the misses and nothing can touch the survivors.
      **Two defects fixed in passing because this commit makes them live:**
      `BoundarySource.to_dict` compared each field against its default without
      normalizing, so a numpy-typed value was written into the payload and it then failed
      BOTH `json.dumps` and `yaml.safe_dump` --
      `snap_within=np.sqrt(vor.gdf_vorPolys.area.median())` is the obvious spelling. It
      runs `_json_value` above the comparison now, which also means a `np.float64` equal
      to its default is correctly OMITTED, so no stored digest moves. And the loop-local
      boundname shadowed the package name being passed to the reporter, so the first
      version of the message named a FEATURE where it meant the package.
      **The deferred-import ratchet goes 77 -> 78, and could not be hoisted**: `specs.py`
      imports from `sources.py` at module level, so `sources.py` cannot import `specs` at
      module level. `_stacklevel_outside_package` moved out of
      `modflow/utils/datatypes/choros.py` into `myflopy/_warnings.py` rather than being
      copied -- a second copy is what the shared-rules consolidation of ledgers 210-212
      exists to prevent.
      **Confirmed adjacent and deliberately NOT fixed here**, each measured:
      (a) `mf.hfb.gpkg` with every trace 50,000 ft off the grid BUILDS an empty package
      with zero warnings -- ledger 211's exact failure in the one package 211 never
      reached, because HFB is face-indexed and outside `package_registry` -- and a NULL
      `hydchr` raises a bare `TypeError: float() argument ...` naming neither file nor
      feature (ledger 247's `_finite` guard never applied there). It needs a miss
      vocabulary of its own.
      (b) `layer_field` naming layer 99 on a 1-layer model with NO `ModelContext.domain`
      writes the record at `(98, 111)` silently; with a domain declared the same input
      raises. The guard exists only by accident of whether a domain was passed, and
      ledger 284 made contextless declarations normal.

289. **A floor that silently was not one, and an elevation divided by area (2026-09-18).**
      Two live silent-wrong-value defects in `GeoPackageSource._value` /
      `CellSurfaceOffset.resolve`, found while scoping the elevation floor (B2 item 8) and
      landed first because the floor would have inherited the first one.
      **(a) A NULL in the `minimum` column silently disabled the floor.** A nullable REAL
      column reads back as `nan`, `max(value, nan)` returns `value` in Python, and the
      result is FINITE -- so ledger 247's own guard let it through. Measured: a drain
      declared `minimum="floor"` over a NULL column wrote output **byte-identical to
      declaring no floor at all**, 11 of 11 records below their own cell bottom, zero
      warnings. That is the worst shape an input defect takes -- **the safeguard the user
      reached for is the thing that vanished**. The other direction was no better: a TEXT
      NULL raised a bare `TypeError` naming neither the feature nor the field, where the
      same NULL in a plain value column gives 247's full named error. Both the `offset`
      and `minimum` columns go through `_finite` now, which is what makes ledger 247's own
      claim -- that it names those columns -- true; that entry is amended.
      The message gained the ROLE as well as the column, because knowing a value is
      missing is no use without knowing which of `offset=`/`minimum=` it was:
      `GeoPackage 'bc.gpkg': feature 'l' (minimum=) has nan for 'floor'.`
      **(b) `Spread` on an ELEVATION was accepted and divided it by the cell's area
      share.** Measured: `elevation=mf.Spread("elev")` on a declared 75.0 wrote **2.06 to
      11.87** across 11 cells -- all of them below their own cell bottom -- with a clean
      build and no warning. `Spread` exists to divide a feature's TOTAL across the cells
      it covers, which is right for a flux or a conductance and meaningless for an
      elevation: there is no total to divide. **Ledger 274 refused exactly this on the
      ARRAY form and never reached the list form.** Refused by name now, for the six
      elevation fields (`chd.head`, `ghb.head`, `drn.elevation`, `riv.stage`, `riv.rbot`,
      `evt.surface`), through `_ELEVATION_FIELDS` -- the shape `_EXTENSIVE_FIELDS` set in
      ledger 288. `rch.recharge` is deliberately absent: a rate column that really holds a
      total volume IS spreadable, which is what `Spread`'s own docstring teaches.
      **The refusal had to be called from BOTH paths**, and a single site would have
      covered half the API: the eager form reaches `_bc_from_features` and a LAZY
      declaration never does (ledger 284/285 made contextless declarations normal). It
      needs no grid, so it belongs at the call -- the rule `_lazy_bc_spec` already follows
      for a missing file and `nper >= 1`. Proved by mutation: removing the lazy-path call
      fails five of the six parametrized cases.
      **Recorded so it is not re-filed:** the LEGACY builders carry a third instance of
      the same family -- `min_elev = min_elev if min_elev is not None else 0` at
      `modflow/mf6/ghb.py:242` and `drn.py:200`, read with `row.get(...)`, turns an ABSENT
      floor column into an absolute floor at DATUM ZERO. Silently correct on a model above
      sea level and silently destructive below it. Legacy layer, and deprecating it is
      already blocked, so it is noted rather than fixed.

290. **An elevation outside its own cell, and nothing said so (2026-09-18).**
      `min_above_bottom=` on `mf.chd/ghb/drn/riv.gpkg` lifts an elevation that resolves
      below its cell's bottom, PER CELL -- plus a **default-on detection** that reports one
      whether or not the floor is asked for. Not `evt` (user decision).
      **The plan's justification was wrong and the earlier correction incomplete.** MF6's
      behaviour splits on `icelltype`, and **both branches are live in this library**.
      At `icelltype = 0` -- which is what `mf.npf(k=10.0)` writes, because it names no
      icelltype at all -- all four packages ACCEPT a below-bottom value, terminate
      normally, and over-drain: **2.17x on a 3x3 bench, 1.09x on a real 64-cell DISV
      model**. At `icelltype != 0` -- which `CanonicalModelConfig` uses and 17 taught sites
      pass -- MF6 **REFUSES by name**, NEWTON does not change it, and the refusal is a
      PER-PERIOD data read, so an offender in period 3 dies after MF6 has solved periods 1
      and 2. On a 72-period model that is a late failure. End to end on a real run: the
      same declaration at `icelltype=1` fails with `DRN BOUNDARY (1) ELEVATION ( 45.000)
      IS LESS THAN CELL BOTTOM` and reaches Normal termination with
      `min_above_bottom=0.5`.
      **What is constant across models is the SILENCE, not the magnitude**, so the
      detection is default-on and the correction opt-in. Nothing reported a below-bottom
      elevation before: no warning, no metadata key, no validator (`surface_water_validation`
      covers LAK stage and SFR streambed only). The count, the worst depth and the lift
      are stamped beside `coverage` in metadata, because on the lazy path the warning
      fires inside `prepare_run` where no stacklevel points at the declaration.
      **Half of the arithmetic already shipped, and the entry says so** rather than let a
      later reader find `max(value, minimum)` and think this was redundant.
      `CellSurfaceOffset("cell_bottom", offset=F, minimum=<declared>)` IS
      `min_above_bottom=F` exactly, for a declared elevation that is a constant or a single
      column -- measured, 0 of 7 mismatches. What it cannot do is floor anything else:
      `minimum` is read once per FEATURE (a scalar and a column behave identically, both
      leaving 3 of 7 records below their own bottoms), and `minimum=<CellSurfaceOffset>`
      and `minimum=[...]` both raise `TypeError`. So the two shapes that could not be
      floored are the per-period column list and a surface-relative value --
      `CellSurfaceOffset("model_top", offset=-35.0)`, "a drain 35 ft below ground", which
      left 5 of 7 records below their own cell bottom. **That is the idiom the docs push
      people toward**: 63 `model_top` + ~50 `cell_top` references across the tree, against
      `minimum=` appearing 5 times in total and never as a real declaration in `src/`.
      **A clearance of 0.0 does NOT mean "at the bottom"**, and cannot. FloPy writes `botm`
      fixed-point and a list-BC value in E format, so a value set exactly equal to its cell
      bottom can round BELOW it in the written file and MF6's strict comparison trips:
      **13 of 24 real runs FAILED** at bottoms drawn from [40, 600], and which way the
      discarded digits fall is a coin flip -- which is why round numbers look immune. A CHD
      set exactly at its bottom is worse: it aborts the SOLVER (`CONSTANT-HEAD CELL WENT
      DRY`) at round magnitudes too. The clearance is nudged by
      `max(|bottom| * 1e-6, 1e-6)`, the relative form already in the MODFLOW-USG importer
      whose comment says exactly this and is now measured true rather than defensive
      (both are `boundary_support.bottom_clearance` since ledger 291, which also
      corrects the RIV pair rule below: carrying the stage up is right only where the
      stage is itself below the floor). A
      plain absolute `1e-6` is NOT enough -- it fails at bottom 3456.789012346.
      **RIV is a PAIR, and the three readings of "the same parameter" are 3.5x apart in
      flux on ONE record.** MF6 checks `rbot` and never names `stage`; raising `rbot`
      alone trips a SECOND check (`stage >= rbot`), so a model that RAN becomes a hard
      failure. Measured, cell bottom 48.0, declared stage 40 / rbot 35: as declared
      q=-868.57 (runs at icelltype 0); rbot alone REFUSED at both icelltypes; both clamped
      q=-380.00 with the river depth collapsed to **0.000 from a declared 1.0**;
      pair-lifted q=-108.57. So the floor lifts `rbot` and raises `stage` by the SAME
      delta, and the declared depth survives (measured exactly 5.000 ft across every
      cell). A declared `stage < rbot` is REFUSED by name instead -- MF6 refuses it at
      both icelltypes and `mf.riv.gpkg`'s own docstring already promised the invariant
      while nothing enforced it.
      **Order matters: the floor runs AFTER the `gaps="nearest"` snap** (ledger 288). A
      snapped point lands in a DIFFERENT cell with a different bottom, so a floor applied
      first would use the wrong one.
      **A regression this commit introduced and a test now guards:** making
      `min_above_bottom` a REQUIRED keyword on the shared `_lazy_bc_spec` broke
      `wel`/`rch`/`evt` on the lazy path outright (`missing 1 required keyword-only
      argument`), because only four of the seven pass it. Defaulted, and the three are
      asserted still to build.
      **Not carried:** the detection needs the layer elevations, so a model that declares
      none is skipped rather than refused -- there is nothing to compare against, and a
      model without surfaces is not an error.

291. **The importer lifted the river's water surface, not its bed (2026-09-18).**
      `to_mf6(fix_for_mf6=True)` clamped RIV's **`stage`** and left **`rbot`** below the
      cell bottom -- and `rbot` is the field MODFLOW 6 checks. `_bc_record` passes a USG
      record's trailing values through in MF6 order (`stage, cond, rbot`), so column 0 is
      the water surface; the clamp read column 0 and the finding read the same column.
      Measured end to end (`docs/reproducers/riv_pair_and_icelltype.py`, cell bottom 48.0,
      declared stage 40 / rbot 35, `icelltype = 1`): as declared REFUSED, stage lifted
      alone **still REFUSED** naming `RIVER BOTTOM`, pair-lifted runs. At `icelltype = 0`,
      where all three run, they read q = -818.18 / -381.82 / -109.09 -- three readings of
      one river, **7.5x apart**. So the option's documented promise was false for RIV in
      exactly the way that looks like it worked.
      **The case it could not see at all is the ordinary one.** A river with its surface
      inside the cell and its bed below it -- stage 55, rbot 40, bottom 48 -- offends on
      nothing the old check read, and MODFLOW 6 refuses it by name. The check is on
      `rbot` now, and on `stage` as well because MODFLOW 6 names both when both offend.
      **RIV moves as a PAIR, but ledger 290's version of that rule was over-general and
      is corrected here -- which changes `mf.riv.gpkg` too.** 290 measured ONE record
      shape, stage 40 / rbot 35 with BOTH below the bottom, where carrying the stage up
      by the bed's delta is the best of the readings (-109.09, against -381.82 for
      clamping both and losing the declared depth), and generalised to every record. On
      the ordinary river -- stage 55 / rbot 40, the water surface INSIDE the cell --
      carrying it up writes a stage of 63.0 against a cell top of 60.0: **three feet
      above land surface**, turning q = 0.00 into **+436.37**. With a deeper bed, stage
      50 / rbot 20, the sign reverses: **-272.73 to +1254.55**. Lifting the bed alone
      reproduces the declared answer exactly and runs at both icelltypes.
      So the stage is carried up **only when it is itself below the floor**, which is
      exactly when MODFLOW 6 would refuse it. `max(stage, floor)` is NOT the rule either:
      on 290's own shape it collapses the depth to zero. `river_pair_lift` /
      `bottom_clearance` in `modflow/mf6/boundary_support.py` (L0) are the single rule
      now -- both layers carried their own copy and the copies had drifted -- and a test
      asserts the two call sites resolve to the same function objects.
      The project's own fixture was already producing the bad case unnoticed: a declared
      stage of 7.0 over a bed at 2.0, in a cell bottomed at 5.0 with a top of 10.0, was
      being written at 10.000005. Found by an adversarial review, not by the tests.
      **`validate()` was silent about a model MODFLOW 6 will not start.** DRN was exempt,
      on the comment that a drain below its cell bottom is simply inactive. Neither branch
      supports that: at `icelltype != 0` MODFLOW 6 REFUSES it by name (NEWTON does not
      change it) and at `icelltype = 0` it accepts it and over-discharges -- **2.00x** the
      same drain placed inside its cell. A converted model inherits `icelltype` from the
      LPF `LAYTYP`, so both branches are reachable from one importer. **`severity` is
      therefore read from the model**: `reject` when any offending record sits in a
      convertible layer, `allow` otherwise -- with `allow` reported, not dropped, because
      the silence is what was constant. The report's `MODFLOW 6 IS STRICTER` heading
      became `MODFLOW 6 DIFFERS`: its `allows` branch had been dead code.
      **DRN had to join the clamp in the same pass**, or `validate()` would name a blocker
      whose stated remedy does nothing. A stage below its own bed is REFUSED at both
      icelltypes and is deliberately **not** repaired -- a pair lift preserves an
      inversion rather than fixing it, and which of the two numbers is wrong is not
      something a converter can know; it is named instead.
      **What was deliberately NOT changed.** The corrections stay unconditional while the
      detection became icelltype-aware, so `fix_for_mf6` means the same thing on every
      model. Two consequences, both accepted: on a confined model it edits boundaries
      MODFLOW 6 would have accepted, and the CHD branch still DROPS records that a
      confined model was actively using -- measured **-1200** ft3/d on the bench, a
      boundary DRAINING that much rather than feeding it, so "inert in USG anyway" is
      true only of a convertible layer. Gating the corrections would have
      changed the converted water balance for confined models, which the one real model
      that exercises this path cannot be re-run here to check. **Open**: gate the CHD drop
      on convertibility once a confined USG model is available to measure.
      The finding tests `< bottom` while the clamp lifts below `bottom + clearance`, so
      a value sitting exactly ON its bottom is corrected but not reported -- it is not
      *below* the bottom, and MODFLOW 6's verdict on it is the coin flip ledger 290
      measured. Asymmetric in the safe direction, unlike the defect above it.
      **An `allow` finding is logged at conversion time, not left to `validate()`.**
      The first draft left it to `validate()`/`report()` on the grounds that the two USG
      notebooks carry conversion warnings in saved output that cannot be regenerated
      without the proprietary model -- but reading that model settles it: Ten Trails is
      `icelltype [1 1 1 1 1]`, carries no RIV and has no below-bottom DRN, so every
      finding there is `reject` and logs exactly as before. Withholding the one warning
      nothing else says out loud would have been ledger 288's defect ("reported through
      a channel nobody hears") one module over. The GHB clamp message is byte-identical
      all the same; DRN and RIV got their own, since one line cannot call a drain invert,
      a river bed and a head the same thing, and the CHD drop message now splits on
      convertibility rather than asserting an inertness that holds on only one side.
      **Each number in a finding comes from ONE period** -- the one with the most
      offenders. Taking count, depth, share and total as independent maxima over periods
      reported a share/total pair belonging to no period at all (a constructed case
      understated it 50x) and a count that read as a record total.
      **Known gap, not closed here:** a non-finite elevation is neither clamped nor
      reported (`nan < floor` is False), so it reaches MODFLOW 6 -- the USG importer has
      no counterpart to the refusal ledgers 247/289 built for the GeoPackage sources.

292. **The bundler half-copied a shapefile, bundled the project into itself, and ran
      before the save was allowed (2026-09-18).**
      Three defects in the SHIPPED grid bundler (ledger 256), found while scoping B2's
      package-source work and landed first because that work multiplies every one of them.
      **(a) A multi-file source was bundled as its named FILE alone, and the project then
      could not be opened.** Measured end to end, on a tree where NOTHING was deleted: a
      shapefile written with five companions (`.cpg .dbf .prj .shp .shx`) was bundled as
      the `.shp` only; the grid that resolved at `ncpl = 28` before the save then failed
      `DataSourceError`, and `SaveReport` reported the bundle as done. **That is strictly
      worse than not bundling** -- it takes a project that builds and makes it not build,
      and says it archived it. A `.gdb` is a DIRECTORY and was already carried whole by
      `copytree`; this is the same mistake in its other shape.
      Companions are matched by NAME PREFIX rather than an enumerated suffix table: a
      shapefile's companion set is open-ended, and a raster sidecar is often a double
      extension (`ground.tif.aux.xml`), whose `Path.stem` is `ground.tif` rather than
      `ground`. The prefix catches both without a table that silently omits the one format
      a user has. Only formats that NEED companions are swept, so a self-contained
      `.gpkg` does not drag in a same-stem neighbour.
      **(b) A source the project ALREADY held was copied into the project.**
      `already_inside` tested `inputs/` and never the project root, so a `method="object"`
      grid -- which becomes a pickle on save -- had its own `specs/grids/g.pkl` copied to
      `inputs/g.pkl` and the recipe repointed at the copy, orphaning the original. On a
      real grid that pickle is the largest thing a saved project holds, so it doubled it.
      **It takes save -> load -> save to reach**: the LIVE grid is still an object and
      names no pickle, so a single save cannot produce it, and the first version of the
      test passed with the fix reverted for exactly that reason. The same one-line
      condition also covers a source the user deliberately keeps inside the project, which
      `usg.export_gis(dir)` (ledger 169) actively encourages.
      **(c) A REFUSED save still copied files and repointed the live registry.**
      `_bundle_grid_sources()` was the FIRST statement of `Project.save`, ahead of
      `validate()` and the `strict=True` raise -- so a refused save left `inputs/`
      populated and the in-memory recipes pointing into it, with no spec file written. A
      state nothing on disk records, and one a later plain `save()` would then persist
      without the user having asked for an archive. Bundling runs after the refusal now.
      **Ledger 256's premise is separately stale** and is amended there rather than here:
      "package sources resolve EAGERLY" was measured true when written and is now false
      for a lazy `.gpkg` (ledgers 279/284/285). Carrying those is the NEXT commit; this
      one is the bundler that will have to carry them.

293. **A saved project now carries what a LAZY package reads, and the digest reads the
      file rather than its address (2026-09-19).** Ledger 292 fixed the grid bundler; this carries the
      other tier. A package declared without a `context=` holds a RECIPE, so
      `bundle_sources=True` had to grow a package pass -- and the interesting part is
      that **there are TWO carriers, and the one that is easy to overlook fails FIRST**.
      The boundary recipes are `DataSourceSpec` objects in `inputs`, which
      `bundle._paths_of`'s walk would have found. The layer stack behind
      `mf.disv(<gridless LayerStack>)` is not a dataclass, names no source spec, and per
      ledger 270 is the ONLY shape a layered model saves in. Measured by deleting the
      sources and rebuilding: the failure is `RasterioIOError` on the stack's raster,
      raised inside the discretization before any boundary condition is built. So a
      bundler carrying only the `.gpkg` recipes reports a complete archive and produces
      one that cannot open -- strictly worse than not bundling, the same shape as 292(a).
      One walker (`specs.repoint_source_paths`) serves both, duck-typed on `_SPEC_TOKEN`
      because `specs` is import layer 1 and `layers` is 6.
      **THE DIGEST WAS WRONG IN BOTH DIRECTIONS AT ONCE.** `package_digest` fingerprinted
      a source by its PATH. So bundling -- which copies the file into `inputs/` and
      repoints the recipe -- moved every lazy package's digest on a byte-identical
      archive (`4c3988e4` -> `113e32d2`), and `runs.drift()` called every stored run
      edited on the day it was archived. And a DIFFERENT file at the same path digested
      IDENTICALLY, which is the `unchanged`-is-the-dangerous-verdict failure: the recipe
      says "read this file", and nothing noticed when the file stopped saying what it
      said. A content hash on the recipe (`BoundarySource.source_sha`, inside `inputs` so
      it is digest-VISIBLE) fixes both, and it is also what makes the lazy form AGREE
      with the eager one -- an eager `.gpkg` stores records, so its digest is
      location-blind and content-sensitive by construction, and the two were drifting in
      OPPOSITE directions from the same declaration. Only `BoundarySource` moves:
      `digest_payload()` defaults to `to_dict()`, so no grid source's digest changes.
      **The path is REPLACED, not joined** -- keeping both reintroduces the churn half
      while looking fixed -- except when the file could not be read at declaration, where
      `source_sha` is `None` and the path stands in, because two unreadable sources
      digesting alike is the blindness again with nothing to replace it. The migration
      was free: 0 tracked files held a lazy recipe, re-checked at the start of the commit.
      `to_dict` still writes the path; only the digest drops it.
      **The anchor belongs AFTER `resolved_packages`**, which is ledger 280's exact miss
      in a different function: a `PackageRef` carries no `inputs`, so anchoring the
      DECLARED list silently skips every package reached through `mf.ref` -- the
      documented library route. Anchoring at LOAD time instead was measured worse twice
      over: it moved the digest, and the next plain `save()` wrote the absolute path
      back, quietly un-bundling the archive. Grids never had this bug --
      `grid_spec_resolver._source_path` has anchored them all along -- which is exactly
      why the package tier went unnoticed. `RunLibrary._library_source_memo` needed the
      same anchor: it hashed `inputs/bc.gpkg` against the current working directory and
      answered `missing` for a file sitting right there.
      **`drift()`'s `source` column was INVERTED, and blind on the wrong half.** The memo
      keys off `metadata['source_path']`, which only the EAGER declaration stamped -- so
      the package whose records are frozen and whose file is never reopened reported
      `missing` when that file moved, while the LAZY one, which cannot build without it,
      reported `—`: "names no source". The lazy spec stamps `source_path` + `source_sha`
      now; both are in `metadata`, which `package_digest` excludes, so the stamp moves
      nothing.
      **`Surface.out` is carried, and it is the one path here that is a WRITE target.**
      It is the GRASS interpolation cache, so an archive without it needs GRASS installed
      to rebuild; with it, `DerivedRaster.status()` reads `stale` -- its provenance key
      records each source by PATH STRING, which bundling changes -- and a stale cache is
      REUSED with a warning rather than regenerated, so the archive still produces the
      same raster. Its `.provenance.json` rides along for free: `.tif` is in
      `_COMPANION_FORMATS` and the prefix match catches the double extension (292). An
      ABSENT cache is not reported missing -- it has simply not been produced yet, and
      listing it would put a fault in the report for a project in an ordinary state.
      **Not carried, and now SAID so:** a `LayerStack` holding a `from_array` surface
      cannot be serialized at all (ledger 193), so it is left exactly as it was and named
      in the new `SaveReport.not_bundled`. Reported rather than raised because such a
      model is skipped by the save anyway, and a bundler that raised would cost the
      caller every other simulation in the project -- the rule `SaveReport` was created
      for. `SaveReport`'s whole reporting surface was invisible to CI until this commit:
      `members()` captures callables and properties only, and this class is all data, so
      `SaveReport.members` is the empty list and every column could have appeared or
      vanished without moving a snapshot row. `SaveReport.fields` is pinned now.
      **Still open, deliberately.** `BoundarySource` has no `*.fields` snapshot row, so
      `source_sha` is pinned only by `test_boundary_source.py`'s own field sweep; the
      eager `.gpkg` path still stamps its metadata in `GeoPackageSource._metadata` while
      the lazy one stamps in `_lazy_bc_spec`, two sites that must agree by hand.
      **AMENDED 2026-09-19 after two independent adversarial reviews, which found six
      defects and two overstated claims in the paragraphs above.** Corrections first,
      because both are claims this entry made about its own evidence:
      * *"it churned ... measured 4c3988e4 -> 113e32d2"* **described a state that never
        shipped.** Before this commit `save(bundle_sources=True)` did not touch package
        recipes at all, so bundling could not move a package digest; the number came
        from a scoping exercise that simulated the bundling this commit then added.
        Latent-within-the-commit, not live before it -- the same correction c877911 made,
        and the same rule as [[a-measurement-belongs-to-what-it-measured]]. What WAS
        live is the weaker form: a user who moved their own GeoPackage moved its digest.
      * *"the migration was free"* is true of STORED payloads only -- a recipe loaded
        from a pre-commit project digests identically, because `source_sha` is absent and
        the path falls back. A LIVE re-declaration moves, so a stored run reads
        `state=edited` the first time its declaring script is re-run. Exposure is small
        (the lazy `.gpkg` landed 2026-09-17) but "0 tracked files held a lazy recipe"
        measures the REPO, not a user's saved project.
      **THE DIGEST FIX COVERED ONE CARRIER OF THE TWO -- a regression this commit
      introduced.** `_canonical`'s `_SPEC_TOKEN` branch still read `to_dict()`, so the
      LAYER STACK -- the carrier this entry's own headline is about -- kept a path-keyed
      digest. Because the commit made bundling reach package inputs for the first time,
      that turned the churn LIVE exactly where it had just been removed: a byte-identical
      archive moved the lazy disv's digest (`c69eb0ad` -> `660c6be0`) while the `.gpkg`
      beside it held still. Blind in the other direction too (a different raster at the
      same path digested identically), and the same for a lazy `mf.evt(surface=...)`.
      Fixed with the same rule: `Surface.source_shas` + `Surface.digest_payload` +
      `LayerStack.digest_payload`, stamped by `stamp_source_hashes` **at LAZY-PACKAGE
      declaration, not in `Surface`** (user decision) -- a bare `Surface.raster(path)`
      opens nothing, and hashing there would put a full read of a multi-hundred-megabyte
      DEM behind the cheapest call in the layer API. `out` is dropped from the digest
      rather than hashed: it is a WRITE target whose content is fully determined by
      `contours` plus the build parameters, which ARE digested.
      **`Surface.zone` NAMES A FILE and the key set missed it.** It is typed `Any` and
      takes either a shapely geometry or a path to a vector file (`Surface.where`, which
      the cheatsheet teaches), so it read as "not a path field" -- and a stack using one
      bundled with `not_bundled` empty and then died `DataSourceError`, the 292(a) shape
      again. Including it is safe because the walk tests the VALUE's type: a geometry is
      not a `str`. Same pass: the new `source_shas` dict is keyed by FIELD NAME, so a
      naive walk read its content hashes AS paths (the bundler reported
      `proj/06464ba5355f3e8e` missing); `SHA_KEY` is skipped by both walkers.
      **THE ANCHOR SILENTLY CHANGED WHICH FILE A RELATIVE DECLARATION NAMED.**
      `_lazy_bc_spec` validated the path against the CWD; `_anchored_packages` re-based
      it against the project root. Two bases for one string: a declaration that passed
      then failed at build, and where a same-named file happened to sit under the project
      root **the model BUILT CLEAN from the wrong one** -- heads 999.0 against a declared
      9.0, normal termination, no warning. Both reviews found it independently. The
      recipe RESOLVES at declaration now (and so does a surface path the stamp could
      read), so the only relative paths reaching the anchor are the ones the bundler
      wrote, which are project-relative by construction. Free of digest consequences
      because the content hash is what the digest reads.
      **`drift()`'s source column answered about the wrong file, in both directions.**
      Bundling repointed the RECIPE and left `metadata['source_path']` -- which the memo
      keys off -- naming the original. A shipped archive read `missing`; and editing the
      bundled copy, the only file the build opens, read **`ok`**. A false clean bill
      produced by the column added to remove exactly that. Bundling repoints the metadata
      and re-hashes now.
      **Two more, smaller:** `bundle_package_sources`' `missing` list was computed and
      discarded (the sole signal was a `logger.warning`, invisible per ledger 288), so a
      project whose source had moved archived nothing, said nothing, and reported
      success -- it goes in `not_bundled`, and the GRID pass's identical discard is fixed
      with it. And the walker rebuilds a token object from its DECLARATION, which drops a
      `LayerStack`'s bound `vor`, producing "needs a grid ... declared without one" about
      a stack declared with one.
      **One of this entry's own guards was CERTIFYING**: the `_anchored` test built its
      state with `dataclasses.replace(spec, metadata=...)`, and the library could not
      produce that state, because bundling left the metadata behind. It passed while what
      it guarded was unreachable. It goes through `save(bundle_sources=True)` now.
      **Still open after the second pass:** a lazy `mf.disv` stamps NO `source_path`, so
      its `source` column reads `—`. That column is single-source by construction and a
      stack names many files; giving it a multi-source answer belongs with B2 item 10
      (source-edited drift state), not here. The `*.fields` snapshot gap was closed in
      the same pass instead of being deferred: `BoundarySource.fields` and
      `Surface.fields` are pinned now, because a field vanishing from either silently
      changes what `package_digest` fingerprints.

294. **Two runs either side of an edit were indistinguishable, and an INLINE package was
      invisible (2026-09-21).**
      B2 item 10. The plan asks for five new drift states; measuring first changed what
      got built, and the ledger records the re-scope rather than the plan text.
      **What was already right, measured before touching anything:** on the taught path
      -- `add_package` -> `mf.ref` -> `save()` -> a fresh `Project.load()` -- `drift()`
      answers correctly: `unchanged|ok` untouched, `unchanged|ok` across save/load, and
      `unchanged|edited` once the GeoPackage moves on, with a rebuild confirming the new
      value. The two-column split of ledger 276 does its job. So `source-edited` and
      `source-missing` are NOT built as `state` values: they exist as the `source`
      column, and promoting them re-hides one of the two questions 276 separated.
      **THE CORRECTNESS BUG.** `package_digests` records the LIBRARY's declaration, so
      two runs of one simulation prepared either side of an edit recorded the IDENTICAL
      digest while building CHD heads of 9.0 and 42.0 -- and `drift()` gave both the same
      verdict, including the run that AGREES with the file. A run now records
      `metadata['built_from']`: the content hash of every source it actually READ, and
      the `source` column prefers it over the library memo. The two runs read `edited`
      and `ok` respectively now.
      **AND AN INLINE PACKAGE HAD NO ROW AT ALL.** `_package_digests` records only
      `mf.ref` entries, on the premise stated in its own docstring that an inline package
      "is baked into the run's own recipe and cannot drift". Ledgers 279/284/293
      falsified that premise: an inline lazy `.gpkg` holds a PATH and opens it at build.
      Measured -- edit the file and `drift()` reported `unchanged` with `source` `—`
      ("names no source") while the rebuild produced 42.0 instead of 9.0. Since
      `built_from` is keyed by the DECLARED entry -- a `PackageRef`'s library key, an
      inline spec's own name (ledger 280's rule) -- the inline half comes free. Such a
      row reads `state` `—`: there is no key, so the question "does this key still mean
      what the run used" has nothing to answer about, and it says so rather than
      answering `unchanged`.
      **ONLY A LAZY PACKAGE IS RE-HASHED AT BUILD**, because only a lazy package reads a
      file there. An eager one resolved at declaration and carries records, so its
      declaration hash IS what the run was built from, and re-reading would describe a
      read that never happened -- `source` for an eager package is PROVENANCE, not
      buildability, and the docs now say so (user decision). That distinction is also
      what keeps the cost honest: hashing is **0.15%** of the work it describes for an
      ordinary GeoPackage (0.07 ms against a 46.4 ms resolve; 1.4-2.4 ms on the real Ten
      Trails files), but a full read of the 3.7 GB LIDAR DEM is **~1.9 s at 2 GB/s**,
      and the build only SAMPLES that raster -- so hashing a file the build never opened
      would be the dominant cost of describing it.
      **Cost this entry also states because the previous one did not measure it:**
      ledger 293's `stamp_source_hashes` put a full read behind `mf.disv(stack)` --
      **2.09 s** on that same 3.7 GB DEM. `Surface.raster(path)` itself is untouched at
      **2.4 us**, identical for a nonexistent path, so the placement argument holds; the
      declaration of the PACKAGE is where the cost landed.
      **A package naming several files gets ONE cell**, so it reports the WORST with a
      count -- `edited (1 of 2)`, `missing (1 of 2)` -- because a lazy discretization
      names one file per surface plus the top, and a stack whose single raster moved must
      not read clean because its others did not.
      **`built_from` lives in `metadata`, not at the top level of the manifest**:
      `save_manifest` writes an explicit key list and `from_dict` reads one, so a
      top-level key is dropped by any rewrite from code that does not know it -- and
      `_record_status` rewrites on every status change. `metadata` round-trips wholesale.
      **NOT BUILT, and why.** `grid-changed` and `unfrozen` are per-RUN and per-MODEL
      facts; `drift()` is per (run, package key) and has no `model` column, so either
      would fan one fact across every row -- they belong in `runs.summary()`, which has
      one row per run. `legacy-digest` has no era marker to read (no version field exists
      anywhere in `src/`, and `myflopy.__version__` is a frozen "0.1.0"), so every
      existing record would have to be ASSUMED into an era; measured, 0 of 84 real stored
      digests move under HEAD, so it would be insurance about the NEXT break rather than
      a fix for this one.
      **A scoping error worth recording, since it nearly set the scope.** The first pass
      leaned on the user's Ten Trails project, where `drift()` emits 88 rows of which 84
      read `removed` and 0 could ever read `unchanged` -- because `specs/packages` and
      `specs/simulations` are EMPTY, the project having been script-built and never
      saved. The user's correction: those runs predate this system and are not the
      standard. The numbers are real and the inference was not: a legacy artifact was
      being allowed to define normal, which is [[a-measurement-belongs-to-what-it-measured]]
      one level up. Re-measuring on the taught path is what showed the verb already works
      there, and narrowed this commit to the two defects that survive it.

295. **A per-cell array moved to another mesh and the report called it `unchanged`
      (2026-09-22).**
      Found while scoping B3. `npf`, `ic` and `sto` take no ``context=``, so nothing
      ever stamped them -- ``CELLWISE_OPTIONS`` is written in ONE place
      (``advanced._array_bc_spec``), which only ``mf.rch.array`` and ``mf.evt.array``
      reach. Everything else carrying per-cell values fell through to
      ``"unchanged", "names no cells"``, which is false: an array names every cell, by
      POSITION.
      **Measured on the form the docs now teach.** A model with a LAZY ``mf.disv(stack)``
      moved between two meshes of the SAME cell count: the discretization reported
      ``rebuilt`` and resolved itself correctly, ``npf`` reported ``unchanged``, the
      build COMPLETED, and the K array was byte-identical to the one written for the old
      mesh. This is ledger 249's defect in the one place 249's own guard cannot see it --
      a range check passes because every index is in range on both meshes -- and B1/B2
      made it MORE reachable, not less: a hand-written DISV was ``stale`` and refused the
      build, while a lazy one rebuilds cleanly and leaves nothing to object to. Sixth
      instance of the pattern in [['unchanged' is the dangerous verdict]]; and the same
      one-carrier-of-two asymmetry as ledger 282 itself, which closed this for the array
      BCs and left the array-valued PACKAGES open.
      **THE DETECTION MUST BE ncpl-EXACT, and that decides where it lives.**
      ``npf(k=[10.0, 1.0])`` is a per-LAYER list and means the same on any mesh, so
      deciding from "is this a sequence?" would refuse a correct move. The exact test
      needs a cell count, and these helpers have no ``context=`` to supply one -- so the
      detection cannot happen at declaration at all. It happens in ``package_move``,
      which ``with_grid`` calls **while it still holds the old grid**: ``with_grid`` does
      not mutate, so ``self.context.grid`` is the mesh the packages were declared on.
      Every scout in the scoping workflow reported "the old geometry is gone" by
      inspecting the RESULT of the move; it is gone from the result and present at the
      call site, and ``ModelSpec.with_grid`` already read it to compute the stamp.
      **The rule moved to import layer 0** (``grid_identity.column_count`` /
      ``cellwise_options``) because three callers in layers 0, 2 and 5 need the SAME one;
      ``advanced`` now delegates rather than holding a second copy.
      ``column_count`` also learned to see a NESTED sequence -- ``k=[[...ncpl...],
      [...ncpl...]]`` is what a per-cell K on a multi-layer model looks like written by
      hand, and reading ``.shape`` alone missed it, which is ledger 282's own gap one
      nesting level down. All four spellings are pinned by a parametrized test.
      **A stamped package now reports its own verdict.** ``package_move`` reads
      ``MOVED_FROM`` before anything else, because the moved spec no longer carries the
      old mesh: without it a report read AFTER the move said ``unchanged`` about the very
      package the build then refused, and ``move_report`` exists precisely to be read
      before ``prepare_run``.
      **What this does NOT do.** It gives the arrays a VERDICT, not a route: a refused
      package must still be re-declared by hand. Routing it is the overlay engine, which
      is deliberately the LAST piece of B3 -- this commit is what gives that engine a
      trigger, and it is worth having on its own because the silence is a live defect
      whether or not the engine is ever built. It also cannot fire for a model whose
      context carries no grid (a deferred-grid model), which is the same limit ledger 271
      already records for hand-written cellids: there is no old mesh to measure against.

296. **An eagerly declared `.gpkg` moves EXACTLY, and needed no overlay engine
      (2026-09-22).**
      B3's second commit, and the one that shrinks what the engine has to cover before
      the engine is designed. An eager `.gpkg` resolves at DECLARATION and holds finished
      records, so `with_grid` classified it `stale` and the build refused it -- and that
      is the LARGEST stale class there is, because declaring with a ``context=`` is what
      every pre-B2 document teaches. It never needed an overlay: everything required to
      resolve it again is present at the call, so it is written down and the move
      re-declares it. Measured: 8 records on ncpl 28 becoming 10 on ncpl 81, verdict
      `rebuilt`, and `mf.Spread(mode="retained")` conserving the feature total exactly.
      **RECORDED, NOT RE-DERIVED, and the difference is not cosmetic.**
      `metadata['fields']` looks like it already holds the recipe, and reconstructing
      from it was the obvious plan. Two measurements refused it. `_metadata_value` is
      deliberately NOT a round-trip format -- ledger 274 recorded two reasons to keep it
      apart from `to_dict`, one of which is that reviving it would change what
      `metadata['fields']` means for every consumer. And it is **three fields short**:
      `nper`, `edges_only` and `boundnames` appear nowhere in metadata. `edges_only` is
      the one that matters, because it decides WHICH CELLS are kept (ledger 246), so a
      reconstruction that guessed it would write a different package in silence. The
      recipe is built from the call arguments instead, where all three are in scope.
      **It rides in `metadata`**, which `package_digest` excludes by contract, so
      recording it moves no stored digest -- verified with and without, live and revived.
      It cannot ride in `inputs`: `PackageSpec.build` splats `inputs` into the builder,
      and an eager package's builder would be handed a `BoundarySource` where FloPy
      wants records.
      **A SOURCE THAT ONLY REBUILDS VIA ONE CALLER IS A TRAP, and this made it live.**
      `BoundarySource`'s own docstring recorded that its nested `Spread` /
      `CellSurfaceOffset` survive ONLY through `options`/`inputs`, because
      `_spec_value(..., int_keys=True)` is what recurses into a source payload; by any
      other route they came back plain dicts with nothing raised. `metadata` IS another
      route, so the documented trap became reachable. `_from_dict` revives its own
      `values` now and is idempotent when they arrive pre-revived. The test that had
      PINNED the trap as behaviour is inverted, deliberately.
      **What the move drops.** The re-lazified spec keeps the caller's real MF6 options
      and drops the two the recipe owns (`stress_period_data`, `boundnames`) -- passing
      either twice is `got multiple values for keyword argument`. It also drops
      `grid_pin`/`grid_pin_options` and `coverage`: a pin describes the resolution just
      replaced, `package_move` reads `GRID_PIN_OPTIONS <= inputs` before anything else,
      and a stale pin beside a fresh recipe is the exact collision ledger 275 voided.
      **The builder is the one thing data cannot carry.** A recipe names its package;
      binding the FloPy class is what keeps the declaration-time option check
      byte-identical to the eager form (ledger 279), so `_relazified` resolves
      `package_api._lazy_factory` through a DEFERRED import -- `specs` is import layer 1
      and `package_api` is 5. A package whose builder cannot be resolved is returned
      unchanged and classified as it stands, rather than half-converted.
      **Scope, stated:** this covers the seven list `.gpkg` forms. `mf.uzf`/`sfr`/`lak`
      still resolve eagerly with no recipe and remain `stale` -- that is tranche C1, not
      this. And re-lazifying is exact only because the SOURCE is re-read: a package
      whose GeoPackage has moved or been edited resolves to what the file says NOW, which
      `runs.drift()`'s `source` column is what reports (ledger 294).

297. **Every input field summed, including the water levels (2026-09-22).**
      All twenty ``FieldSpec`` entries read ``agg="sum"``, elevations among them -- so a
      cell holding two CHD records of 100.0 and 102.0 rendered **202.0** on
      ``packages.chd.inputs.head.map()``. Summing a flux is right and summing a level is
      not, and nothing distinguished them. It reaches the INPUTS VIEW
      (``package_inputs.py``), so it mis-draws a map and a table; it does not change what
      MF6 runs.
      **Fixed by declaring what the number IS, once.** ``FieldSpec.kind`` --
      ``extensive`` (a flux or a conductance: MF6 superposes them, so they ADD),
      ``elevation`` (a water level or an invert), ``intensive`` (a length, a fraction, a
      coefficient) -- and ``agg`` became a PROPERTY of it rather than a second field
      beside it, because two fields that must agree are two fields that drift. The
      closed kind set is checked at construction: a typo would otherwise fall through to
      the intensive default and quietly change how a field aggregates. Twenty fields:
      8 extensive, 6 elevation, 6 intensive. A caller who wants something else still
      passes ``agg=`` at the call; this is the DEFAULT, not a restriction.
      **TWO NAMESPACES, and three of seven packages differ between them.**
      ``_ELEVATION_FIELDS`` and ``_EXTENSIVE_FIELDS`` are keyed by the HELPER's argument
      names (``drn.elevation``, ``ghb.head``, ``wel.rate``); the record names are
      ``drn.elev``, ``ghb.bhead``, ``wel.q``. Both sets match their call sites and the
      code was correct -- but the local holding those names was called ``record_fields``
      and the comment above the set called them "record field" pairs, which is the other
      namespace and reads as authoritative. **That cost a wrong diagnosis during this
      commit**: comparing ``("wel", "q")`` against a set holding ``("wel", "rate")`` says
      the branch is dead, and running it shows the loss total is reported correctly. The
      locals are ``gpkg_field`` now and the comments name the namespace. The hazard the
      names created is real for anything rebuilt against ``FieldSpec``: such a set would
      match NOTHING for those three and raise nothing -- ``refuse_spread_on_elevation``
      would simply stop refusing -- so a test pins that the two namespaces differ.
      ``_ELEVATION_FIELDS`` is DERIVED from ``kind == "elevation"`` now (measured
      identical to the literal it replaces), so one hand-kept list is gone.
      **``_EXTENSIVE_FIELDS`` is deliberately NOT ``kind == "extensive"``**, which is
      eight fields against its one. Two different questions share the word: ``kind`` asks
      "do several records on one cell ADD?", which a conductance does; that set asks
      "does the DECLARED column hold a total we can report a shortfall against?", which
      an unwrapped conductance does not -- it is copied WHOLE to every covered cell, so
      declared-minus-written calls a clean build a -300% loss (ledgers 169, 288).
      Collapsing them would put a false loss figure on every drn/ghb/riv warning. Pinned
      as a strict subset, so the relationship is asserted rather than remembered.
      **Not done:** a mean HIDES that a cell held several records, where the old sum at
      least produced a number a reader might question. Reporting multiplicity beside the
      value is a view-layer change of its own and is not attempted here.

298. **What a move would have no data for, in ft2 rather than as a coverage fraction
      (2026-09-22).**
      B3's C4: the measurement to read BEFORE ``with_grid``. ``move_report`` says what
      happens to each PACKAGE; this says what the new mesh would have nothing for at all.
      Pure geometry, so it is the same number whatever is being moved:
      ``model.coverage_on(grid)`` and ``sim.coverage_on(grid, on=)``.
      **AREA IN MODEL UNITS, and that was the user's call** -- it dissolves a tolerance
      question rather than answering it. Polygon intersection is exact to ~1e-15
      relative, so on a mesh refined over the SAME footprint, where nothing is missing,
      comparing ``coverage < 1`` flags **765 of 2,352 cells (32.5%)** as short by 4e-15
      of themselves; at 1e-12 it flags zero. Any `uncovered=` default built on that
      fraction would have been meaningless without a tolerance nobody had specified. The
      same residual in area is ~1e-11 ft2 and reads as the nothing it is, and a threshold
      a modeller might actually want ("more than 50 ft2 of this cell has no data") is
      then expressible in units they can judge. Measured against a hand-checkable case:
      a footprint grown 1,200 ft eastward reports 3,600,000 ft2 uncovered, which is
      exactly 1,200 x 3,000.
      **A DISJOINT PAIR IS A DIFFERENT FACT FROM A GAP**, and nothing else can tell them
      apart. ``grid_pin`` hashes CONNECTIVITY only, so the same mesh shifted to a local
      origin -- what a USG conversion produces by design (ledger 159), and B3's headline
      customer -- pins IDENTICALLY while overlapping nothing. Reporting that as "100%
      uncovered" is what would invite C6's ``nearest`` to fill every cell from a source
      1.5 million feet away. ``CoverageReport.disjoint`` says so instead, and the two
      boxes and both CRSs are worded by ``where_they_are``, the helper ledger 211
      already uses for every other miss in this library.
      **The noise floor is RELATIVE** (1e-9 of a cell's own area), so it means the same
      on a 4 ft2 cell and a 40,000 ft2 one, and it sits five orders of magnitude above
      the measured residual -- it can only ever hide something already invisible.
      **A refusal rather than a guess** for a model carrying no grid: a deferred-grid
      model has nothing to overlay, and "nothing is covered" would be indistinguishable
      from a real total miss.
      **One line was removed because a mutation could not kill it.** The first draft
      clipped the per-cell shortfall at zero before thresholding it. Removing the clip
      changed no test -- and could not, because the threshold excludes a negative
      residual for the same reason it excludes a tiny positive one. It read as careful
      and was unfalsifiable, which is the same defect as an assertion that certifies.
      **Not built here:** nothing CONSUMES this yet. It reports; C6's engine is what will
      act on it, with ``uncovered="nearest"`` as the default the user chose and the frame
      guard above as what keeps that safe.

299. **A polygon map could fill an array, but the model could not then be saved or moved
      (2026-09-23).**
      B3's C5: ``mf.Polygons(path, column=...)`` in ``mf.npf(k=)`` / ``k22`` / ``k33``,
      ``mf.ic(strt=)``, ``mf.sto(ss=, sy=)``. A serializable RECIPE resolved at BUILD
      against whatever grid the model supplies, in ``PackageSpec.inputs``, carrying
      ``path`` + ``source_sha`` and digested by CONTENT (ledger 293's rule, both
      directions).
      **The justification is NOT "nothing else can do this"** --
      ``GeoPackageSource.k_array`` has painted K from polygons for a long time, still
      does, and is not deprecated by this. What it cannot be is LAZY or SAVED, and both
      halves are measured, not argued: it takes a live ``ModelContext`` so it resolves at
      DECLARATION, and it returns an ``ndarray``, which ``to_dict`` refuses (ledger 193)
      -- so ``Project.save()`` reported ``simulations=0, skipped=1`` for a model painted
      that way and ``load()`` returned an empty project, silently, because ``save()``
      reports rather than raises. The recipe form reports ``simulations=1, skipped=0``
      and rebuilds to the same two values. This is ledger 270's defect two packages over.
      **It converts the array class from ``unverifiable`` to ``rebuilt``.** A per-cell
      array names cells by POSITION and carries no cellid to check, so ledger 295 could
      only give it a verdict, not a route: ``npf`` holding a plain array reads
      ``unverifiable`` ("its values still mean mesh 639cf118"). Holding a ``Polygons`` it
      reads ``rebuilt`` and builds correctly at ncpl 36 and ncpl 100 from ONE
      declaration.
      **The rule is NAMED, because there are three and they disagree.** ``majority``
      (default), ``mean``, ``centroid``. The fork is ``mean`` against the other two: on a
      64-cell grid with one geology contact it wrote **12 distinct conductivities where
      the map holds 2** -- ten values no mapped unit has -- and across 19 contact
      positions its area-integral ran between 0.0% and 60.5% from ``majority``'s. That is
      the arithmetic-versus-harmonic problem in miniature, which is why the default is
      the rule that INVENTS NOTHING. ``majority`` and ``centroid`` are close but not one
      rule: over those same 19 positions they differed on **at most ONE cell of 64**, the
      cell whose centre and whose bulk fall on opposite sides. A single fixture therefore
      proves nothing about them, and the test sweeps the 19 rather than asserting on one.
      **The DENOMINATOR is the trap.** ``cell_shares`` normalizes by the whole FEATURE
      (share of the polygon falling in each cell, what ``mf.Spread`` needs to divide a
      total) and drops slivers doing it. Filling an array needs share of the CELL -- the
      same intersection, a different denominator -- and must KEEP the slivers, since a
      sliver is still the only thing covering its own sliver of cell. So this uses
      ``gpd.overlay`` like ``cell_coverage`` (ledger 298), not ``cell_shares``.
      **An uncovered cell is REFUSED without ``default=``.** ``k_array`` cannot make that
      mistake because its ``defaults`` is required; here it is optional, and an unfilled
      cell is a NaN that MF6 answers with a NaN budget under normal termination -- ledger
      247's failure exactly.
      **Two things the slot accepted and could not use are now refused at the
      DECLARATION**, which the user asked for as part of this: ``mf.npf(k=<Surface>)``
      was accepted and died at BUILD inside FloPy with an ``MFDataException`` naming
      neither the slot nor the type (measured; same for a ``LayerStack``); and a recipe
      sitting beside an option of the same name reached FloPy as ``got multiple values
      for keyword argument 'k'``. The second is the older defect and it was INVERTED:
      ``_check_input_collisions`` deliberately EXEMPTS a source shadowing its own option,
      on the recorded premise that "a future resolver will consume one into the other",
      while refusing a non-source collision with a good message -- so the shape the
      comment called supported got the worse error. The resolver has arrived and it
      REPLACES the option rather than merging with it, so the state is unbuildable and
      ``PackageSpec.build`` now says so, for every package rather than just these.
      **The refusal is narrow on purpose**: it names the two types measured to fail
      rather than allowing a list, because the array slots genuinely accept a scalar, a
      sequence, an ndarray, an ``OPEN/CLOSE`` path string (measured: it builds, reads
      back, and writes ``OPEN/CLOSE ... FACTOR 1.0``) and FloPy's own layered dicts. A
      rule written the other way round would refuse something that works today.
      **Integer FLAGS are refused rather than half-supported.** ``icelltype`` and
      ``iconvert`` are not measured values and every rule here returns a float -- there
      is no cell type 0.4. ``majority`` and ``centroid`` would in fact be meaningful on
      them, but supporting that means shipping a cast this commit did not measure, so
      they are named and refused instead.
      **An allowlist, not "anything that is a ``Polygons``"**: a helper's ``**options``
      tail also carries ``steady_state``, ``transient`` and filerecords, and silently
      painting one of those produces an array where MF6 expects a period dict.
      **The deferred-import ratchet goes 81 -> 82, and it cannot be hoisted.**
      CLAUDE.md's rule for a rising count is "hoist the import to module level instead",
      and here that is impossible rather than merely inconvenient: ``to_dict`` needs
      ``specs._json_value`` to normalize a numpy-typed field before comparing it against
      its default (``default=np.float64(...)`` is an obvious spelling, and the
      unnormalized value fails both ``json.dumps`` and ``yaml.safe_dump`` -- ledger 288's
      trap on ``snap_within``), while ``specs.py`` imports ``sources`` at module level.
      Hoisting would be a cycle. It is the third of exactly this import in the file;
      ``BoundarySource.to_dict`` makes the other two for the same reason.
      **The rule names are stated TWICE and a test holds them together.**
      ``POLYGON_RULES`` is in ``sources.py`` (import layer 0) so a declaration is refused
      at the call; the resolver is in ``grid/geometry.py`` (layer 1) and cannot import it
      without the edge running upward. Placing the class in ``sources.py`` is also what
      keeps the import ratchet completely still: ``specs.py`` already imports that module
      at module level, so there is no new edge and no new deferred import.
      **One line was deleted because a mutation could not kill it**, ledger 298's rule
      again. The majority branch first summed areas per (cell, zone) before picking the
      winner, justified by "a multi-part polygon reaches one cell as several pieces".
      Measured: it does not -- ``gpd.overlay`` returns ONE row per (cell, zone) and keeps
      a multi-part intersection WHOLE (a two-lobe unit covering 60% of a cell comes back
      as a single MultiPolygon of area 60, not two pieces of 30). Swapping the ``sum``
      for a ``max`` passed every test. The groupby went, and the behaviour it claimed to
      protect is held by a test that fails loudly if ``overlay`` ever changes.
      **The adversarial pass found a defect of its own, and it is the interesting one.**
      The builder first recorded its resolved arrays on a private attribute of its own
      (``_myflopy_resolved_arrays``) that read as the obvious sibling of
      ``_myflopy_resolved`` and was DEAD: nothing anywhere reads it. ``ModelSpec.build``
      harvests exactly ``_myflopy_resolved`` into ``BuiltModel.resolved``, and
      ``Run._freeze`` hands that to ``freeze_simulation(resolved=)`` -- so the snapshot
      held the RECIPE, and a reopened run went back to the polygon file and died once it
      was gone. **That is ledger 270's defect, one package over**, reintroduced by a
      plausible name. It now records an eager ``PackageSpec`` carrying the arrays, and a
      thaw with the source file DELETED comes back with the right values. A mutation
      restoring the private attribute fails both new tests by name.
      **Three subsystems needed no per-type wiring, which is the payoff of the shape:**
      ``project.save(bundle_sources=True)`` archives the polygon file and reports
      ``not_bundled=()``; ``runs.drift()`` reads ``source`` ``ok`` and then ``edited``
      after the file changes; and ``move_report`` classifies it. All three work because
      the recipe rides in ``inputs`` as a ``DataSourceSpec`` with a ``source_sha``, which
      the ledger 293/294 walks already find. Pinned by tests anyway -- nothing else here
      would fail if a refactor stopped it being found.
      **A shadowed name that reached a running build.** ``package_api.py`` already had
      ``_lazy_array_factory`` / ``_build_lazy_array`` for ``mf.rch.array`` (ledger 285) at
      ~line 5890; a second definition of the same name at ~line 1000 was silently
      overridden by it, so the new calls dispatched into the recharge builder and died on
      ``_ARRAY_FIELDS[<flopy class>]``. Renamed to ``_polygon_array_factory`` /
      ``_build_polygon_arrays``. The file is 5,900 lines; grep before adding a private
      helper to it.
      **Deliberately NOT here, and each for a reason:**
      * **Layer ELEVATIONS from a polygon map.** The user scoped it out for a follow-up.
        Nothing does it today -- ``Surface.where(zone, inside, outside)`` is a two-way
        inside/outside choice on centroids, not a value looked up per unit -- but it is a
        DIFFERENT route (through ``Surface``/``LayerStack``), not another keyword.
      * **Boundary-condition conductances and elevations.** Already covered, and covered
        better: the seven ``mf.<pkg>.gpkg`` forms read a polygon's attribute columns and
        have been lazy since ledger 279. A second way to do it would be the duplication
        the plan exists to avoid.
      * **A ``remap`` slot on ``FieldSpec``.** ``kind`` (ledger 297) is the natural place
        for a per-field default rule, but nothing needs one yet: C5's rule is per
        DECLARATION. Keep it separate from ``agg`` when it lands -- ``agg`` combines
        records already sharing a cell (no weights), ``remap`` combines old cells into a
        new one (area weights).
      * **A generic ``_SOURCE_TYPES`` completeness sweep existed nowhere**, only two spot
        checks, so a new source class could ship registered nowhere and be found by the
        first user who saved a project containing one. Added here because this commit is
        what made the registry grow.

300. **A calibrated array could not follow its model to another mesh (2026-09-23).**
      B3's C6 and its last commit: the overlay remap engine.
      ``sim.with_grid(grid, remap=True, rule=, uncovered=)`` intersects the OLD grid's own
      cell polygons with the new grid's and carries per-cell arrays across on the
      resulting areas. ``npf`` ``k``/``k22``/``k33`` and ``ic.strt``/``sto.ss``/``sto.sy``;
      ``unverifiable`` becomes a fifth verdict, ``remapped``.
      **It exists for an array with NO recipe** -- a PEST-calibrated K field, an array read
      out of an imported model. **And it is the WORSE route wherever a source exists,
      measured**: re-declaring a polygon map on the new mesh (ledger 299) held to a
      maximum 7.1% and a median 2.1% boundary-flux error against the fine mesh, where the
      best reducer's own worst case was 12.5% and the worst four orders of magnitude. So
      ``remap=`` is OPT-IN, the default behaviour does not move, and the warning names
      re-declaration as the better route. That also amends ledger 169's bullet, in place.
      **K HAS NO SAFE DEFAULT, AND THAT IS THE HEADLINE.** The correct average for a
      conductivity depends on the FLOW DIRECTION, which is a property of the SOLUTION and
      not of the field -- so no per-field declaration can ever carry it, and
      ``FieldSpec.remap`` (reserved in ledger 299) would have been the wrong shape.
      Measured in MF6 on one 2:1 coarsening: with the contrast ACROSS the flow the
      arithmetic mean gave **264x** the fine-mesh boundary flux and the harmonic mean was
      nearly exact; with the SAME contrast rotated 90 degrees the arithmetic mean was
      EXACT and the harmonic wrong by about 250x. **The ordering reverses.** ``geometric``
      is the default on the user's call -- never best, never catastrophic (median 7.2%,
      worst 81.7%, and the classical answer for a heterogeneous 2-D field) -- and the
      engine computes the arithmetic and harmonic means ALONGSIDE it and WARNS naming the
      cells where they diverge by more than 2x. The choice is surfaced where it matters
      instead of having to be known in advance.
      **TWO DENOMINATORS, and only one of them is here.** An INTENSIVE quantity divides by
      the new cell's COVERED area; an EXTENSIVE one divides by the OLD cell's area. They
      are not scalings of one another. The covered-area denominator is what makes a
      partially covered cell right rather than diluted -- measured on a constant 7.0 field
      over a grown footprint, it returns 7.000000 where the new cell's own area returns
      0.0066 to 6.9878.
      **EXTENSIVE IS DEFERRED, and ``kind`` is why it cannot simply be added.**
      ``kind == "extensive"`` holds a RATE *and* a TOTAL, and they need opposite
      treatment: measured in MF6 on a 2:1 refinement, "split and renormalize" gives 45.0
      where the area-mean gives 90.0 for RCH -- half the water -- and the area-mean
      DOUBLES a WEL total (-50 to -100). A reducer keyed on ``kind`` picks the wrong one
      for four of the eight extensive fields. **And ``npf``/``ic``/``sto`` are not in
      ``_PACKAGE_EXPLORER_SPECS`` at all**, so no ``FieldSpec`` exists for ``k`` or
      ``strt``; what enumerates them is ``grid_identity.cellwise_options``, which is what
      this uses.
      **INTEGER FLAGS are refused by name** -- ``icelltype``, ``iconvert``, ``irch``,
      ``ievt``. Measured on an 8x8 -> 5x5 coarsening of an ``icelltype`` contact: the mean
      gave 5 of 25 cells values like 0.3851, and even ``majority``, which invents nothing,
      moved the convertible AREA fraction from 0.4949 to 0.4569. ``irch``/``ievt`` are
      zero-based LAYER INDICES, so averaging them is meaningless in a way nothing
      downstream catches.
      **THE FRAME GUARD NEEDED BUILDING; ``CoverageReport.disjoint`` IS NOT IT.** The B3
      scope note recorded "the frame guard IS ``CoverageReport.disjoint`` -- already there,
      already tested", and that is measured false: two identical footprints declared
      EPSG:2927 and EPSG:2926 come back ``disjoint=False, uncovered_area=0.0`` with
      ``summary()`` saying "every cell of the new mesh has data under it", while
      ``gpd.overlay`` warns and proceeds. ``disjoint`` catches only the zero-pieces
      (translated) case. So ``refuse_a_different_frame`` compares CRS FIRST and then
      ``disjoint``; neither is sufficient alone. A grid is REFUSED rather than reprojected,
      unlike a ``.gpkg`` source, because two model meshes are both the modeller's own and
      one in another frame is far more likely an error than an intention.
      **The blind spot, stated out loud:** a mesh rescaled into other UNITS while keeping
      the same declared CRS passes both tests -- it sits inside the old footprint, every
      cell is covered, and the remap is self-consistent; it simply describes a tenth of
      the domain. Nothing geometric distinguishes that from a legitimate SUBDOMAIN
      refinement, which is supported work, so a test that fired on it would fire on
      correct work. Ledger 211 records the same blind spot for a source. A test PINS the
      limit so it is a decision rather than a surprise.
      **``CoverageReport.uncovered`` IS NOT THE FILL LIST**, and reading it as one destroys
      good data. It names cells that are SHORT -- one measured at 98.9% covered -- so
      nearest-filling from it threw away 15 correct area-weighted values out of 51 named.
      The fill predicate is ``~reached``: this new cell got NO pieces at all.
      **MASK THE WEIGHTS, NEVER THE VALUES.** Handing an idomain-inactive old cell through
      as a ``NaN`` poisons the new cells above it and ``reached`` does not say so --
      measured on a pinching wedge, ten reached new cells came back ``NaN``, THREE of them
      ACTIVE on the new mesh. The active set genuinely differs between meshes, so the mask
      is per-LAYER.
      **``replace``, not ``with_options``.** That verb VOIDS the pin of a certified package
      and ``package_move`` then reports "its records were edited after the library resolved
      them on mesh X" -- a lie about a correct remap. Measured on ``mf.rch.array``.
      **``REMAPPED_FROM`` is stamped INSTEAD of ``MOVED_FROM``, not beside it**:
      ``moved_package_complaints`` fires on that stamp's presence alone, so leaving it
      would refuse the very package the remap just fixed. ``PIN_VOIDED`` is deliberately
      NOT cleared and a voided package is not remapped -- its values were never verified on
      the OLD mesh either, so an overlay would carry an unverified guess forward while
      stamping it certified (ledger 275).
      **A fifth verdict rather than reusing ``unchanged``**, because a reader deciding
      whether to trust a run needs to know the values were INTERPOLATED and how many cells
      were filled from a neighbour. ``rebuilt`` would also have been a lie: that means
      re-derived from a recipe and exact.
      **A latent bug fixed in passing.** ``cell_coverage`` bincounted by index LABEL and
      read the result by POSITION -- correct only for a ``RangeIndex``. A row-permuted new
      frame reported 63 uncovered cells where the truth is 0, and a sliced one raised a
      broadcast error. Unreachable because ``gdf_vorPolys`` is always a ``RangeIndex``, and
      sharing the overlay is what would have made it reachable; ``cell_overlay`` assigns
      positions with ``np.arange``.
      **A refusal is not swallowed into a silent no-op.** ``remap=True`` on a package the
      engine cannot serve RAISES. Catching it and leaving the package stamped
      ``unverifiable`` would tell the caller the move was fine, which is ledger 295's
      failure one verb over. The first version of the candidate test read only the
      ``CELLWISE_OPTIONS`` stamp, and ``npf``/``ic`` carry none -- so ``remap=True``
      silently did NOTHING for exactly the packages the engine exists for, measured as two
      ``unverifiable`` verdicts and zero warnings.
      **A test that could not tell two rules apart.** ``harmonic <= geometric <= mean`` is
      satisfied by EQUALITY, so a mutation making the harmonic branch return the geometric
      mean passed all 32 tests. The test now also asserts STRICT inequality on the cells
      that actually hold both materials -- selected by a relative threshold, because on a
      uniform cell the three agree only to float noise (the harmonic mean of identical
      10.0s came back 9.999999999999998) and an exact-difference test failed on correct
      code.
      **The deferred-import ratchet goes 82 -> 83, and here it is FORCED rather than
      preferred.** ``grid/remap.py`` imports ``grid/geometry.py`` (import layer 1) and so
      sits at layer **2**, while ``specs.py`` is at layer **1** -- a module-level
      ``specs -> remap`` edge would point UPWARD, which the ratchet refuses outright.
      CLAUDE.md's rule for a rising count is "hoist it instead"; that is not available, and
      the same is true of ledger 298's reason for keeping ``cell_coverage`` deferred
      (hoisting makes a bare ``import myflopy.specs`` pull geopandas).
      **Deliberately NOT here:**
      * **Hand-typed list-BC records.** ``unverifiable`` too, but there are no per-cell
        source VALUES to weight -- an overlay has nothing to average.
      * **``mf.uzf``/``sfr``/``lak``/``hfb.line`` and the eager array-form ``rch``/``evt``.**
        Measured ``stale``, not ``unverifiable``: they carry a ``grid_pin``, so the overlay
        does not reach them and re-declaration is their route.
      * **A ONE-STEP saveable remapped model.** Two obstacles, and this entry first
        recorded them as a flat "cannot be saved", which overstated it -- corrected the
        same day. (a) The remapped values are an ``ndarray``, which ``to_dict`` refuses
        (ledger 193). **But the model was ALREADY unsaveable before the move**, measured:
        ``mf.npf(k=<ndarray>)`` gives ``simulations=0, skipped=1`` either side of it. That
        is not incidental -- it is why such a model needs remapping at all, since a
